events.title: UFC CEO Dana White says it's 'impossible' to build a successful business while working from home
events.summary: UFC CEO Dana White said people who want to protect their free time are better suited to a 9-to-5 than entrepreneurship. Mike Roach/Zuffa LLC Dana White said he doesn't believe successful businesses can be built by working remotely. The UFC CEO said managing a company means tackling new demands at any time of day. He also said aspiring entrepreneurs often get one thing wrong about working for themselves. UFC CEO Dana White said the dream of flexible hours is a trap for aspiring entrepreneurs. Speaking to Steve Bartlett on Monday's episode of " The Diary of a CEO " podcast, White spoke about why he doesn't believe that a successful business could be built by working from home. "It's impossible. You can't do it. I'm in the office from 8:30 in the morning, and I don't leave the office till 7, 8, 9, 10 sometimes," White said. Even on days when his schedule was fully planned, spontaneous conversations with colleagues could surface new issues, spark ideas, and change the course of his day. "A lot of good ideas come from everybody being at work," White added. White said entrepreneurship is a poor fit for anyone whose priority is protecting their free time, because business demands can arise at any time. "There is no such thing as a day off when you run your own business. There are no birthdays, there's no Christmas, there's no Thanksgiving," White said. Running a business means dealing with a fresh set of problems every day, "but when you like what you do, it's fun," he added. White said he believed many young people have the wrong idea about what entrepreneurship involves. "'You know, I'd really like to work for myself, and own my own business because I'd love to plan my schedule.' Oh, you're going the wrong way," White said. "What you need to do is find a 9-to-5 job where you have weekends and holidays off. That's your move." White has pushed back on the idea that entrepreneurship offers an easier, more flexible life in past interviews. He said in a March 2024 appearance on the  "Lex Fridman Podcast"  that he works "just as hard now" as he did when he was starting out. In a May 2024 appearance on the " In Search of Excellence " podcast, White said that entrepreneurs who want their businesses to succeed must be prepared to become "a slave" to the company in the early years. Other business leaders have also pushed back on remote work. Skims cofounder Emma Grede , for example, has said that working from home is "career suicide." Jason Lemkin — also known as the "Godfather of SaaS" — has said that he's only interested in investing in "small, high paid teams that work in the office over six days a week." events.title: Will Cristiano Ronaldo play for Portugal after a row with coach Jesus?
events.summary: Ronaldo sparked controversy last week when he walked out of the camp after learning that he would not start a game. The drama surrounding Cristiano Ronaldo’s international future took another turn after Portugal head coach Jorge Jesus left the door open for the 41-year-old superstar’s return following his abrupt departure from the national team’s training camp. The sentiment is shared by the Portuguese Football Federation president Pedro ⁠⁠Proenca, who believes the episode is a mere misunderstanding that could be resolved internally. list 1 of 3 ‘Lego race’: Formula One to probe software bug behind Bahrain GP chaos list 2 of 3 Who were the top teen athletes at the Asian Games? list 3 of 3 France hosts neighbours Belgium, but De Bruyne to miss battle with Olise But how did the apparent rift start, and will Ronaldo ever play again for Portugal? What happened between Ronaldo and Jesus? Ronaldo left the Portugal squad late on Wednesday, shortly after the head coach’s news conference, where Jesus confirmed that the five-time Ballon d’Or winner would be left out of his starting lineup for the match against Denmark, marking a second consecutive Nations League game absence. Ronaldo’s decision to walk out came as a shock, as he had been due to train with his teammates at the Parken Stadium in Copenhagen. Portugal’s leading scorer had already spent the entirety of the 2-1 Nations League win away to Norway on September 27 on the bench, having captained the side in the 1-0 home victory over Wales three days before. The game in Oslo was the first time since November 2024 that Ronaldo had not featured for Portugal despite not being injured or suspended. Ronaldo appeared to indicate that the reasons behind Jesus’s decision to bench him ran deeper and hinted at a departure from the national team he has graced for more than two decades. “In due course, I will tell the truth to all the Portuguese people about my reasons for leaving the national team, to which I have always been dedicated,” Ronaldo said in a cryptic Instagram post, announcing his sudden exit from the camp. Spanish sports daily Marca said Jesus and Proenca followed Ronaldo to Copenhagen airport in an attempt to persuade him to stay with the squad, before the player boarded his private jet. There were reports that Portuguese Prime Minister Luis Montenegro had even discussed the issue of Ronaldo’s involvement with the coach on Wednesday. Jesus insisted that there was no rift between them, although the 72-year-old, who was appointed in July, acknowledged that his captain was disappointed to remain on the bench against Norway. How did Portugal play without Ronaldo? Despite his absence, Nations League title holders Portugal won, defeating Denmark 4-2 in Copenhagen and Norway 2-1 in Porto. They also became the first team to qualify for the quarterfinals, ensuring a top-two finish in Group A4. Forward Goncalo Ramos stepped up in Ronaldo’s absence, scoring three goals to be the team’s joint top scorer along with Joao Felix, while the AC Milan player also bagged an assist. What did Portugal’s coach say about Ronaldo? On Sunday, coach Jesus said Ronaldo could return to the national team ⁠⁠if he chooses ⁠⁠to. “If he wants to, he’ll return to the national team. We can talk before the next call-up, but Cris is the one who’s going ‌‌to decide,” said Jesus, who also coached Ronaldo at Saudi Arabian club Al-Nassr. “He’s the one who should decide how he wants to end his time with the national team. In my first call-up, I said, ‘I need you, I need you to be close to me, playing or not playing, I need you’. And now I’m saying ⁠⁠the same thing.” Jesus expects the forward to be available for the next international window if he wants to return. What have the Portugal players said about Ronaldo? Midfielder Bruno Fernandes said on Saturday he had spoken to Ronaldo and dismissed suggestions of a rift within Portugal’s squad. “I had a chat with him and what I said to him is ‌‌what I’ll repeat here: the most important thing is that, whatever happens, Cristiano Ronaldo will never cease to be the greatest symbol of our national team, of our football and of the country,” Fernandes told a news conference. “For what he has achieved not only in Portugal, but all over the world. He has a place reserved not only amongst the all-time greats, but also in the hearts of all Portuguese people.” “The most important thing is that we ⁠⁠stop stirring up trouble; there are no divisions within the national team. It is ⁠⁠one team and will remain so, despite any noise that may come from outside.” Fernandes called for unity after a tumultuous few days in which Portugal fans’ opinions have been split over Ronaldo’s decision. “We are outside of this controversy, but what I ask is that the country does not divide itself, does not make choices, that it respects all sides, but, at the same time, Cris is and will be the biggest icon of our national team.

events.title: What is Beam? The buzzy American AI model being called the 'DeepSeek of the West'
events.summary: Reflection AI is a New York-based AI lab. kolderal/Getty Images Reflection AI's first model is here. Beam is a text-based model designed for coding and reasoning tasks. Beam is being seen as a competitive Western alternative to open weight models. A New York AI startup founded by two former Google DeepMind researchers has released its first major model — and is pitching it as a homegrown answer to China's increasingly powerful open AI systems. Reflection AI on Monday unveiled Beam, an "open-weight" model designed for coding, reasoning, and AI-agent tasks. The company says it rivals some of China's leading open models while using far less computing power. Here's what to know. What is Beam? Beam is Reflection AI's first frontier open-weight model. Open-weight means developers can download the model's parameters, run them on their own hardware, and modify or fine-tune them for specific use cases. That is an alternative to using models from companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic, which are generally accessed via their own Application Programming Interfaces (APIs). Reflection says Beam, a text-only model, has 501 billion total parameters, but activates only 23 billion at a time — a design intended to make it cheaper and faster to operate. The model can handle coding, multi-step reasoning, and other agentic work. For now, Beam is in final safety testing and available through a waitlist. Reflection says it will release the model's weights, a technical report, and developer tools later this month. Who is behind Beam? Reflection was founded in 2024 by Misha Laskin and Ioannis Antonoglou, both former DeepMind researchers. "The only way to own intelligence is, by definition, if it's open — because if it's open, you can run it on your stuff, you can own it, you can control it, you can customize it," Laskin, the CEO, said in a podcast released on Monday. The startup has raised billions of dollars and is backed by investors including Nvidia, Sequoia , and Citigroup. In June, it confirmed a funding round at a $25 billion pre-money valuation. How does Beam compare? Reflection said Beam is competitive with Z.ai's GLM-5.2 on coding and agentic tasks, and is approaching Alibaba's Qwen 3.8-Max. It said that Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 remains ahead on raw capability. The startup is pitching itself on efficiency. It said Beam can achieve results comparable to GLM-5.2 on advanced reasoning benchmarks while using three to four times less inference compute — the processing required for a model to answer a prompt. How are tech and business leaders reacting? Beam's launch is being welcomed as a potentially important US response to China's open-model lead. It arrives in a crowded field that includes open models from Meta, Mistral, Nvidia, and Thinking Machines Lab. Beam also faces obvious competition from powerful models released in China by companies including DeepSeek, Alibaba, Z.ai, and Moonshot AI . The Wall Street Journal reported in March that some investors had described Reflection as the "DeepSeek of the West." That comparison to DeepSeek has become the shorthand used in many X posts surrounding Beam's buzzy launch. On Monday, Nvidia AI's official X account congratulated the company on the launch. Investors, including Deedy Das and Shaun Maguire, also expressed their enthusiasm for the launch on X. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: DeepSeek set to raise at least $15 billion in Tencent-backed funding
events.summary: DeepSeek’s funding sets the stage for one of the most highly anticipated Chinese market debuts in years. DeepSeek is set to raise at least 80 billion yuan (S$15 billion) in Tencent-backed funding, exceeding its initial target ahead of a planned IPO in early 2027. The company plans to build a massive AI data centre in Inner Mongolia using 160,000 Huawei AI chips, aiming to advance its large language model technology. DeepSeek's founder prioritises pushing AI technology boundaries over monetisation, reflecting China's ambition to compete globally in artificial intelligence. DeepSeek is close to securing at least 80 billion yuan (S$15 billion) in its latest round of funding, blowing past its own capital-raising target ahead of a landmark initial public offering in early 2027 . Battery pioneer Contemporary Amperex Technology and WeChat-operator Tencent Holdings have committed among the largest amounts in the current financing, which closes soon, sources familiar with the matter said. DeepSeek initially sought about 50 billion yuan, but interest outstripped expectations after the successful release of its latest AI model, the sources said, asking not to be named as the details are not public. Based on term sheets signed, the final tally could approach 100 billion yuan, they added. The company is riding high after the release of the V4 Flash large language model, which reset expectations for cost versus performance against leaders Anthropic and OpenAI. That caps a strong run for founder Liang Wenfeng , whose start-up has forged a reputation for technical breakthroughs since a 2025 model that matched the capabilities of Silicon Valley offerings at a fraction of the cost. As with other artificial intelligence players, DeepSeek requires huge amounts of capital to bankroll its ambitions in a potentially revolutionary technology. The company plans to deploy at least 160,000 of Huawei Technologies’ top accelerators at a massive data centre it is building in Inner Mongolia, which may create one of the largest known clusters of Huawei AI chips. It has publicly released software created with Huawei to program AI chips, a foray into a new arena in close partnership with the hardware leader . Rival Moonshot, meanwhile, is also targeting an early 2027 IPO after closing funding at a US$50 billion (S$64 billion) valuation. Liang pledged in at least one meeting with investors in 2026 that he will keep developing open AI models while pursuing a broader goal of achieving artificial general intelligence. The hedge fund manager made it clear his main goal was to push the boundaries of the technology rather than monetisation, Bloomberg News has reported. While discussions around the current deal are near an end, details may still change in final talks, the sources said. DeepSeek had originally targeted a valuation of about 500 billion yuan in its financing. A CATL representative declined to comment, while Tencent had no immediate comment. DeepSeek did not respond to an e-mailed request for comment during a Chinese public holiday. DeepSeek has drawn enormous interest from would-be investors because it is one of a clutch of companies that sit at the heart of China’s effort to compete globally on AI. Once the round closes, the next step should be to restructure the company to prepare for an IPO, the sources said. Tencent, which also landed the biggest investment in the start-up at 10 billion yuan in a previous round of financing, aims to integrate AI into its platforms. CATL may be eyeing an increasingly lucrative business of supplying components to the industry, including for data centres. The AI lab’s capital-raising had attracted its share of controversy. DeepSeek briefly suspended the deal after comments widely attributed to Liang about US-Chinese AI competition went viral on social media. Chinese media outlet Yicai reported in July that the billionaire entrepreneur had talked about a reliance on Nvidia chips and China’s persistent lag in AI sophistication relative to the US. Liang’s net worth more than doubled to around US$36 billion when DeepSeek closed its first round of external fund-raising this summer. The AI start-up grew as an offshoot from his hedge fund High-Flyer, which provided much of the initial support. Liang contributed again in the previous 50 billion yuan round, which valued DeepSeek at roughly 350 billion yuan at the time. BLOOMBERG

Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters OpenAI to flood your eyeballs with visual ads 15 hours ago Brighter isn't better and more is less. The AI slowdown is nigh, no matter who says what 22 hours ago OpenAI alerts 100+ orgs that its 'misaligned models' attempted to break in - or worse 3 days ago OpenAI's wandering AI agents earn it a California subpoena 3 days ago OpenAI shows three staff the door over alleged information misuse 3 days ago OpenAI is now offering API customers the option to watermark the output of certain models in order to comply with the letter of Europe's AI Act. And within a few weeks, the biz plans to apply a form of digital watermarking – like it or not – to eligible ChatGPT and Codex text output in the European Union. But unlike rival Anthropic, it isn't applying its watermarking technique to content generated outside of Europe, though API customers can choose to have the marks applied to content made anywhere. Moreover, OpenAI is using technology that misses a fair number of instances of AI-generated text and can easily be tricked. The EU AI Act requires generative AI service providers to make model output identifiable in a way that's readable by machines. Anthropic was the first major AI company to announce its approach to AI Act compliance, which involves the application of Google's SynthID-Text algorithm. It's doing so globally. Microsoft and Meta have been working on similar technology for image-based AI because the EU is not the only market in which people have raised concerns about content provenance and the potential to use AI-generated content to produce misinformation. OpenAI already applies other content provenance signals to AI-generated images, audio, and video. In keeping with the letter of the AI Act, OpenAI is now offering a text watermarking approach called textGrain [PDF] that "adds an invisible statistical signal to the model’s word choices. Our detector looks for that signal to assess whether a passage contains an OpenAI watermark." Large language models predict word tokens one at a time from a probability distribution of potential words. By picking a different word to emit periodically – ideally a synonym – the resulting text deviates from the statistical pattern produced by an unbiased model. A watermark detector, which OpenAI is making available only to approved researchers and organizations, should flag that vocabulary divergence. That's the theory, but in practice results vary. The target error rate is one percent, but in short passages of 200 words, the detector may only flag 80 percent of the watermarks, compared to 95 percent in a 400-word passage. The results are also worse in texts that are functional, like passages about math or code, as substitutions are more likely to introduce errors. The textGrain paper does not address the likelihood that a statistically altered word choice might alter the meaning of a given passage. That's a possibility if the algorithm were to alter some salient fact or figure. Anthropic's approach, which also replaces certain output words though using a different algorithm, brings similar risks. In any event, OpenAI's watermark is easily defeated by word substitution. In tests on 400-token passages, swapping out 10 percent of the words with synonyms reduced watermark detection from 92 percent to 66 percent. And when replacing 25 percent of words, the watermark signal could only be detected in 17 percent of cases. events.title: Nvidia-backed start-up Reflection unveils open AI model to rival China offerings
events.summary: The AI model is designed to perform well for business customers and developers on coding and AI agent tasks. Reflection AI, founded by ex-Google DeepMind researchers, launched Beam, an open-weight AI model rivaling leading US and Chinese options for business and coding tasks. Beam matches China's GLM-5.2 in reasoning benchmarks and is cost-effective, with more technical details due in October. Backed by Nvidia, Reflection secured major deals with SpaceX and Nebius, supporting US efforts to promote AI exports and counter Chinese tech influence. SAN FRANCISCO – Reflection AI, an artificial intelligence start-up from two former Google DeepMind researchers, has unveiled a new open-weight model that it says rivals leading options in the US and China. The model, called Beam, is designed to perform well for business customers and developers on coding and AI agent tasks while costing less than many competitors, the company said on Oct 5. It said Beam scores comparably on advanced reasoning benchmarks to GLM-5.2, a flagship open model from China’s Z.AI. Reflection intends to release more technical details about the model later in October. While China is still widely viewed as behind the US in AI, Chinese developers like DeepSeek and Moonshot AI have gained ground by offering cheaper and customisable open model. Top US firms, including OpenAI and Anthropic, have primarily focused on closed or proprietary offerings as they work to build up their enterprise businesses. Reflection emerged from stealth in 2025 with a focus on developing open AI models. The firm is backed by Nvidia and other investors. It has held talks to raise US$2.5 billion (S$3.2 billion) at a valuation of US$25 billion, the Wall Street Journal previously reported. The start-up has also struck billion-dollar deals with Elon Musk’s SpaceX and cloud provider Nebius Group to secure computing power to develop its models. The model release stands to boost the American government’s efforts to export the US and its allies’ AI abroad. Earlier in 2026, Reflection was part of a US-brokered deal to build sovereign AI in Korea. Officials are planning to cobble together more of these deals promoting exports of US tech, which are designed to prevent the spread of Chinese alternatives. BLOOMBERG

events.title: ‘Pull the plug’: protesters resort to direct action against AI firms
events.summary: Campaign groups report surge in membership after a spate of AI safety alerts and apocalyptic warnings In a bar below Waterloo Bridge, a cell of a fast-growing anti-AI protest movement met last week to plot their latest move: disrupting a tech industry dinner being addressed by a senior executive from the chip maker Nvidia. Emma, a 28-year-old bartender, had never before taken direct action and was the most nervous of the four plotters from Pull The Plug, one of a growing number of AI-focused campaign groups around the world. Around the table were a former climate protester and a campaigner versed in the anti-nuclear movement. Emma signed up after a summer of feeling rising alarm at the catastrophic risks of AI, first when a swarm of OpenAI agents escaped their training “sandbox”, cheated, deceived and conspired to hack into the Hugging Face website and then as Jacob Coxon, an Anthropic researcher, quit with an apocalyptic warning that superintelligent AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade”. As darkness fell they crossed the Thames to the Claremont hotel where Emma filmed while two others unfurled a banner in a function room, shouting “Pull the plug on Nvidia” and “Pull the plug on Palantir”. Hundreds of protesters also staged a rally in front of Palantir’s London HQ last Thursday. “We did not consent to the kind of build-out that you are planning here,” the activists yelled as they were wrestled out of the door. They edited a video clip – “activist disrupts elite AI network dinner – Nvidia edition” – and uploaded it to Instagram. It was a small gesture, but they had made their stand. “I want to show other people that they don’t have to feel powerless among all of these articles coming out [about AI doom],” said Emma. “It’s easy to fall into a spiral that it’s too late. This shows people they can address the tech executives, disrupt their meetings, make them feel uncomfortable and get some answers.” Pull The Plug was launched in January and has about 300 members – mostly aged from 20 to 40. It is backed by an anonymous funder who works in the AI industry, organisers said. Several campaigns resisting AI acceleration are funded by tech insiders . Pull The Plug advocates direct action – a tactic other AI campaigns have rejected. Last month, one of its members climbed on to a chair in a packed AI conference in London addressed by speakers from OpenAI and Amazon and delivered an impassioned speech. “Best case scenario: the men handling this technology are completely incompetent,” the female activist said in an outburst that garnered 153,000 Instagram likes and was picked up by the Washington Post. “Worst case scenario: we are all being led into a disaster.” Other AI protest movements are gaining momentum after a torrent of news about AI dangers. Anthropic told investors this week that advanced AI could pose “existential risks to humanity”. Pause AI, a confederation of campaign groups in 17 countries, saw a fourfold jump in sign-ups when worrying news about rogue AI agents was breaking in August and last month. “We have had a lot of volunteers who have suddenly decided to dedicate way more of their time to the cause,” said Maxime Fournes, a Cambridge-educated mathematician and deep learning engineer who is chief executive of PauseAI Global. Volunteer sign-ups doubled to about 100 a week after the Hugging Face incident and soared to 681 in the week of Coxon’s “kill us all” warning, when PauseAI organised protests in Paris, London and Berlin. Donald Trump may be one of the movement’s most important recruiting sergeants. He announced last week that he wanted AI companies to “self-police” despite widespread demands, including from the companies, for federal and international rules to limit AI-enabled cyber-attacks and bioweapons. The surge in worrying news has given campaigners like Fournes hope that “we could actually survive this situation”. He added: “Suddenly we have a large fraction of the world population that is waking up.” Joseph Miller, an AI safety researcher who has suspended his doctoral studies at Oxford University to run Pause AI’s UK branch, noticed the shift while campaigning outside Brixton tube station in London. He said: “It was the easiest flyering we’ve ever done, because people would just come and talk to me … one every few minutes.” People he spoke to were worried about cognitive decline in schools and AI resulting in sloppy work in the office. “I heard ‘killing everyone’ more from young people,” Miller added. Pausing or halting AI is a cause that cuts across political and generational boundaries, according to campaigners. University students sign up because they fear AI will wreck career paths, while older conservationists rally against datacentre construction.

events.title: Australian consumer confidence plunges to worst level since 1990s after RBA rate rise
events.summary: Key indicator dropped about 20% after the Reserve Bank last month announced the highest interest rates since 2011 Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Australian households are the most persistently pessimistic they have been since the early-1990s recession, after a fourth rate rise this year. Confidence among Australian consumers has plunged about 20% since the Reserve Bank of Australia lifted interest rates to the highest levels since 2011, according to the Westpac–Melbourne Institute consumer sentiment index. The survey, conducted between 28 September and 1 October, showed the confidence index dropped by 4.7% to 80.4% in October – the worst level since the outbreak of the Middle East conflict in early April. But for respondents surveyed after the RBA call on 29 September, the index dropped to 67.2% – the lowest level since the late 1990s. That was broadly in line with the weekly ANZ-Roy Morgan consumer survey, which fell about 5% to 67.1 points. Westpac’s head of Australian macro-forecasting, Matthew Hassan, said sentiment had been extremely weak for the longest period since the “disastrous” recession of the early 1990s. “Australian consumers remain stuck in a cost-of-living nightmare that seems to have no end in sight,” Hassan said. “The latest RBA move looks to have badly rattled consumers. Responses over the course of the survey week show a very sharp deterioration after the decision was announced.” Assessments of family finances and buyer sentiment were the biggest categories affected. Expectations about the economic outlook fell less sharply, but assessments about the economy in the next five years were back to lows not seen since August 2020, shortly after Melbourne’s second lockdown and before jobkeeper subsidies were expanded. AMP economist My Bui said the decline was unsurprising given the September rate hike and rising fuel prices. “On our calculation the weekly petrol bill for a typical Australian household has gone up by $20 versus the beginning of the year,” Bui said. “The worry with declining confidence is that it tends to correlate with household spending on a per capita basis: the downtrend in confidence over the past 12 months suggests consumption per person will likely fall further into contraction this year.” Mortgage holders were the most pessimistic home ownership subgroup given rising borrowing costs at 77 index points. Those who own their home outright experienced the largest decline in sentiment in the month, as the housing market downturn extended for a sixth month. Renters were the most optimistic, unchanged at 84.8 points. Hassan said fears of job losses were rising, with unemployment expectations ticking up 1.9% higher. But there are still signs the labour market is holding strong. Citi analysts Josh Williamson and Faraz Syed said “job vacancies have increased to a two-year high of 122 points, which accords with business sentiment expectations of positive employment growth”.

events.title: Widowed twice: A Gaza mother’s story of loss and survival
events.summary: Shackled, bleeding, raped: Abuse in Israeli prisons Does Trump have real leverage over Netanyahu? A young mother has lost two husbands and two children during Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza. Gaza City, Gaza — For three years, Nisreen Touman has gone to bed every night in tears, remembering all she has lost since the start of Israel’s war on Gaza in October 2023. By the time Nisreen was 34, she had been widowed twice. First, she lost her husband and her two children in June 2024. Then in July 2025, eight months after she remarried, Nisreen lost her second husband while she was pregnant. list 1 of 4 Satellite images show Gaza in ruins three years into Israel’s genocidal war list 2 of 4 Israeli settlers attack Jalud village in occupied West Bank pogrom list 3 of 4 Palestine weekly: Israeli politicians vie to look toughest before election list 4 of 4 Palestinian archaeologists race against time to save Gaza’s heritage Before Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, Nisreen lived a happy and stable life in her home in Nuseirat, central Gaza, with her husband, Sami, 35, and their two children, Mahmoud and Laith, who were aged five and two at the time of their deaths. “I had a home and a complete family. I got along with my husband, and we were friends,” she says, fighting back her tears. On June 8, 2024, Nisreen was returning home with her husband and children after visiting extended family, who had been displaced to al-Mawasi in Khan Younis. “We arrived and the children were playing in the street. Everything was normal. I was upstairs with my husband when suddenly we started hearing heavy, very close, bombing and gunfire.” Her husband rushed outside to bring their children and his brother’s and sister’s children inside, where 25 members of her family were staying. He then went outside again to see what was happening, as aircraft flew overhead. “That was the last time I saw him. I later learned that he had been killed by a gunshot to the head from a quadcopter that was flying over the area that day,” she said. Minutes later, while trying to calm the children as the bombing and gunfire continued, the house was targeted by an Israeli aircraft. “I lost consciousness for a few moments, then woke up to thick dust that completely blocked my view,” she said. “As the dust began to clear, I started to understand our place was bombed. I heard the family screaming and saw blood and body parts. I started shouting, ‘My children, my children.’” Nisreen breaks down as she recalls seeing her two children lying on the ground. One had suffered severe head injuries, while the other appeared to be sleeping. “I knew from that moment that I had lost them. It was clear that they were dead,” she says, recalling how she was unable to move from the shock. Her husband’s brother came and placed the children in her arms. “I could not speak. I was completely unable to speak, just tears running silently,” she said. “Everyone around me was screaming and crying.” For two hours, Nisreen held her children in her arms as the family, including those who were injured, remained trapped in the damaged home as gunfire and bombing continued. After repeated requests to the International Committee of the Red Cross for help, the family were eventually evacuated to a hospital. The killing of Nisreen’s family came on one of the bloodiest days of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza. On June 8, 2024, Israeli forces launched a military operation in the Nuseirat refugee camp, central Gaza, to rescue four Israeli captives who had been held following the Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel on October 7, 2023. The United Nations said 89 inhabited houses and residential buildings were targeted in nearly four hours of bombing. Gaza’s Health Ministry said that 274 Palestinians were killed and 698 wounded on that day alone. Eighteen members of Nisreen’s husband’s family were killed, including her husband and children, her sister Sabreen, 36, her mother-in-law, two of her husband’s brothers and their children, as well as members of the extended family. Nisreen returned alone to her family’s tent in al-Mawasi south of Gaza, where she struggled with the trauma and grief of losing her family. Four and a half months later, Nisreen found herself facing a difficult decision when her late sister’s husband, who was also her first husband’s brother, proposed to her. He wanted to marry Nisreen and have her help take care of their four children, who had lost their mother. “I strongly opposed it at first. I did not want to start a family or get married,” Nisreen said. She eventually agreed because she wanted to care for her departed sister’s children, especially the youngest, who was only one year old. Nisreen does not hide the fact that there were no romantic feelings behind her second marriage. “I had lost my husband, and he had lost his wife. I had lost my children, and the four children had lost their mother,” she said. The marriage allowed two people to fill the roles of the ones they lost.

events.title: Erling Haaland faces injury scare ahead of Man City vs Liverpool
events.summary: The Manchester City star asked to be substituted and was replaced in the 67th minute of the 2-1 defeat in Porto. Norway coach Stale Solbakken has revealed that he had a “heart-to-heart conversation” with Erling Haaland regarding concerns about the striker’s heavy workload ahead of a Nations League loss to Portugal, in which the Manchester City star asked to be substituted. Haaland gestured to Norway’s bench that he needed to come off and was replaced in the 67th minute of the 2-1 defeat in Porto on Sunday. list 1 of 4 ‘Everyone knew’: Canada boss Marsch wants Man City relegated for breaches list 2 of 4 Ronaldo-less Portugal beat Norway 2-1 to reach Nations League quarterfinals list 3 of 4 ‘Sham’: What will happen to Man City after Premier League’s guilty verdict? list 4 of 4 Ramos fires holders Portugal to 2-1 Nations League win in Norway He was seen limping on the field in advance of the substitution, raising concerns about his fitness before his return to City — a club under heavy scrutiny as the subject of a huge financial scandal in the Premier League. Speaking after the Portugal match, Solbakken did not say Haaland had sustained an injury but talked about the heavy workload the striker had been facing after playing the full game in each of Norway’s first three Nations League fixtures — a win over Denmark and losses to Portugal and Wales. That came after a busy start to the English season with City, after reaching the World Cup quarterfinals with Norway over the summer. “He [Haaland] was tired against Wales. That’s why we had a heart-to-heart conversation yesterday. We went through the possible options,” Solbakken said in quotes carried in the Norwegian media. “He might have played the last 45 minutes against Portugal. That was a discussion. But he has very bad vibes and feelings about it … I am very pleased that he managed to pull out 60 good minutes.” Haaland did not score on Sunday or against Wales on Thursday — the two games Norway has played since the verdict by an independent commission on City’s financial case was published. He had scored in the first two games in this international break and is on a record 65 goals in 59 appearances for his country. Haaland is the only senior, out-and-out striker in City’s squad whose first match back after the internationals is at Liverpool on Sunday. “He plays pretty much everything on the club team,” Solbakken said.

events.title: Irish budget to tackle childcare and energy costs
events.summary: The Irish government is expected to announce measures to help with energy and childcare costs when it delivers its budget later. The threshold at which people start paying the higher rate of income tax is also expected to be increased from its current level of €44,000 (£37,000). The Taoiseach (Irish Prime Minister) Micheál Martin said the budget has to be about "trying to ease the pressure on families and households". The broad shape of the budget was set out in the Summer Economic Statement , external , promising tax measures worth €1.5bn (£1.27bn) and extra spending of €7bn (£5.92bn). Government party leaders, including the taoiseach, are expected to sign off on the budget Much of that additional spending is "standstill" funding to cover the rising costs of current services. Ireland is in a stronger fiscal position than most European countries as an ongoing corporation tax windfall means it is collecting more in taxes than it is spending on services. Figures released last week showed the country is expected to run a surplus of €6.9bn (£5.84bn) this year, lower than the €9.2bn (£7.79bn) forecast in April. That smaller forecast surplus reflects the introduction of fuel supports and additional spending to cover budget overspends, particularly in health. Some of the surplus is being invested in national wealth funds to help with future spending commitments. A spending watchdog, the Irish Fiscal Advisory Council, has criticised the government for not saving more. Other measures expected to be announced on Tuesday are a new tax-free savings scheme, similar to the UK ISA. A proposal for a "culture card" for teenagers, to spend on events like concerts, is also set to be announced though the value and eligibility are unclear. events.title: Last call for the mall? How shopping centres are reinventing themselves
events.summary: Keith Ely remembers the Brunel Centre's heyday but is looking to the future The Brunel Centre was once a thriving retail destination, attracting shoppers from far and wide. "It was incredible," says town councillor Keith Ely, who remembers its opening in Bletchley, Buckinghamshire, in 1973. Back then, centre:MK, a large destination shopping centre four miles away in Milton Keynes, did not exist, and the Brunel was quite the draw. Now, like many other medium-sized shopping centres, it is struggling. Vacant units and graffiti-daubed shutters dominate, and it has just one store left. That remaining shop, a Boots Opticians, is set to close later this month ahead of the centre's planned demolition next year . But Ely, 87, is not upset to see the Brunel make way for flats and a health centre, with only some retail space. "It is a sad old building, isn't it?" he says. "There is no nostalgia from me." The Debenhams store in the Grafton Centre in Cambridge closed in 2021 In the Grafton Centre, Cambridge, it is a similar story, with shuttered units, a large empty former Debenhams department store and a permanently closed cinema. There are long-term plans for a redevelopment to include retail but also a life science centre. This may work in Cambridge, a global leader in life sciences, but it is not an option in much of the country. So, in the age of online shopping, what lies ahead for these medium-sized malls? "There are too many in the UK and many don't have a future," is the stark assessment of Subjit Jassy, a director at Pioneer Group, which owns the centre. "The old model of retailers expanding to improve turnover has now disappeared because of the internet." Image source, Milton Keynes Living Archive Image caption, Before the Brunel Shopping Centre was built in the 1970s, people in Bletchley would travel to Aylesbury or Bedford to shop Image source, Milton Keynes Living Archive Image caption, The centre initially had little natural light, before the roof was replaced with glass Image source, Qays Najm/BBC Image caption, In 2021 Milton Keynes City Council was awarded £22.7m from the government's Town Deal Fund to redevelop the site Image source, Qays Najm/BBC Image caption, Boots Opticians, the last remaining store in the centre, is already closed on Wednesdays Analysis by commercial property firm CBRE , external found that while the vacancy rate across UK shopping centres in the second quarter of this year was 16%, it was "significantly lower" at major centres. Meanwhile, research by estate agents Savills found between April and June 2026 almost 73% of consumer spending in shopping centres was in the biggest sites, with less than 18% in secondary, or medium-sized centres. Dr Kardi Somerfield says centres that have leisure businesses can "extend the day" and attract customers into the evening "It is not just that shopping centres have one destiny; they really don't," says Dr Kardi Somerfield, a lecturer in marketing at the University of Northampton. Some destination shopping centres are running at "almost 100% occupancy", she adds. Back at the Brunel, Labour's Ed Hume, responsible for housing at Milton Keynes City Council, says: "We do need shops. "The change here is about making sure we have a town centre that is much more open." The hope is that more town centre homes will increase the number of people to use local businesses. Similar plans in Norwich will see the Anglia Square development primarily replaced by housing. Characters from TV show The Flintstones were at the opening of the Weston Favell Shopping Centre in 1974 But there are other options rather than just tearing a centre down. Market Walk in Northampton is t o become a leisure and entertainment space . "Other shopping centres have a really important purpose as a community hub," says Somerfield, outlining another potential use. This is what management are trying to achieve at another site that opened in the 1970s: Weston Favell, on the eastern edge of Northampton. Footfall – the number of customers entering the building – has increased every year since the pandemic, says centre manager Kevin Legg. "We are still relevant today," he says. "Other shopping centres are trying to emulate and create what we've got." What they have got is a mix of a large supermarket, a number of big national brands and smaller independent businesses, as well as other community facilities. Not far from the library inside the centre is a church. It is currently being used by Silhouette Youth Theatre, a charity that aims to make the arts more accessible. Next year it plans to create a 250-seat theatre inside part of a former Wilko store. Silhouette Youth Theatre currently holds sessions in the Emmanuel Church, inside Weston Favell Shopping Centre George Grande, voice lead at Silhouette, says being located in a shopping centre means more people can easily arrive by public transport and gives the group more visibility.

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Death of a star may not be game over for the inner solar system after all Google launches first datacenter satellite and research that finds orbiting bit barns can work 4 days ago Boeing's Calamity Capsule gets another shot at the ISS taxi business 6 days ago Starship finally makes orbit but engine trouble cuts the victory lap short 6 days ago Astronomer watches Starlink satellites sinking to build a ‘planetary barometer’ 11 days ago Google's TPUs to catch some rays in orbit next week 11 days ago When yellow dwarf stars like our sun die, they swell to an enormous size and destroy their inner planets by either crushing them with massive gravity or evaporating them with astounding heat. While these suns later settle down to become a white dwarf, the process is nearly always game over for planets in an inner solar system. Or maybe not, according to a paper published on Monday titled “Discovery of a second-generation planet candidate accreting onto a white dwarf.” As explained by NASA’s Hubble Mission team, the paper’s authors pored over Hubble Space Telescope observations of white dwarf star HS 0209+0832 from 1999. According to the paper, data from those scans “revealed the presence of carbon, aluminum, silicon, calcium, titanium, nickel and zinc in the atmosphere, as well as ~100 lines that could not be identified.” The authors of this paper used new techniques to identify the mystery matter, and concluded that there’s plenty of the element niobium present in what looks like a gas giant orbiting HS 0209+0832. In NASA’s post, co-author Nicholas Stone, a theoretical astrophysicist at the University of Wisconsin, pointed out that “Niobium and other elements heavier than iron are astronomically special because, unlike many common elements, they are not formed in the cores of stars by thermonuclear fusion.” “Instead, these heavy elements can only be synthesized in the exotic conditions that briefly emerge inside dying stars. The presence of niobium is a signpost of these ‘death’ throes, and the expulsion of the dying star's innards into space.” Finding niobium is also notable because, as the paper explains, “the canonical rock-forming elements [are] silicon and iron.” The paper explains that its authors compared the material observed at HS 0209+0832 with all known examples of rocky material around white dwarfs, and to all meteorites in our Solar System, but could find “no compositional matches.” That finding suggests that the niobium-rich gas giant at HS 0209+0832 represents both a secondary planet – which are rare – and a body composed of material we’ve not previously seen becoming a planet. It also shows that planets can form close to a star after the hellish red giant phase. Oh, and let’s not forget that HS 0209+0832 is also an exoplanet, a class of body humanity first spotted in only 1992. The paper suggests the niobium gas giant is about the size of Jupiter, but that the white dwarf is blasting away its atmosphere and perhaps creating “a comet-like tail of material that would form a disk around the white dwarf star and fall back on to its surface, leading to Hubble detecting the niobium when studying the star” Co-author Jamie Williams, from the Department of Physics at the University of Warwick, told NASA he thinks the niobium world will stick around. “If the second-generation planet is there, I think it is likely to survive. Eventually the white dwarf will cool and then maintain a consistent temperature, with the planet in its stable habitable zone for millions of years,” Williams said. ® Only the finest Swedish Bork will do for Stockholm station No, this is not GRUB of the meatball variety OpenAI rolls out weak sauce watermarking for AI text The VMware exit is a protection upgrade PARTNER CONTENT: VergeIO says an exit is also an opportunity Brighter isn't better and more is less.

events.title: Banks still refusing credit cards, watchdog says
events.summary: The Government of Jersey said whether credit cards were offered to islanders "remains a commercial decision" Islanders are still struggling to get credit cards despite personal data changes to make it easier to apply for one, a consumer council has said. The changes which came into force on 30 July meant the government could securely share personal data with UK credit reference agencies, which had been seen as the main barrier to successful applications . However, the Jersey Consumer Council said several providers had still refused applications and called for the government to work closer with businesses and banks. A spokesperson for Jersey's government said it had "engaged with providers throughout this process" and whether products were offered in the island "remains a commercial decision". Carl Walker from the Jersey Consumer Council said credit card companies may need convincing to bring their business back Carl Walker, from Jersey Consumer Council, said credit card companies would need to be reminded of the change which had allowed more information to be shared. "The last time they were involved... Jersey was slamming the door shut, so they have switched off and turned their attention elsewhere," he said. "We're pushing the government to write them an official letter to say this piece of legislation has now changed, Jersey's now open for business... and then leave it up to them whether they decide they to come back or not." Listen to the latest news for Jersey A spokesperson said the government had "successfully delivered a project to share islanders' data with credit reference agencies". "This was a key issue identified by the industry as an obstacle to providing credit cards in Jersey," they said. "It remains a commercial decision for providers to decide whether to offer their products or services, including credit cards, in Jersey. "The government has engaged with providers throughout this process... and will continue to do so." Follow BBC Jersey on X , external , Facebook , external and Instagram , external . events.title: UK regulator FCA to investigate how it handled Epstein whistleblower who took his own life
events.summary: British banker Simon Andriesz helped to expose alleged ties between late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and US commerce secretary Howard Lutnick A top UK regulator has launched an investigation into how it handled a whistleblower – who highlighted alleged ties between the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and the US commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick – after he took his own life. The British banker Simon Andriesz died late last month aged 57, the campaign group Transparency Task Force, of which he was a member, confirmed over the weekend. Andriesz had formerly worked as a managing director at BGC Group, the financial brokerage where Lutnick had been chief executive. He had accused the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) of failing to hold his former employer to account for alleged wrongdoing, and had been wrongly told he did not qualify for whistleblower protection. The banker had spent years raising concerns about his former employer: first in regards to accounting irregularities – which he raised internally at BGC in 2016, a year before he was sacked – and then in 2020-21, when he reportedly told the FBI that Lutnick had undeclared business ties with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Lutnick has since said he had no “personal or professional relationship” with Epstein. He was named Donald Trump’s commerce secretary in late 2024. Andriesz, who had been living in Cornwall, later unearthed an email chain in the Epstein files that suggested Lutnick and Epstein had discussed the prospects of a startup business they were both involved in, in 2018. Epstein died in jail in August 2019 while awaiting trial on sex trafficking charges. However, Andriesz told the BBC’s File on 4 Investigates this summer that authorities in the US and UK had failed to hold BGC and its parent company, Cantor Fitzgerald, properly to account, or protect him from potential retaliation. He also later accused the FCA of mistreating whistleblowers, and raised concerns about the toll that whistleblowing had taken on his family, career and health. The FCA had also given Andriesz misleading information, saying he would not qualify for whistleblower protection because his identity had become known. The regulator apologised to him and said that further guidance and training would be provided to its whistleblowing team. The FCA confirmed it had now tasked a new board member to investigate how staff handled Andriesz’s concerns. “We are very sorry to hear of Mr Andriesz’s death,” an FCA spokesperson said. “Our thoughts are with his family and friends. Since expressing our condolences, we’d asked Lea Paterson, who has just joined our board as a non-executive director, to review how we interacted with Mr Andriesz to learn any lessons for the future.” However, the all-party parliamentary group (APPG) on investment fraud and fairer financial services is concerned that the FCA is being allowed to “mark its own homework” and called on the regulator to pay an independent party to “forensically and objectively evaluate its handling of whistleblowers”. The APPG’s chair, the Labour MP John McDonnell, said: “It is vital that this time a truly independent and non-conflicted organisation carries out the work needed. If the FCA refuses to respond positively, the APPG will consider all alternatives, including conducting its own call for evidence from whistleblowers who have interacted with the regulator.” Lutnick has not been accused of any wrongdoing in relation to Epstein, and has previously said: “I unequivocally condemn the conduct attributed to Jeffrey Epstein and everyone who participated in his illegal activities. The survivors of his crimes deserve our respect and support.” A BGC spokesperson said: “BGC has long disputed Mr Andriesz’s allegations but does not intend to relitigate these matters at this sad time. BGC is sorry to hear this tragic news and expresses our condolences to Mr Andriesz’s family.” In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline on 988, chat on 988lifeline.org , or text HOME to 741741 to connect with a crisis counselor. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org

events.title: ‘It really hammers people’: Scottish islanders hit by highest diesel prices in UK
events.summary: Inhabitants of the Hebrides and Shetland tell of how fuel costs are putting the squeeze on commuting, services, food and more A s fuel prices reach the highest level in the UK since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Scottish islanders are feeling the pain more than most. On the mainland, the price of diesel has soared to a record high of 200.01p a litre, bringing the cost of filling an average family car to more than £110, according to the RAC. Petrol has risen by a third since the start of the Iran war at the end of February, averaging 174.71p – increasing to 195.64p in motorway service areas. In the Hebrides and Shetland, prices at the forecourt have jumped even higher, with some fuel stations selling diesel for more than 220p a litre during the initial rise. While European governments appear to have staved off a US export ban that could have sent prices even higher, in Shetland the lack of competition and the cost of shipping to remote areas have made it the most expensive place in the UK for fuel. The ramifications for island life have been immediate. Adam, 43, who lives in North Uist in the Outer Hebrides, said diesel had reached £2.28 a litre on the island, making his 45-mile round commute particularly expensive. He and his wife have diesel cars that they need for work and transporting their three children. “You accept that things are more expensive, especially food because there’s more distance to travel and we are further from distribution centres. Same with getting things delivered here because you have to drive more miles. But when something like the price of diesel skyrockets, it really hammers people here more than other places around the country,’” he says. In between work and dropping children off with his wife, Adam says they really rack up the miles. To cut costs, Adam says the family is having to buy the cheapest food they can, given that food prices are also dependent on the price of diesel that haulage companies pay. “It’s come down a bit in the last week or so. I never thought I’d look up at a £2.18 diesel price and think: ‘Oh, quick, I better fill up now.’ It’s really bad. Although people think of this place as really tiny, you’re in your car all the time. I average 15,000 miles a year, and my wife does even more because she’s a health visitor. She gets the same mileage as someone who’s a health visitor in the central belt, yet we pay a lot more,” he says. About 26,000 people live in the Outer Hebrides, mainly on the largest islands of Lewis and Harris. Adam says rising prices have also hit accessibility to public services, which are already difficult to reach for islanders. “The Scottish government say they want to help repopulate places like this but in reality, they are not offering much practical support. For example, my daughter had a referral to a paediatrician for a hearing test so I had to take her to Stornoway for that. It involved booking ferries, driving more than 100 miles and staying in a hotel. We can claim some money back from the patient travel scheme but they only offer you £40-£50 for a hotel. Because of the costs getting there, the NHS stops being free at the point of use because we can’t be treated locally,” he says. Bob, a postman who lives in Shetland, said that people in the North Sea archipelago were frustrated by rising fuel prices while also being a hub for the oil and gas industry. “You are resigned to it. It’s always been slightly more expensive than everywhere else, so you have to pay the prices. What can you do? Fuel poverty has always been an issue up here. It’s ironic in a sense given we are near where a lot of the oil and gas arrives from the North Sea. Yet, we are paying higher prices than anyone else. It’s the same with the windfarms,” he says. Bob says that islanders often have no other choice but to drive, especially when getting to work. “Most jobs are in Lerwick so unless you live in town, you need to drive. There is a bus service but people who work don’t use it much because it’s difficult to make their hours,” he says. “I only ever drive small cars. I have a Fiat 500 so it’s not too bad. But an awful lot of people have big 4x4s up here because of the weather. Diesel prices will be having a big impact on them.” Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Ryan, 25, from the Isle of Benbecula in the Outer Hebrides, says the soaring costs mean many islanders are having to cut back. “A lot of family and friends up here are taking fewer journeys than they would normally outside work. For a lot of people, it’s a case of just going to work and going to the shops. Even those journeys are not short. The Western Isles span 130 miles. South Uist itself is about an hour top to bottom. A lot of us easily get through a few tanks a month on fuel. It’s a lot of the money that’s getting spent up here,” he says. Ryan works in a nearby hotel and is paid close to the minimum wage.

events.title: Burnham’s surprise EU-turn could deliver the Tories from a generational mess | Gaby Hinsliff
events.summary: Burnham’s surprise EU-turn could deliver the Tories from a generational mess Badenoch would never have reopened the door on Brexit, but now that the PM has, it suits the Conservatives to let him walk through it T here’s no way on earth it should have worked, but somehow he may have got away with it. Last week, the actor Richard E Grant became the first contestant on The Traitors – a show whose only unbreakable rule is never to let anyone know you’re the murderer – to gleefully announce within minutes of being selected that yes, haha, it’s him! Yet even then many of his fellow contestants seemed to like him too much to recoil. And that, roughly speaking, is now Andy Burnham’s Brexit strategy. After years of Labour politicians – not least Burnham himself, in the Makerfield byelection , without which he would not now be prime minister – trying to hide their real feelings about Brexit, Burnham has decided just to tell the truth and hope people roll with it. Leaving hasn’t worked, he said bluntly last week in Liverpool , and Britain should consider the alternatives. If you’re a leaver who suspects him of being out to unwind Brexit – well, yes, he is. This bold strategy seemingly surprised much of his own cabinet , an early lesson in how he likes to work for those who hadn’t studied his Manchester operation closely enough. But the oddly muted initial response to what would once have been a seismic shock suggests it’s wrongfooting some opponents, too. Nigel Farage has been the only one to react with unfettered glee . Reform’s next manifesto is basically now written for him: save Brexit, stop the boats and don’t vote for Restore because it can’t win. Things are more complicated for the Lib Dems and Greens, who, having pitched themselves as the only real pro-Europeans on the left, are now stuck with trying to take credit for pushing Labour into doing the right thing. But it’s the party currently holding its conference in Birmingham that faces the most interesting dilemma. Kemi Badenoch doesn’t mention Brexit much these days – only elected after the referendum, she seems to regard the generational Conservative trauma of that period as history now – and it gets only brief mentions in The Right Way , the 95-page personal essay she says would form the bedrock of a Tory government. In his platform speech on Monday, the shadow chancellor, Andrew Griffith, chose to focus on accusing Burnham of supposedly dragging Britain back to the 1970s, rather than back to 2015. On this they echo much of what’s left of the Tory vote, who are more interested in tax, the costs of doing business, small boats and what exactly Labour has against labradors in pubs than in relitigating the Brexit deal. Yet the Conservatives are still promising to reverse any Labour unravelling of Brexit, regardless of how that affects the economic growth Badenoch simultaneously insists is everything to her. It makes no intellectual sense, which arguably didn’t bother previous Tory leaders. But it’s a mistake for one pitching herself as a rigorous thinker, approaching power with the same robustly worked-through theory of the world as Thatcher in the 1970s. Growth is now Badenoch’s rationale for everything, from scrapping the Environment Agency – accused of being a drag on developers, although that’s precisely what some rural Tory voters like about it – to giving parents earning over £100,000 free childcare (on the grounds that, currently, high earners will cut their working hours rather than lose that nursery place). It’s her defence for some potentially unpopular choices, her alpha and omega. Yet by ignoring the ongoing damage Brexit is doing to trade and GDP, Badenoch is chopping her self-professed growth mission off at the knees. In her 1976 essay The Right Approach , which Badenoch’s treatise consciously echoes, Margaret Thatcher declared that her party “has always been outward-looking, while concerned with the security, the economic interests and the honour of Britain”, and lambasted Labour’s lack of enthusiasm for the then European Community. The context now is obviously different, but Thatcher in 1976 was still a pragmatist arguing for Europe “to concentrate on what is practical and what is attainable”, where Badenoch in 2026 is an ideologue. The Tory brand remains toxic despite its leader’s relative popularity mostly because voters got sick of endless Brexit-related drama consuming Westminster, while none of the practical benefits materialised. There’s no point dangling policies such as free childcare for bankers over the remain-voting former Tory shires without acknowledging all that. But if she can’t bring herself to do so, then Badenoch’s next best bet is to let Burnham rescue her party from a dead end of its own making. Though they would never have opened this door, in truth it suits the Tories to let Burnham walk through it, while blaming him for whatever goes wrong.

events.title: World Bank says Middle East economy to contract 2.1% in 2026 on Iran war
events.summary: The World Bank on Tuesday lowered its 2026 forecast for the economies in the Middle East , saying the region's overall GDP will contract by 2.1 per cent for this year. The revision was the latest downgrade the World Bank has forecast for the region as the Iran war continues to constrain energy supplies. Economists had previously lowered their 2026 forecasts from 3.6 per cent in January to 2.1 per cent in April. Global growth, meanwhile, is projected to slow to 2.5 per cent this year, the World Bank had said in June. The seven-month conflict has affected a wide variety of sectors as the closure of the Strait of Hormuz initially choked off much of the region's energy supplies. This also led to setbacks in tourism, aviation and logistics, with uncertainty in financial markets, the World Bank said in its latest Economic Update for the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan (Menaap). “This conflict is very painful and it has concentrated the losses of the conflict in our region while the global economy and other regions are upgrading their forecasts, and we are downgrading significantly,” said Roberta Gatti, Menaap chief economist at the World Bank. Economies in the Gulf Co-operation Council are projected to contract by an average of 4.3 per cent for 2026, down 5.7 percentage points from April, driven by lower export volumes due to the Strait of Hormuz's closure, leading to significant losses in output and government revenue. Economies in the UAE and Saudi Arabia are set to slow from 6.2 and 4.6 per cent in 2025 to minus 1.6 and minus 2 per cent in 2026, respectively, the World Bank said. Qatar is forecast to have its weakest economic performance in five decades, slowing from 1.8 per cent growth in 2025 to minus 20.9 per cent this year after its average monthly gas production fell by about 67 per cent between March and July due to damage sustained at its sites. Kuwait's economy is forecast to contract by 14.6 per cent, a downwards revision of 8.2 percentage points from April. The war has hit oil exporters particularly hard, with the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and attacks across the region. Oil production in the Gulf dropped from its prewar average of 26 million barrels a day to about 16 million in March, the World Bank said. The IMF's PortWatch monitor showed just three tankers moved through the strait in the seven-day moving average ending September 27. “It's a volume story. It's a quantity story for us. It's a price story for the world,” Ms Gatti said. Oman, which is less reliant on the Strait of Hormuz, is the only GCC member projected to experience positive growth this year, at 3.1 per cent. Iraq 's growth prospects also faced a downwards revision of 3.8 percentage points since April with a negative growth rate of 12.4 per cent. Iraq, which is Opec's second-largest producer, depends on oil for about 90 per cent of its government revenue. Iran's economy also expected to shrink by 7.7 per cent in 2026. The World Bank report works on the assumption that the Strait of Hormuz will gradually reopen beginning on December 31. Under this scenario, economic activity in 2027 for the UAE will rebound to 8 per cent, Saudi Arabia by 6.1 per cent, Qatar by 25 per cent, Kuwait by 20.5 per cent and the GCC as a whole by 8.6 per cent. The UAE has embarked on a “ Zero Hormuz ” strategy to diversify its supply chains, while Saudi Arabia has relied on its East-West Pipeline to move oil to Yanbu Port on the Red Sea. Oil prices have swung wildly since the onset of the war on February 28, with global benchmark Brent crude trading at about $118 a barrel in March and in May. Saudi Aramco chief Amin Nasser credited the East-West Pipeline for keeping oil prices at about $100 a barrel. Mr Nasser also warned it could take up to two years to refill global inventories that were reduced under emergency measures. He was speaking at an energy conference in London on Monday. Oil importers, by contrast, are expected to fare better in what Ms Gatti described as a “reversal of fortunes” compared to the 2022 energy shock after Russia's invasion of Ukraine. The World Bank anticipates Egypt's economic activity to pick up at a 5.1 per cent pace after growing by 4.4 per cent last year. It also raised its 2026 forecast for Morocco by 0.2 percentage points to 4.4 per cent, and 0.7 percentage points for Pakistan at 3.7 per cent. Its projection for Jordan remained unchanged at 2.7 per cent, while Tunisia received a slight downgrade of 2.3 per cent growth, 0.2 percentage points lower than its April forecast. Compounding effect Ms Gatti said the Iran war is placing a compounding effect on economies already mired in conflict, harming recovery prospects and contributing to long-term economic pain. Renewed hostilities between Israel and Hezbollah are reversing Lebanon's economic recovery of 4.2 per cent growth in 2025 to a contraction of 6.4 per cent this year. Forecasts for growth in Afghanistan and Yemen were also lowered to 3 per cent and 1 per cent respectively, while the World Bank anticipates Syria's economy to pick up between 8 and 10 per cent this year. The World Bank estimates GDP growth in the West Bank and Gaza will slow from 4.3 per cent in 2025 to 1.5 per cent this year, a downwards revision of 3 percentage points compared to April. The poverty rate in the area remains an estimated 41.9 per cent. It also said Gaza's economy is still in a state of “near-total collapse” despite the October 2025 ceasefire, owing to flare-ups in tensions, continued restrictions and stalled reconstruction preventing recovery efforts. “There were ongoing fragilities and now we see less humanitarian aid. We see a need to keep the attention,” Ms Gatti said. She said the economic costs of fragility were being compounded by the conflict, with reduced humanitarian aid making it important to maintain attention and investment in affected countries to prevent the consequences from being felt by future generations. AI productivity gains The report also said that, despite the conflict, artificial intelligence remains a key avenue for opportunity in the region. Economists said it could boost the productivity of up to 20 per cent of the region's jobs. The World Bank has previously urged developing countries to quickly adopt AI or risk falling behind on the economic gains it can deliver. It said developing economies can avoid mistakes by adopting available tools, adapting them to local conditions and advancing towards frontier AI development. “Some of the complements that are needed to fit the benefits of AI might not require money, but they require political will and vision. You need regulation and ethical regulation for AI to operate well,” Ms Gatti said.

events.title: Wood Group offshore workers launch 48-hour strike in row over pay
events.summary: At its peak in 2013, Wood reached a market valuation of more than £5bn and employed more than 50,000 people in oilfields around the world Offshore workers on a number of North Sea platforms are taking strike action in a dispute over pay and conditions. The Unite and RMT unions said they are in dispute with the Wood Group over its decision to "slash" the pay and conditions of dozens of offshore workers, including through the threat of issuing fire-and-rehire notices. The strikes will affect a number of installations run by Harbour Energy, including the Britannia, Jasmine, Judy, Lomond and North Everest platforms. The Wood Group said it had been notified of the action and added that staff and operational safety remained its "top priority". Production, instrument and mechanical technicians are among those set to walk out for a total of six days in October and November, beginning with a two-day walk-out which started at midnight. Vic Fraser, Unite regional officer in Aberdeen, said his members had been left with no choice but to strike Further walkouts are expected on 20 and 21 October and 3 and 4 November. The RMT has also instructed its members not to work any overtime from 8 October until further notice. The news comes after a warning that separate strike action by offshore workers at energy firm Apache could "severely disrupt" UK fuel supplies. Unite general secretary Sharon Graham said: "Unite will not allow the Wood Group to slash and burn our members' pay and conditions. "This is a profitable company and it is despicable that it is threatening to fire and rehire its workers. This is corporate greed in its worst form." Vic Fraser, Unite industrial officer, said: "Industrial action will inevitably impact the operation of Harbour Energy's offshore assets. "The workforce has been left with no option but to strike against the Wood Group's threats and intimidation. "Our members are saying enough is enough." "Strike action is always a last resort, but our members have clearly shown that they are prepared to stand together to defend their livelihoods and the terms and conditions they have worked under for many years. events.title: Community supermarket opens in shopping centre
events.summary: Gina English from the SEK Community Food Shop in Chatham says the store is open to everyone A new community supermarket offering access to affordable and healthy food has opened in a Kent shopping centre. The store run by SEK Community Food Shop welcomed the public to its home on the first floor of The Pentagon Centre in Chatham. Gina English from SEK says the shop is open to all as "in addition to supporting people with food insecurity, people will also be able get wraparound support from us, help with employment, looking at CVs and interview skills. We're also going to help people with budgeting and money management and signposting to other local services". Initial funding to set up the supermarket was provided by Medway Council through the Crisis and Resilience Fund. Shoppers can walk straight into the social supermarket, with no prior booking required, to access a wealth of budget-friendly groceries, including a £1 fruit and vegetable bag. Cost are kept low as the store redistributes surplus food to reduce waste, helping to protect the environment at the same time. SEK already operates two similar stores in Kent. English said: "We've had Ramsgate for about three years, Ashford just for just over a year and across the two shops in the last year alone we saw 55,500 transactions and we were able to save 170 tonnes of perfectly good food from going to waste, so they do work." Rod Taffs and Shirley Graves from Chatham were among the first customers into the newly opened community supermarket Some of the first to experienced the store were Shirley Graves and her partner Rod Taffs who have already filled their basket with bargains. "People want to come down and see what they've got, it's amazing," says Graves. "I've got a box of 20 samosas for £1.50 and a big huge bag of chicken for £6. Times are quite tight at the moment, being pensioners, it's cheap and the chicken is amazing." "That's going to do us three or four meals," adds Taffs. Medway Council leader, Vince Maple, said: "I think most people across Kent and Medway would want to see food not going to waste, so the ability to have good quality food at a reasonable price, helping not just our families and individuals on low incomes but helping all families has got to be a good thing." The shop also has a confidential, soundproofed office pod at the back of the store where customers can seek personal advice and guidance. The SEK Community Food Shop in The Pentagon Centre, Chatham, is open Monday to Saturday between 10:00 and 18:00. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Tells users ‘action required’ – but maybe don’t make that action a Jira ticket, because it has this bug ServiceNow under siege as Atlassian adds to ITSM take-outs May 1, 2026 Atlassian’s new data collection policy protects rich customers while AI eats the rest April 18, 2026 Atlassian gussies up Confluence for the AI era April 9, 2026 OpenAI now gets to decide which type of product assassin it will become March 25, 2026 Atlassian to shed ten percent of staff, because AI March 12, 2026 Atlassian has told its users to patch its datacenter products, pronto, to prevent attackers accessing their files. The Australian collaborationware company on Monday sent users an email that opens with the words “Action required” and points to a security bulletin that explains CVE-2026-21589 . The 9.3-rated arbitrary file access vulnerability is present in the datacenter versions of its Bitbucket, Confluence, Jira Service Management, Jira Software, Bamboo, Crowd, Crucible, and Fisheye products. Atlassian says the vulnerability “allows an unauthenticated attacker to access specific files within the web application root directory in affected versions.” That’s scary because Atlassian warns “In some configurations, there may be sensitive files present that increase your risk.” There’s also some good news in that attackers must know the exact filename and path to exploit the vulnerability, and the mess doesn’t allow anyone to see the contents of a directory. Another piece of good news is that Atlassian has updated its products – so users only need to find a change window in which to upgrade to a safe version of their software. Atlassian advised those who can’t patch ASAP to remove their instances from the internet, if possible. “Instances accessible to the public internet, including those with user authentication, should be restricted from external network access until you can take action,” the company warned. Its advisory also includes mitigations and advice on how to determine if your instances need the fix. Users who made the move from datacenter products to the Atlassian cloud have nothing to do, as Atlassian fixed the flaws in its own SaaS. That state of affairs rather vindicates Atlassian’s 2020 decision to stop developing its low-end server products and require users to shift into its cloud , and last year’s sequel in which it decided to discontinue its datacenter software , too.
