events.title: World Bank warns of AI concentration risks as it lifts East Asia and Pacific growth outlook to 4.5%
events.summary: The World Bank upgraded its growth forecast for East Asia and the Pacific to 4.5% in 2026. AI-related goods drove more than half of export growth in most of the region's economies. The bank warned that a reversal in AI spending, which is expected to be partly financed by $800 billion of private credit, would remove "a key pillar" supporting growth. The World Bank has raised its growth forecast for the East Asia and Pacific region on the back of artificial intelligence-related exports, while warning that its reliance on the AI boom leaves it vulnerable to a potential global tech spending reversal. The region includes 23 economies, including China, Vietnam, Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand. The EAP economy is expected to expand 4.5% this year, 0.3 percentage point more than the bank projected in April, according to its latest report released Tuesday. Growth is forecast to ease to 4.4% in 2027 and 4.3% in 2028. Vietnam received the biggest forecast upgrade among major economies of the region, up 1.1 percentage point to 7.4%. The region's strength, however, is highly dependent on AI-related manufacturing and exports. Trade growth, excluding AI-related goods, has been "weak or negative," the bank said. Those products accounted for more than half of the export growth in most of the region's economies and more than 70% in Malaysia, the Philippines, Thailand and Vietnam. China, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Thailand and Vietnam shipped $1.4 trillion of AI-related goods in the 12 months through April, according to the report. Official data showed that South Korea's exports grew 83.5% in September to a record $120.9 billion , with chips making up half of those shipments. Reflecting the dominance of semiconductors in the country's market, the World Bank highlighted that just two chipmakers — Samsung and SK Hynix — accounted for 43% of the benchmark Kospi index's value as of end-April. The AI risk is on the spending side. AI-related capital expenditure has reached about 6% of U.S. GDP, similar to the 2000 peak in information-technology investment, and the current cycle "has risen faster than either previous cycle and is still gaining speed," the bank said. The Bank for International Settlements in its annual economic report in June had warned that the boom's scale and pace bears resemblance to the dot-com frenzy of the 1990s and other "manias." The financing driving the boom is also less transparent. Of the $2.9 trillion in AI capex planned for 2025-2028, $800 billion is expected to come from private credit, the bank said, where AI-related lending rose to 34% of activity in 2025 from an 18% average over the prior five years. Private credit portfolios have experienced markdowns, outflows and defaults this year. Private credit markets are "less visible, and have not been tested by a severe downturn," the bank said. That said, the AI boom supported by abundant liquidity could slow due to the latest tightening of financial conditions as major central banks raise rates for the first time since 2023, according to the report. The U.S. Federal Reserve raised rates last month , its first increase in more than three years, and signaled one more to hike this year. A correction may not necessarily mean a bust for the AI supercycle, but that investment "had run ahead of realized demand," the organization said. A slowdown by 1 percentage point in U.S. growth cuts other emerging-market growth by an estimated 0.6 percentage point, with the hit to investment about twice as large, the bank said. "A slowdown concentrated in AI would be material for East Asia because of the region's prominence in the AI supply chain." Bank funding is the broadest exposure. Foreign-currency-denominated liabilities of banks appeared significant in some countries — 29.2% of GDP in Malaysia, 20.7% in the Philippines. Taiwan's statistics bureau recently raised its 2026 growth forecast to 11% from 9.6% on AI demand, while warning in June that "if the high-tech sector faces headwinds, the negative impact on the local economy could be bigger than expected."

events.title: The butter boom – how the world fell back in love with the glorious golden spread
events.summary: It’s being sculpted for fashion parties, collected by tourists and hoarded in freezers. There are even entire shops devoted to it. What’s behind the revival of the much-maligned foodstuff? T emperatures in Paris were nudging 41C when Erwan Leo opened Le Butter this summer. Wildfires had already been tearing through France and the city was quiet, particularly in the less touristy 8th arrondissement, a flex-your-wealth area near the Eiffel Tower known as the “golden triangle”. The last thing it needed, you would think, was a shop that sold loads of butter. “We were just so worried about the fridges,” says Leo, the 34-year-old owner. “We didn’t think anyone would even turn up.” I visit Le Butter, the first shop in Paris dedicated to selling the stuff, two months later in September. It’s a quaint, photogenic spot between a wine shop that was opened by Leo eight years ago and a cafe famous for being blown up in Christopher Nolan’s Inception. Inside there are candy-striped walls, little shopping baskets, a shelf of Instagrammable buttery merch (knives, hats, totes) and two double fridges containing 50 different types of butter. It’s a lot cooler today; the fridges purr away at an exacting 3C. And the past few months have been busy – so much so that Leo has had to erect a bench for those waiting outside, and a retractable barrier to manage the queues. Outside today, I find a gathering of butter fans comparing purchases. Among them is Clifford Yellen, a 66-year-old Italian-American chef and consultant who has bulk-bought “only pure stuff – salted”. He opens his paper bag to show me multiple packets, vacuum-packed for his flight home. “We chefs have a real thing about butter,” he says. He usually eats Italian, or the famously creamy Hokkaido from Japan. Inside the shop, tourists from Brazil and Korea are gathered around a glass display cabinet on the counter where staff dispense quenelles of wild garlic butter on to wooden tasting spoons. The tasters follow it with raspberry flavour, and chocolate. “I call Le Butter an ice-cream shop for butter!” Leo says with a laugh. And while British tourists have been banned from bringing French butter to the UK since 2025, to stop farm animal diseases spreading, as a nation we, too, revere butter. Earlier this year, the Pembroke Club in Belgravia, London, placed an advert for a butter sommelier in Country Life magazine, looking for someone able to confidently “curate our butter assortment and assist in training staff using our silver butter trolley”. For those who can take butter home with them, there are entire threads on Reddit discussing the best way to transport it via plane (frozen, vacuum-packed, ziplocked) and where to buy it. Guided by one, I head to La Grande Épicerie de Paris to lay eyes on its famous “wall of butter” where 150 types are sold. The two most popular varieties, according to the staff, are Le Beurre Bordier and Beillevaire. Like most good French butters, they have a fresh, rich flavour with tangy depths, which you could probably put down to their high butterfat content and the grass-fed cows from which they come. Even the high-end butter is relatively cheap, and right now, in this “little treat” economy , eking out €8 for a wheel of butter sprinkled with fleur de sel feels more manageable than buying a decent bottle of wine. The latest thing, Leo says, is people serving butter as they would cheese after dinner, on boards with crackers. “It’s also cheaper.” While I’m reporting from Paris fashion week, my Instagram becomes a cavalcade of ambrosial butters laid out on event tables with great loaves of bread, or pummelled into submission and piled up into small hills as table centrepieces. I watch influencers biting into whole sticks of butter, or being served plates of medjool dates stuffed with slivers of the stuff. It’s at once beautiful and grotesque. It has even become a material for food artists. Laila Gohar, the American-Egyptian artist, treats it like marble, and once carved it into a fragment of Michelangelo’s David. During a design festival, the food artist Imogen Kwok built a foot-high cone from whipped butter and foraged herbs. It was the threat of shortage that turned South African journalist Safia Patel, 35, into a self-described “butter hoarder” who now collects and categorises it. At home in Istanbul she keeps cooking butter, eating butter and “ornamental” butter (too precious to eat), the last of which she stores in her freezer. Her love of butter comes from her grandmother, who ate it in thick, cold slices on bread. But it was during the pandemic that she realised how much it really meant to her. She’d buy Lurpak locally in Istanbul – but as the pandemic wore on, it became harder to find. “Once things returned to normal, I began coercing people into bringing me butter from around the world in case I ran out.” Most days she carries two or three portion-sized packs in her handbag, “just in case. Yes, it can get messy.

events.title: Arizona welcomes new Taiwan representative office, rejecting warning from China
events.summary: Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs joined Taiwanese leaders at the opening of an office in Phoenix to aid Taiwanese businesses and citizens in the region PHOENIX -- Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs joined Taiwanese leaders at the opening of an economic and cultural office Monday to aid Taiwanese businesses and citizens in the region, despite pressure from the Chinese government to block it. Taiwanese authorities have said the new Phoenix office — their 14th in the United States — will promote collaboration in technology, especially in semiconductor manufacturing, and better serve a growing number of Taiwanese migrants in the city. After the plans for the office were announced in July, Hobbs received two letters from China’s consulate general in Los Angeles asking her to object to the proposal, according to documents the governor’s office shared with The Associated Press. In a July 3 letter, the Chinese authority called the governor to “refute such an attempt by the Taiwan authorities and stop any political gimmicks to harm the friendship and cooperation between China and the State of Arizona.” The stance was reiterated in an Aug. 21 letter. The letters were first reported by Phoenix radio station KJZZ. Hobbs highlighted Arizona’s ties with Taiwan at Monday’s opening. “Every Arizona elected official should show the courage necessary to support the partnership between Arizona and Taiwan,” Hobbs said. “As our economic partnership grows, we are mobilizing every available resource to support Taiwanese companies expanding here in Arizona.” Beijing claims the island as a breakaway province inseparable from China, while Taiwan considers itself separate from the Chinese mainland and has its own government. Scholars say that local-level collaborations with the Chinese government and Taiwan have become more politicized as U.S.-China relations have deteriorated over the years. Taiwan has been increasing its economic footprint in Arizona, with advanced chipmaker Taiwanese Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, or TSMC, pledging $100 billion to expand its operation in northern Phoenix. That brings its total investment in the city to $265 billion, the largest foreign direct investment in U.S. history. Around 500 Taiwanese engineers are working to ramp up production at TSMC in Arizona, according to Jason Hsu, a former lawmaker in Taiwan and a senior fellow at the public policy think tank Hudson Institute. Phoenix Mayor Kate Gallego also said the city is seeing a sort of “baby boom” in its Taiwanese communities, with several labor and delivery rooms even launching Mandarin language programs. events.title: OKX debuts a platform that turns 50 currencies into digital dollars, betting emerging market investors want stablecoins
events.summary: Crypto exchange OKX launched a standalone app on Tuesday that lets users convert more than 50 local currencies into U.S. dollar-backed stablecoins, as the company tries to expand its offerings beyond just being an exchange. OKX Money, which went live at the company’s OKX Now Product event in Singapore, is aimed at emerging markets in Latin America, Africa, South Asia, and the Middle East. OKX argues that currency swings, limited banking access, and foreign-exchange fees in those regions make it difficult to “protect savings and spend globally.” “The key gap for people and institutions is settlement,” Haider Rafique, OKX’s global managing partner, tells Fortune. He specifically cites two friction points: a small business shouldn’t wait days for a bank to settle a payment and a traveler shouldn’t have a credit limit frozen by pending hotel deposits. “I grew up in Pakistan,” he says. “I still have all the receipts of my mom and dad sending me money through Western Union ,” along with the memory of the fees paid from their “hard-earned savings.” OKX Money will allow customers to hold three dollar-backed stablecoins: Paxos’s USDG, Circle’s USDC, and Tether’s USDT. According to OKX, the platform offers up to 10% annual yield on eligible USDG balances, virtual and physical cards with no foreign-exchange markup, and referral rewards. Compared to legacy technologies, “crypto has one moat: We are technologically more advanced than traditional finance, whether it’s money or markets,” Rafique says. OKX Money is the latest launch in a series of new products by the cryptocurrency exchange, sparked in part by a March funding round with Intercontinental Exchange . The owner of the New York Stock Exchange invested in OKX in a deal that valued the cryptocurrency exchange at $25 billion. (The total investment was undisclosed, but Bloomberg reported the figure to be roughly $20 million).  On Sunday, the OKX-ICE joint venture–co-chaired by former New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo—filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission to launch a separate platform for round-the-clock trading of more than 60 tokenized U.S. stocks.  In recent weeks, OKX also introduced an account-protection program, named OKX Shield. In addition to security safeguards, Shield promises to reimburse up to $100,000 for regular users, and up to $500,000 for its highest class of VIP users, in the event of a third-party takeover. The launch comes as crypto platforms have lost an estimated $2.7 billion to hacks this year, according to security firm CertiK, including nearly $388 million stolen from rival exchange Bitget last month through a vulnerability in a third-party security product.  Roughly 97% of global stablecoin market value is tied to the U.S. dollar, a dominance drawing attention in Washington—where officials hope dollar-backed tokens will fuel demand for U.S. assets—and beyond, where several economies are exploring their own alternatives. “Every nation should be thinking about this technology,” Rafique says. “But the question is: What is the world willing to put their money towards?” He says he would welcome an Asian rival to the dollar stablecoin: “If there’s an Asia-based, fiat-pegged stablecoin that has stability, people will absolutely trust it.” In particular, he cites a Singapore-dollar-based stablecoin as something he’d be interested in. Rafique sees the crypto industry at an “inflection point.” Even as Bitcoin has rebounded, he says, liquidity in the altcoin market “is just not there.” Consumers in markets like Venezuela and Turkey once “YOLO-ed” into crypto to hedge inflation and chase fast-rising assets Yet now, with access to U.S. markets, energy markets, and pre-IPO price exposure, Rafique says emerging market investors are asking a different question: “Do I really need to bet on the next ape coin?” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Moonshot said to eye Hong Kong IPO in early 2027 after value hits US$50 billion
events.summary: Moonshot is one of the biggest stars of China’s AI scene, bursting onto the global stage in July with the debut of Kimi K3. HONG KONG – Moonshot AI has closed the final round of private fund-raising at a valuation of about US$50 billion and is heading towards an initial public offering in Hong Kong in the first quarter of 2027, according to sources familiar with the matter. The Chinese artificial intelligence champion has also begun laying the groundwork to start gauging investor sentiment through early look meetings starting as early as October, some of the people said, asking not to be identified because the information is private. Moonshot is one of the biggest stars of China’s AI scene, bursting onto the global stage in July with the debut of Kimi K3 , an open model that goes nearly toe to toe with leading platforms from the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic on some metrics. Its planned IPO is one of the most hotly anticipated deals in Hong Kong , where fund-raising driven by the industry is setting fresh records. The company is considering raising up to US$5 billion in the deal, people familiar with the matter have said. It is unclear how the valuation or the IPO timeline may be affected by tighter oversight of China’s AI industry after regulators opened a data security probe into DeepSeek and Moonshot, according to The Information, adding to broader concerns over governance and safety. Deliberations are ongoing and the timing of the IPO might still change, the sources said. Moonshot representatives did not respond to requests for comment during a Chinese public holiday. The company’s valuation has risen steadily through a series of fund-raising efforts. A previous round this summer valued it at US$31.5 billion. Moonshot’s annual recurring revenue (ARR), a gauge of future sales, is expected to rise to US$2 billion by December from the current US$1 billion, people familiar with the matter have said. The company achieved US$300 million of ARR in June, Bloomberg News reported earlier. The Beijing-based AI lab previously added Bank of America as overall coordinator for the transaction alongside sponsor banks China International Capital, Deutsche Bank and Goldman Sachs Group, people familiar with the matter said previously. The company has filed confidentially for the IPO , they said. Founded in early 2023 by Yang Zhilin, a former Tsinghua University professor who previously worked at Meta Platforms and Alphabet’s Google, Moonshot counts Alibaba Group Holding, Tencent Holdings and 5Y Capital as its backers. events.title: Oprah-backed True Food Kitchen files for bankruptcy after expansion
events.summary: Oprah Winfrey had decided to invest in True Food Kitchen and joined the board after dining in its Palo Alto, California, location. True Food Kitchen, backed by Oprah Winfrey, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy due to management turnover, Covid-19 impacts, and a cyclospora outbreak, closing a dozen locations. The chain plans to recapitalise or sell, has secured a US$20 million bankruptcy loan, and ended its ghost kitchen delivery strategy. Founded in 2008 with a wellness focus, remaining locations continue serving health-conscious food with natural ingredients amid restructuring efforts. True Food Kitchen, a health food focused restaurant chain that counts American media mogul Oprah Winfrey among its investors, has filed for bankruptcy after struggling with management turnover and lingering effects of the Covid-19 pandemic. The company said in court papers that it had closed a dozen locations after filing for Chapter 11 protection on Oct 4 and will seek to either recapitalise or sell the business. The chain said it grappled with “significant management turnover, which resulted in frequent changes to expansion strategy, brand direction and menu offering”. The chain has sought permission to end leases in Miami, New Jersey, Southern California, Columbus, Ohio, New Orleans, Chicago, Bethesda, Maryland, Reston, Virginia, Scottsdale, Arizona and Long Island, New York. True Food Kitchen’s advisers have already entered into separate transactions for certain unexpired leases, chief restructuring officer Nathan Cook said in a court filing on Oct 5. Winfrey decided to invest in the restaurant and joined the board after dining in its Palo Alto, California, location, former True Food Kitchen chief executive Christine Barone said in a 2018 interview with Bloomberg. Barone now leads the Dutch Bros Coffee chain; Jeff Chandler was appointed CEO of True Food Kitchen in July. In 2022, True Food Kitchen announced a US$100 million (S$127.9 million) investment round led by new investors HumanCo and Manna Tree and support from Centerbridge Partners. A True Food Kitchen spokeswoman said on Oct 5 that Winfrey remains a minority investor and that Centerbridge is no longer a shareholder in the company. Like most restaurants, Covid-19 era lockdowns significantly impacted True Food Kitchen at a time it was expanding. To offset the loss of in-person dining, the chain used some of its locations as “ghost kitchens” and opened one off-site kitchen for delivery service, only, Cook said in the filing. The strategy, which has since ended, impaired staffing and the dining experience at its restaurants, he said. A True Food Kitchen lawyer told a bankruptcy judge on Oct 5 that the cyclospora outbreak in July “also didn’t help”. True Food Kitchen has lined-up a US$20 million Chapter 11 loan to help fund operations during the bankruptcy. The financing is being provided by an affiliate of HumanCo. The brand was founded in 2008 by wellness author Andrew Weil, who has appeared on Oprah’s talk-show, and restaurateur Sam Fox. True Food Kitchen’s remaining locations are open and serve items that are cooked without seed oil, grass-fed beef, pasture-raised eggs and antibiotic-free chicken, according to court papers. events.title: Secessionist party wins Quebec election in Canada
events.summary: Parti Quebecois returns to power, promising a third referendum on Quebec’s independence from Canada. The secessionist Parti Quebecois has won the most seats in Quebec’s election and will form the next government in the predominantly French-speaking Canadian province, according to media reports. The result on Monday revives the question of whether the province should leave Canada, testing Prime Minister Mark Carney’s message of national unity. list 1 of 2 US coastguard suspends search for six on board crashed medical jet list 2 of 2 Trump defiant about midterm chances as he rallies for Republicans in Ohio Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, the party’s leader, is set to become premier. During the campaign, he promised a third referendum on leaving Canada during his first term, although he said he would wait until US President Donald Trump leaves office in January 2029. It was not yet clear whether the party had reached the 64 seats needed for a majority in the 127-seat National Assembly. If it falls short, it would lead a minority government and need support from opposition lawmakers to pass major legislation and survive confidence votes. The Parti Quebecois, or PQ, last governed the province from 2012 to 2014. Monday’s victory marks a sharp recovery for the PQ, which won just three seats in the 2022 provincial election. Its return also ends eight years in power for the Coalition Avenir Quebec, or CAQ, a centre-right Quebec nationalist party that does not support independence. Daniel Beland, a political science professor at McGill University in Montreal, told The Associated Press news agency that the victory reflects Quebec’s multiparty system, where support is divided among several parties, rather than a surge in secessionist sentiment. Support for independence remains at about 30 percent, low by historical standards, he said. Still, Beland said a secessionist government in Quebec represents a new national-unity challenge for Carney, particularly with another independence-related vote approaching in Alberta. “Seeing that a pro-independence party won in Quebec barely two weeks before an independence-related referendum takes place in Alberta might suggest to the Trump administration that national unity remains a major issue in Canada despite the popularity of Mark Carney,” Beland said. Quebec held two previous referendums on independence, in 1980 and 1995, and voters rejected secession both times. The second vote was decided by a narrow margin, but there has been no further referendum in the three decades since.

events.title: 'Can I be in the UAE after overstaying my visit visa?'
events.summary: Question : Can a telecoms company impose a travel ban over an unpaid bill? I owe a telecoms company money and haven't paid it for months. I have been sent a message saying that I owe Dh2,930 and that my account is now 190 days overdue. It also said: “We hereby inform you that legal proceedings may be initiated to recover the outstanding amount.” The message was from a credit management company. Can they make a case against me and put a travel ban on me for this? Is there any other action they can take? JC, Abu Dhabi Answer : For an unpaid telecom debt of Dh2,930, a full court case is unlikely, but JC can still face consequences. The account has probably already been cut off, and the company will follow up as he owes it money. Companies can pursue debts in court but, for in this case litigation costs would be disproportionate relative to the amount owed. A travel ban will not happen. Under Article 324 of the UAE Civil Procedure Law (Federal Decree Law No 42 of 2022), a creditor – a person or company that is owed money – can only apply for a travel ban against a debtor if the debt is Dh10,000 or more. Below that threshold, a civil travel ban cannot be issued, regardless of the risk of a person leaving the country without settling their debts. It is common for UAE companies to hand over small debts to collection agencies. That will lead to regular telephone calls, emails and even WhatsApp messages. These companies are licensed and regulated, and there are rules that they must follow. The agency must not overstep by making repeated calls designed to intimidate rather than to communicate, as that constitutes harassment under UAE law. They are only allowed to make contact between 9am and 8pm, and must not disclose information to any third party. That includes calling a place of work and telling anyone the call is about a debt. If the collection agency breaks these guidelines, a complaint can be made, first to the telecoms company, but if that doesn’t stop it, then to the Central Bank of the UAE. JC needs to start making repayments in order to stop follow-up calls and messages. Non-payment of any debt will affect a person’s UAE credit record . This will affect a person's ability to borrow and open financial accounts. Since the change in legislation this year, landlords can now ask for confirmation of a credit score, which can also affect a person's ability to rent a home. Q : I have overstayed my visit visa after my employer failed to arrange a work permit. What can I do? I have a question about overstaying a visit visa. I came to work for a company, and although the team promised me a visa, it never happened. I don’t have a contract, and they have now said they do not want me to work for them any more. What can I do about this? I want to find another job and stay in the UAE. Will I get in trouble or have to pay a fine? MP, Dubai A : The important point here is that MP has been working illegally since arriving in the UAE. From the outset, the employer should have given MP a proper offer of employment and a labour contract, and applied for a residence visa and a work permit. As this did not happen, the company has been employing MP illegally, so she has been working illegally. Sadly, this means that she has no protection under UAE law. This means that MP is unable to make a legal complaint against the company, even if it has broken the law. No doubt the employer will know that this is not permitted, but the company can be reported for breaking the law. Any company that takes on staff without a visa can be fined up to Dh50,000 and may have difficulty obtaining visas in the future. As MP has been in the UAE without a valid visa, MP will have overstay fines. Since February 2026, the UAE has unified overstay fines across all visa types and emirates. They are now the same for all visas, whether tourist, visit or residence visas, and there is no variation by emirate. The fine is Dh50 per day. If an overstay exceeds 30 days, an additional exit permit, known as an “outpass”, at a cost of Dh250 to Dh300, including base and service fees, is required before leaving the country. It is possible to pay the overstay fines and stay in the UAE without leaving the country, provided a new employer initiates the visa process immediately. If not, MP will need to leave and return on an employment entry permit from a new employer. MP should visit an Amer centre, a division of the General Directorate of Residency and Foreigners Affairs, for advice and to find out how much MP owes. Once the overstay fine has been settled, MP can find a new job and be employed with a visa in order to stay legally in the UAE. events.title: UN rights council condemns attacks on civilians in Sudan, calls for truce
events.summary: Resolution demands an immediate ceasefire and extends the mandate of the mission investigating abuses in Sudan. Sudan's army advances in North Kordofan as RSF drone attacks intensify The United Nations Human Rights Council has condemned drone strikes and other attacks on civilians in Sudan, warning warring parties that there is “no military solution to the crisis” in the country. The statement on Monday came as the World Food Programme said an air attack had hit a truck carrying food supplies in North Kordofan, killing one person. list 1 of 3 Is the Sudanese army gaining momentum against the RSF? list 2 of 3 Air strike in Sudan kills UN aid truck driver: WFP list 3 of 3 Four African leaders issue joint declaration as Ethiopia war escalates In Geneva, the 47-member council adopted a resolution extending the mandate of its independent international fact-finding mission for Sudan by a vote of 28 to 10, with nine abstentions. Sudan urged member states to reject the measure, stating the council had failed to take its reservations into account. The war between Sudan’s army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, which began in April 2023, has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced more than 13 million, according to estimates cited by human rights groups. The resolution demanded “an immediate and complete ceasefire by all parties, without preconditions”, along with an independent monitoring mechanism and the restoration of basic infrastructure. It condemned widespread violations of international humanitarian law by both the Sudanese Armed Forces and the RSF, citing “indiscriminate attacks against civilians” and “indiscriminate aerial bombardments and drone strikes resulting in civilian deaths and the destruction of critical infrastructure”, including schools and hospitals. Both sides have sharply increased their use of drones in recent months. UN figures show that drone strikes killed more than 1,100 people in the first five months of the year alone. The council also condemned outside interference in the war, warning that illicit financial networks, illegal arms transfers and foreign mercenaries continue to fuel the fighting. The fact-finding mission, which gathers evidence of abuses by both sides, concluded in February that the RSF’s siege and capture of the North Darfur capital, el-Fasher, bore “the hallmarks of genocide”. As the last military stronghold in Darfur to fall after a months-long siege, el-Fasher saw civilians systematically deprived of food and medicine before facing mass summary executions, investigators found. They documented ethnic killings aimed mainly at non-Arab groups, widespread sexual violence and the destruction of medical facilities. Separately, the WFP said in a statement that the airstrike that hit its convoy travelling between Dilling and Kadugli in South Kordofan killed one driver and damaging life-saving food. The agency stressed that the vehicles were clearly marked with official humanitarian logos. The attack took place on Saturday and came just 24 hours after another WFP vehicle detonated an explosive device in Dilling following a food distribution run, it said. “Humanitarian workers and aid assets are not targets,” the WFP said, demanding a transparent probe to hold perpetrators accountable under international law.

events.title: Little room for ‘giving and taking’: India’s finance minister confirms trade impasse with the U.S.
events.summary: Indian finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman on Monday said trade talks with the U.S. had plateaued. After months of negotiations, there has been growing skepticism recently around the finalization of the U.S- India trade deal. Sitharaman questioned the extent to which negotiations can continue if reducing the trade imbalance is the ‘sole criteria.’ The trade balance between the two countries favors New Delhi, and Washington is keen to change that by selling more to India. India's Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said trade talks with the U.S. had reached a plateau, adding to growing skepticism around a deal between New Delhi and Washington. "Negotiations are still ongoing, although we'd like to believe that both sides have reached a plateau beyond which giving or taking might be very very difficult," Sitharaman said, speaking to the press at the Munich Leaders Meeting in New Delhi on Monday. The finance minister's comments come just after U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer last week said a trade agreement was not 'imminent' even as the negotiations were ongoing. Sitharaman's comments mark the first time India has acknowledged the challenges it faces in closing the trade deal with the U.S. She said the U.S. wants to "reduce" its trade imbalance with India, and they want to make up "for all that they've lost over these years." "When you're talking of trade and trade imbalance being the sole criteria to reduce the imbalance, to what extent beyond negotiation can you go," Sitharaman said. The U.S. goods trade deficit with India was $58.42 billion in 2025, a 27.8% increase ($12.7 billion) over 2024. In the first seven months of 2026, this figure was $28.4 billion , as per U.S. data. Last week, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi had reviewed bilateral trade, defense, energy and critical technologies during a call with U.S. President Donald Trump. While Greer said the call was "constructive," and Modi called it "productive," Trump did not comment on it. Trump in February announced an interim trade deal with India, outlining that New Delhi had agreed to " BUY AMERICAN " at "a much higher level." India, meanwhile, has been seeking preferential tariffs from the U.S. that make its exports to Washington more competitive. "Both countries stand to lose if no deal is finalized," Mark Linscott, former assistant U.S. trade representative and senior advisor at the U.S.-India Strategic Partnership Forum, told CNBC. "US exports currently face higher tariffs in the Indian market," he said, adding that if India did not strike a deal soon, "it could face much higher tariffs than other countries, and that could be a real problem given that the U.S. market is critical for India." Currently, Indian exports to the U.S. face a 10% tariff , following the conclusion of USTR's investigation into the acts, policies and practices of forced labor in 60 countries. As per the Indian government, a substantial share of the country's exports to the U.S., such as generic pharmaceuticals and smartphones, remain outside the scope of the 10% duty.

events.title: Pentagon says Trump approves Army firing squad execution of Fort Hood killer Nidal Hasan
events.summary: The Pentagon said President Donald Trump has approved a recommendation by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to have convicted Fort Hood mass killer Nidal Hasan executed by a U.S. Army firing squad. Hasan, 56, would be the first person executed after a U.S. armed forces court-martial since 1961, when Army Pvt. John Bennett was hanged at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas, for the rape and attempted murder of a girl in Austria. Hasan, a psychiatrist, was convicted and sentenced to death after a 2013 court-martial for the Nov. 5, 2009, shooting spree that killed 13 and injured 32 others at the Army base in Killeen, Texas, while he was an Army major. The Pentagon on Monday evening said that President Donald Trump has approved a recommendation by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to have convicted Fort Hood mass killer Nidal Hasan executed by a U.S. Army firing squad. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment from CNBC. During his court-martial, Hasan told a judge that he was motivated in the shooting to defend the "leadership of the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan, the Taliban." Hegseth in September 2025 said that he had asked Trump to approve Hasan's execution. Federal law says that a person convicted through court-martial and sentenced to death cannot be executed until approved by the president. "Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has recommended — and President Donald J. Trump has approved — death by U.S. Army firing squad for convicted terrorist Nidal Malik Hasan, the jihadist who opened fire on unarmed American soldiers at Fort Hood in 2009," Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in a post on X on Monday. "He killed 13 people and wounded 32 others while shouting 'Allahu Akbar' during the attack," Parnell said. The spokesman also said the secretary of the Army "will set the time and place of the execution." "Judgement day for Hasan has finally come," Parnell wrote. Hegseth retweeted Parnell's post, writing "Justice." Russian lab worker dies amid plague reports — here's what we know Trump's nemesis in Europe: Why Spain's Sanchez is calling a snap election Trump tells South Korea to sign on to Alaska LNG deal or 'I'll just charge them more' Supreme Court Justice Alito said he's 'thought about' retirement as Senate control hangs in balance Trump taps Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton as AI czar The Supreme Court on March 31, 2025, denied a petition by Hasan to hear an appeal of his conviction, clearing the way for him to be executed. In September 2025, Hegseth told The Hill in a statement, "I am 100 percent committed to ensuring the death penalty is carried out for Nidal Hasan." "This savage terrorist deserves the harshest lawful punishment for his 2009 mass shooting at Fort Hood," Hegseth said at that time. "The victims and survivors deserve justice without delays." events.title: Ukraine claims to have taken out more than half of Russia's oil refining capacity
events.summary: Ukraine said long-range strikes have put more than half of Russia’s oil refining capacity out of action KYIV, Ukraine -- Ukraine says its long-range strikes have neutralized more than half of Russia's oil refining capacity, hampering Moscow's ability to supply its forces during its 4 1/2-year-old invasion. The Defense Ministry said late Sunday that recent strikes on refineries in cities, including Moscow, Yaroslavl, Ust-Luga, Perm, Saratov and Syzran, had disabled 51% of Russia’s oil refining capacity. The claim could not be independently verified. Moscow and Kyiv have intensified their aerial assaults as progress along the 1,200-kilometer (750-mile) front line has largely ground to a halt. Ukraine has launched repeated attacks on refineries from Moscow to Siberia, sparking a widespread fuel crisis in Russia earlier this year that forced authorities to restrict gasoline sales. Russian officials have not released figures on damage to the country’s oil infrastructure. But in a rare acknowledgment of the strikes’ economic impact, President Vladimir Putin said on Oct. 1 that they had cost Russia roughly 1% of its gross domestic product. “They started attacking oil refineries and openly declared the goal of damaging our economy. Did they achieve their goal? Partially,” Putin told a meeting of the Valdai Club forum of international foreign policy experts. Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara said analysts from Ukraine’s intelligence services, the General Staff and the Defense Ministry had assessed the strikes' effects. “Fifty-one percent of struck refining capacity is a significant blow to the enemy’s economy, to its ability to carry out aggression and supply its troop groupings. Our deep strikes continue to bring the war to Russian territory,” he said. Russia has historically been the world’s third-largest producer of refined fuel products from crude, after the U.S. and China. Some of Russia’s 32 refineries have been hit as many as 15 times since the start of the war, and one refinery has been hit every three days in recent months, creating a cycle of damage and emergency repairs that could degrade units long term, according to the International Energy Agency. Ukrainian strikes have also increasingly targeted the more complex equipment that removes impurities from fuel, which takes months to repair. The IEA says diesel output has fallen by about 30%, and drivers have had to wait up to 40 hours to fill up at gasoline stations. Russian refiners have tried to compensate by delaying scheduled maintenance and bringing mothballed units back online. Another response has been to lower fuel quality standards to maintain gasoline supplies, which risks damage to engines and pollution control equipment. The Kremlin has also banned diesel exports, pushing global prices higher and prompting U.S. President Donald Trump on Sept. 13 to urge Ukraine to stop hitting refineries. A Russian attack with a guided aerial bomb killed at least three people and wounded 39 others, including three children, in the Ukrainian city of Kharkiv on Monday, Mayor Ihor Terekhov said. “There may be people under the rubble of the residential building that was hit. A search and rescue operation is underway,” Terekhov wrote on his Telegram channel. An earlier Russian drone attack on the city's Industrialnyi district also killed one person, Terekhov said late Sunday. Vehicles and an administrative building were set alight and apartment buildings were damaged, he said. Another person was also killed in a separate Russian attack on the Sloviansk community in Ukraine’s Donetsk region, said Vadym Liakh, head of the Sloviansk city military administration. He urged residents not to wait for a mandatory evacuation order but to leave the area. Russia’s Defense Ministry said in a statement on Monday that it had struck an electrical substation in the Kharkiv region, in addition to energy and port infrastructure and maritime vessels used by Ukraine's military elsewhere in the country. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a Russian drone attack caused a fire on board a commercial vessel that later sank in the Black Sea . Two people died and 11 crew members were rescued, Romanian authorities said. In a post on X on Monday, Zelenskyy described the attack as “a horrific strike by two Russian drones on a civilian vessel” in neutral waters. He said the vessel was Turkish-owned and carrying corn. events.title: Asian shares track Wall Street higher, Treasury yields near multi-decade highs
events.summary: MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan rose 0.2%, while Japan’s Nikkei gained 0.7%. European stock futures climbed 0.5%. SYDNEY – Asian stocks rose on Oct 6 after a tech-fuelled rally lifted the Nasdaq to a record close , with a retreat in oil prices offering further support even as longer-dated Treasury yields hovered near multi-decade highs. The euro languished near 17-month lows after briefly touching US$1.116 overnight, pressured by mounting fiscal concerns in France. Investors dumped French government bonds after an underwhelming budget, while political uncertainty deepened after Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez called a snap election . Brent crude was little changed at US$100 a barrel after losing 1.9% overnight as exports from the Middle East increased and the Group of Seven nations pledged to boost supplies. Nasdaq futures edged up 0.2% and S&P 500 futures rose 0.1%. The Nasdaq notched up a record close overnight, buoyed by softer-than-expected jobs data that dampened expectations for a rate hike from the Federal Reserve in October. Artificial intelligence heavyweight Nvidia climbed 2.1%, reaching a record-high close and boosting its market value to $5.76 trillion. “The rally in the market was tech-led once again, with the marginal easing of interest rate uncertainty along with a slight moderation in geopolitical risk allowing market participants to focus on the extraordinary earnings growth being delivered by AI names,” said Kyle Rodda, a senior analyst at Capital.com. The third-quarter earnings season kicks off next week. Goldman Sachs estimated consensus forecasts point to 27% growth in S&P 500 earnings last quarter, with more than half that growth from companies benefiting from AI infrastructure spending. Latin American markets also climbed, led by a rally in Brazilian stocks and the real currency, after right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro outperformed poll predictions in the first round of the presidential election and advanced to a run-off against leftist incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva. The relentless climb in Treasury yields continued even as markets scaled back bets for an interest rate rise in October from the Federal Reserve to just 23% from 71% a week ago, after top policymakers stressed the need for more data before tightening again. US 10- and 30-year Treasury yields hit fresh 24-year highs overnight, capping a steady climb since mid-August driven by inflation and debt concerns. An ISM survey showed a measure of prices paid by services businesses for inputs jumped to the highest level in more than four years. The 10-year Treasury yield was steady in Asia at 5.3089%, after climbing 3 basis points overnight to hit 5.3493%, the highest since 2002, while 30-year yields held at 5.6622%, having briefly reached 5.7029% overnight. The sell-off in French bonds calmed a little, with the premium investors demand to hold French 10-year bonds over safer German debt narrowing to 137 basis points on Oct 5. The euro nursed losses at US$1.1215, after falling as much as 0.8% to US$1.116 overnight, its weakest since May 2025. It traded at 177 yen, having been down for seven straight sessions, around the lowest since November 2025. “Deep divisions in France’s parliament raises the risk that the proposed fiscal consolidation is diluted or that the government faces a no-confidence vote,” said Joseph Capurso, head of international economics at the Commonwealth Bank of Australia. “EUR/USD will likely test support at 1.1109.” That kept the US dollar firm, with the US dollar index at 102.2 after a weekly rise of 0.9%. Spot gold was little changed at US$4,141.31 an ounce. REUTERS

That nasty news came from security researcher Paulos Yibelo, who on X shared a screenshot of a bug bounty award he won for discovering what he described as “Full VM escape zeroday (guest>host root in industry standard hypervisors)!” The bug bounty Yibelo participated in is run by Vercel, a company that provides MicroVMs as sandboxes for AI agents to work inside. The company’s Sandbox uses Firecracker MicroVMs, a technology created by AWS , which relies on Linux KVM – the kernel level hypervisor in Linux. Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch named KVM as the hypervisor identified by Yibelo. “We’ve confirmed a KVM 0day through our Vercel Sandbox bounty program. Affecting the industry’s gold standard solution for Linux virtualization,” he wrote. And that’s all the info that has made it into the public view at this time. The Register can find no chat on relevant mailing lists. We have asked Rauch and Yibelo for additional details. Hopefully, we don’t hear from either of them for days or weeks, for two reasons. One is that guest-host escapes are the nightmare virtualization scenario because they mean whoever runs a guest VM could take over an entire server, and perhaps gain the ability to control other guests. The other is that KVM is astoundingly prevalent: AWS and Google both use it to power their public clouds. Enterprise virtualization players Nutanix, HPE, and Proxmox also rely on KVM. And of course KVM is also in Firecracker, which is open source and could therefore be running in all sorts of places. Whatever Yibelo discovered therefore very much needs a responsible disclosure process, because if hints about the flaw emerge it could allow attackers to do a lot of damage. Once a fix is found, the next question is whether implementing it will require disruption or downtime. It’s possible to hot-patch KVM, and to migrate live VMs from vulnerable hosts to machines running a patched version of Linux. Hopefully those techniques will work. This might be the second nasty bug discovered in KVM this year, after the so-called Januscape flaw. Beyond the potential risks this bug created, observers have suggested the potential seriousness of the flaw means Yibelo’s reward should exceed the $50,000 available under Vercel’s bug bounty program. ® Only the finest Swedish Bork will do for Stockholm station No, this is not GRUB of the meatball variety OpenAI rolls out weak sauce watermarking for AI text The VMware exit is a protection upgrade PARTNER CONTENT: VergeIO says an exit is also an opportunity Scientists find planet made on new matter recipe, and it formed after a Red Giant ate a solar system Death of a star may not be game over for the inner solar system after all Brighter isn't better and more is less.

events.title: Trump says MAGA Inc. PAC will pay for controversial TV ads that government funded
events.summary: President Donald Trump said he and his political action committee will pay for controversial television ads that praised him and had been funded by the U.S. government. The White House later clarified that the super PAC — MAGA Inc. — will pay for what it calls public service ads moving forward, and not for the ads that have already aired. Trump's announcement came after continued backlash to the ads, which had run in the weeks leading up to November's midterm elections. Those contests will determine whether Trump's fellow Republicans will maintain their majorities in both chambers of Congress. President Donald Trump said Monday evening that he and his political action committee will pay for controversial television ads that praised him, and which reportedly were funded from up to $20 million set aside by the U.S. Department of Homeland Security . Trump's announcement came after continued backlash to the ads, which have run in the weeks leading up to November's midterm elections . Critics say the ads mirror Republican campaign talking points. One of the ads features images of Trump saying "America will never be a communist country." "The Radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking Ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A., and paying for them with U.S.A. money," Trump said in a post on Truth Social on Monday. "This is a rather standard thing to do but, rather than doing that, although nothing will make them happy, I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc.," Trump said. AdImpact has tracked roughly $9.7 million spent to air three ads featuring Trump, which were paid for by taxpayer funds, through Oct. 5. Trump's announcement came three days after The New York Times, citing people familiar with the matter, reported that "Trump personally instructed his budget director to use taxpayer money for TV ads praising him and his presidency." Russian lab worker dies amid plague reports — here's what we know Trump's nemesis in Europe: Why Spain's Sanchez is calling a snap election Trump tells South Korea to sign on to Alaska LNG deal or 'I'll just charge them more' Supreme Court Justice Alito said he's 'thought about' retirement as Senate control hangs in balance Trump taps Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton as AI czar The Times said that federal money to pay for the ads became available on Sept. 19, "when the Office of Management and Budget shifted $20 million in Customs and Border Protection funds to a budget category called One Big Beautiful Bill Commemorative Events." Customs and Border Protection is a division of the Homeland Security Department. Sen. Maggie Hassan , D-N.H., in a Sept. 24 letter to White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, wrote, "The advertisement does not have a clear official government purpose and appears to run afoul of federal prohibitions against the use of appropriated funds as part of 'a general propaganda effort designed to aid a political party or candidates.'" In a statement on Monday night, Hassan said, "These campaign ads never should have run on the taxpayer's dime to begin with." "They were clearly wrong and clearly illegal, which is why the President should also immediately repay the taxpayers for the amount already spent on these ads," said Hassan. "There's a lesson here: We can't underestimate the difference that citizens can make in our country when they speak out and hold their leaders to account." Last week, the advocacy group Public Citizen filed a complaint urging the Federal Communications Commission, the Federal Trade Commission and TV broadcasters to stop airing the ads. Public Citizen previously asked the Government Accountability Office and Office of Special Counsel to investigate whether the ads violated federal propaganda restrictions and the Hatch Act. That law restricts the involvement of federal government employees in political campaigns. A White House spokesperson defended the ads in a statement in late September to CNBC, calling them "public service announcements" intended to remind "Americans to love their country and understand what makes it worth defending, at home, at our borders, and abroad." "The ad is educational and unapologetically patriotic. We should be proud of our country," the spokesperson said. MAGA Inc. has raised $424.4 million and spent $32.4 million during the 2025-26 cycle through Aug. 31, leaving the Trump Super PAC with $415.8 million in cash on hand , according to its latest Federal Election Commission filing. MAGA Inc. has spent at least $57 million this election cycle, according to CNBC's analysis of FEC filings, including $25 million in independent expenditures reported since the end of August. — CNBC's Luke Fountain contributed to this article

events.title: Trump offers U.S. help to Russia after plague death; WHO assesses the situation as low risk
events.summary: Trump said the U.S. would help Russia, calling the illness a “rough disease.” WHO said the cause of death has not been confirmed and assessed the risk to the general public as low. "We encourage Russian authorities to share accurate information quickly and openly," State Department spokesperson. U.S. President Donald Trump has offered to help Russia after a laboratory worker died following an illness at a plague research institute in Siberia, while the Russian authorities said the situation was under control. "We'll help," Trump told reporters at the White House on Monday when asked about the case. "Everybody who has that kind of a problem, we'll always help," according to a Reuters transcript. A laboratory worker at an anti-plague research institute in the Irkutsk region of eastern Siberia fell ill and died in undisclosed circumstances, reportedly prompting authorities to quarantine nearly 200 people and fueling public health concerns. Trump said he had not spoken to Russian officials about the case, but described the plague as a "rough disease." "That's a disease we used to be able to control," Trump said, adding that "somehow those microbes have gotten stronger and stronger, they're like an army." "We are monitoring the situation closely with the CDC and our other interagency partners. Many details have not been confirmed. We encourage Russian authorities to share accurate information quickly and openly," a state department spokesperson who did not wish to be identified told CNBC. Trump said the U.S. would do what it could to help Russia. He has previously said he considers Russian President Vladimir Putin someone he can work with, despite tensions over Moscow's war in Ukraine. The World Health Organization in an email response said the cause of death had not been confirmed and testing was underway. It said it was in contact with Russian authorities, and has offered support if needed, while assessing the risk to the general public as low based on available information. It remains unclear whether Moscow has sought or would accept any assistance.

events.title: Exclusive: OpenAI is piloting a ‘mission interview’ for job candidates
events.summary: Candidates interviewing for certain teams at OpenAI will now go through a new step in the process, knowing as the “mission interview.” The company is currently introducing it as a new pilot program, starting with the marketing and human resources teams, OpenAI told Fortune on Monday. The goal is to give job candidates a dedicated space to talk about how they will contribute to OpenAI’s mission, which is “to ensure that artificial general intelligence (AGI) benefits all of humanity.” Specifically, OpenAI wants to gauge how candidates think, including their judgment and ability to weigh trade-offs—traits that are increasingly critical as artificial intelligence companies work to control technology with great benefits as well as potential dangers. There is no “right” answer, an OpenAI representative said; skepticism and disagreement are welcome, as is intellectual diversity. The person conducting the interview will be from a separate team from whatever role the candidate is applying for. OpenAI is also creating a training program that interested employees can complete to become certified to conduct the interviews, though the program is just starting to ramp up. The evolution in OpenAI’s recruiting process is a marker of the company looking to standardize its evaluations as it matures and balloons in size. The company, which has roughly 8,000 employees worldwide, has 830 open roles as of this writing. By standardizing the process, OpenAI aims to have a consistent measure to evaluate new employees across teams. Many tech companies, including Meta and Amazon , have their own version of a “mission interview,” which is somewhat akin to a test of cultural fit. For example, Amazon employees can be trained as “bar raisers”—interviewers from outside the hiring team, who assess whether a candidate meets Amazon’s company-wide “Leadership Principals.” In Anthropic’s version, interviewers reportedly test if candidates are joining the AI lab for its mission or the money, according to Axios. Jobs at leading AI companies are incredibly lucrative, with many positions at OpenAI currently offering over $300K salaries, and much more with stock included. One software engineer with six years of experience reportedly received an offer from OpenAI for $935,000 total compensation, with a $385,000 base, and $2.2 million of restricted stock shares (RSUs) vesting over four years, according to the anonymous professional network Blind. Anthropic allegedly offered another person $620,000 in total compensation, according to another Blind post. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Singapore’s DayOne files for US IPO joining data centre rush
events.summary: DayOne Data Centers is part of a wave of firms in the sector eyeing IPOs as soon as 2026. DayOne Data Centers, headquartered in Singapore, filed for a US IPO to capitalise on strong demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure, aiming to raise up to US$5 billion with a US$20 billion valuation. The company reported a net loss of US$81.9 million on US$512 million revenue for the six months ended June 30, expanding rapidly across Asia Pacific and Europe with over 1.5 gigawatts booked since 2022. Backed by major investors like Coatue Management, Hillhouse, SoftBank Vision Fund, and Citadel, DayOne operates in multiple countries and plans to list on Nasdaq under the symbol DODC, amid a wider data centre IPO wave. NEW YORK – DayOne Data Centers filed for a US initial public offering, setting the Singapore-headquartered firm up to capture investors’ resilient demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure. The data centre operator had a net loss of US$81.9 million (S$104.8 million) o n revenue of US$512 million for the six months ended June 30, compared with a net loss of US$13.5 million on revenue of US$151.5 million in the corresponding period a year earlier, according to its filing on Oct 5 with the US Securities and Exchange Commission. Once an international affiliate of Chinese data centre operator GDS Holdings, DayOne was known as GDS International before rebranding in 2025. The company filed confidentially in August for a US IPO that may seek to raise as much as US$5 billion at a valuation of about US$20 billion, Bloomberg News has reported. The data centre operator is part of a wave of firms in the sector eyeing IPOs as soon as 2026. Others include Switch, which is seeking a valuation approaching US$50 billion including debt, and London-based Nscale, which could raise as much as US$3 billion, people familiar with the matter have said. DayOne closed a US$4.5 billion Series C funding round in June, led by its biggest shareholders, Coatue Management and Hillhouse, and also including new backers Achi Capital Partners and the Indonesian Investment Authority. Since its inception in 2022, DayOne has secured more than 1.5GW of bookings for capacity in Asia-Pacific and Europe. Along with GDS, which remains an investor, its backers also include SoftBank Vision Fund and Citadel’s Ken Griffin. DayOne is running or developing data centres in Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, Hong Kong, Japan, Finland and Spain, its filing shows. The offering is being led by Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan Chase & Co, Bank of America and Citigroup. The company expects its American depositary receipts to trade on the Nasdaq Stock Market under the symbol DODC. BLOOMBERG

events.title: Nvidia backs startup Reactor as buzz grows for world models
events.summary: World models are capturing the tech industry’s attention and investment dollars, amid growing expectations that AI will soon move beyond our screens and into the physical world of cars, robots, and other objects. A slew of new startups are developing world models, which are typically based on video data rather than the text-based large language models like OpenAI’s GPT and Anthropic’s Claude. In just the last week, AMD announced plans to acquire World Labs for $8.2 billion in stock and video AI startup Runway unveiled the first open-weight version of its world model. And just as generative AI helped bring about a broader industry to train and run LLMs, the rising popularity of world models is spurring new innovation and startups. On Monday, San Francisco-based Reactor said that it added Nvidia’s venture capital arm and Sapphire Ventures to its cap table, adding to a Series A round announced in May and bringing its total funding to $74 million.  Reactor, which emerged from stealth in May, develops software to make world models run faster and cheaper, and sells a cloud service that manages the computing capacity.  “Once the model exists, how do you actually run it?” co-founder and CEO Alberto Taiuti told Fortune , describing the question that led him and co-founder Bryce Schmidtchen to start Reactor. Both previously worked on Apple’s Vision Pro. Taiuti also co-founded the AI video generator startup Luma AI, where he served as chief technology officer. Reactor says Hollywood studios, advertising platforms and streaming services have active projects on the platform. But the company sees robots as a major area of focus.  Building conventional simulations for robot testing can be time-consuming and costly, Taiuti said, requiring developers to create three-dimensional objects and configure scenes. He said world models could reduce some of that work by generating environments from prompts. Reactor says it can run world models that respond to robot actions, allowing developers to test their software in those generated environments. Running the models in the cloud can give developers access to more computing power without adding that hardware to each robot. It also lets them upgrade the computers running the models without replacing hardware across a fleet, he said. Taiuti said the company can adapt technology developed for interactive media to robotics because “similar models and similar workloads can also be run on the same core engine”. Reactor plans to use the investment to secure more computing capacity, expand its team and buy robot hardware to test its systems, Taiuti said. Nvidia, which invested in Reactor via its NVentures VC arm, has developed its own Cosmos world models, alongside Isaac tools for robot simulation and Jetson computers that run AI on robots. Its investment in Reactor gives it a stake in infrastructure for running interactive models. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Elon Musk is a trillionaire again
events.summary: Elon Musk is once again a trillionaire, a title he first held briefly in June after the SpaceX IPO. Finn Gomez/Getty Images Elon Musk has regained his trillionaire status thanks to a boost in SpaceX's stock price. Musk became the world's first trillionaire after the SpaceX IPO, but the stock price later fell. The stock price has rebounded, along with Musk's net worth. Elon Musk has regained his title as the world's only trillionaire. The Tesla CEO made history earlier this year by becoming the first person worth 13 figures after SpaceX's blockbuster initial public offering in June. Musk's wealth came back down a little closer to Earth after SpaceX's stock price fell following an initial surge. The rocket and AI company's stock price has been creeping back up since early August, reaching $171.09 as of Monday's market close. The nearly 8% boost on Monday brought Musk's net worth back over the trillion-dollar threshold, according to Forbes, which estimated his wealth at $1.046 trillion. Musk's wealth previously peaked on June 16 at $1.32 trillion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. While Musk had long been counted among the richest people in the world, the SpaceX IPO put him in another stratosphere. The second- and third-wealthiest people in the world as of Monday were Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and Google cofounder Larry Page, worth $371 billion and $284 billion, respectively, according to Forbes. Much of Musk's net worth comes from stakes in SpaceX and Tesla, so it is typically tied to the success of those companies. SpaceX's stock reached its highest level since June on Monday. events.title: S’pore beauty salons bank on value-adds, convenience as RTS spells more competition from JB
events.summary: Crystal Lee, CEO of Peachy Skin Bar, recently renovated the salon with pink walls and an open lounge area where customers can enjoy a free drink. SINGAPORE – Lower prices have long drawn Singapore customers to beauty salons across the Causeway, and this is only set to increase when the Johor Bahru–Singapore RTS Link opens in 2027 . With the journey between Woodlands North and Bukit Chagar taking just minutes, the new service could lead to Singapore consumers making 51% more round trips to JB a year, with beauty services listed as one of the top spending categories, a study released in July found. In anticipation of this, some salons here have opted to improve their in-store experience and take their services directly to clients’ homes, betting that convenience and service quality will help them retain customers. One example is Singapore facial salon Peachy Skin Bar, which offers facial treatments priced between $180 and $500. “Instead of competing purely based on price, I’m finding ways to differentiate my facial business from other competitors in Singapore and Johor Bahru,” said owner Crystal Lee. Her salon in Queen Street, founded in 2019, was recently renovated with pink walls and an open lounge area where customers can enjoy a free drink. “The lounge is so that customers won’t feel trapped in a small room. I wanted my salon to resemble a summer destination where people can come to unwind,” said Lee, adding that her business is focusing on the overall customer experience rather than just the service itself. As a value-add, she has also trained her staff to give customers a shoulder massage between stages of a facial, rather than leave them alone while waiting for the next step. She noted that even before the RTS came into the picture, competition from JB had always existed, and that building good relationships with her customers has kept them coming back to her salon despite the higher price. Asked if she would consider opening an outlet in JB, Lee said that she prefers to observe the market first. “Opening an outlet in JB would require a lot of money and logistics. I’m not a hasty person, so I prefer to focus on my Singapore outlet for now,” she said. Still, she noted that customers are now more price sensitive and unpredictable. “The RTS intensifies the convenience factor, but we can’t predict how they will behave once it opens. We can only brace ourselves,” she said. Other local beauty businesses are also upping their game by doubling down on the Singapore market. Eyelash salon Perky Lash, which has four salons in Singapore, has operated an outlet in Johor Bahru City Square mall since 2024. “Prices at our JB outlet are 20 to 30 per cent lower than our Singapore outlets,” said founder Jasmin Tay, adding that 80% its customers are Singaporeans. But rather than opening a second outlet in JB, Perky Lash plans to give its customers here less reason to make the trip across the Causeway. In April, it launched a home visit service here, where staff offer lash services in homes, offices and even hospitals. Jasmin Tay, CEO of Perky Lash, has launched a home visit service in Singapore, where staff offer eye-lash services in homes, offices and even hospitals. “Singaporean customers are very time-starved. Even by opening more outlets, our reach to customers who may not have time to travel to us is limited. With home visits, we hope to broaden our customer base,” said Tay. She added that lashes are a regular maintenance beauty service rather than a one-off service. “Customers tend to stick to the lash artists they already know and trust,” said Tay. “They value trust and consistency, rather than just the price.” Shiyun Teo, founder of Picasso Hair Studio, which opened in 2014, said that as competition from across the Causeway intensifies, businesses here must give customers compelling reasons beyond price to choose them. Shiyun Teo, founder of Picasso Hair Studio, reckons that convenience and time will play an important role in attracting customers. “We don’t have any immediate plans to open in Johor Bahru, although I wouldn’t completely rule it out in the future,” said Teo. Like Tay, she reckons that convenience and time will play an important role in attracting customers. “Our Novena outlet, for example, is surrounded by condominiums and tuition centres. We have parents who drop their children off for tuition and use that time to get their hair done,” Teo said. “For these customers, maximising their time can sometimes be more important than saving money. “Even with the RTS making JB more accessible, there is still travelling time involved, so I don’t think the decision to cross the Causeway will be purely about comparing prices.” Teo said that choosing a local hair studio gives customers the assurance that their salon and stylist are nearby should any adjustments be needed, saving them another trip across the border.

events.title: Moroccan journalists recount years of surveillance amid new Amnesty claim
events.summary: Amnesty cites a whistleblower’s account of how Morocco allegedly uses surveillance to silence journalists. Rabat, Morocco – “I was surveilled not because of a specific article. I was investigating land dispossession in Morocco. I then learned I was a Pegasus target,” Omar Radi, a journalist and human rights defender, told Al Jazeera, referring to the mobile surveillance tool developed by Israeli company NSO Group. The findings emerged in June 2020, when Amnesty International Security Lab examined his phone. Radi, now based in Germany, said he had spent two years, from 2018 to 2020, noticing signs including his phone’s battery draining quickly, its temperature rising and the network slowing down. The physical surveillance, he said, was barely discreet. “They came every day to get a daily report from the parking attendants in my street, the shops I used to go to, and my friends,” he said. “I would sometimes turn around and walk towards the people following me to take photographs, but they ran quickly and hid their faces.” His case is among four detailed in a new Amnesty International report, We Start With the Verdict: Inside Morocco’s Surveillance Machine, produced with 14 media organisations and coordinated by the international network of journalists Forbidden Stories. The other three are Fouad Abdelmoumni, a veteran activist; Abdessadak El Bouchattaoui, a human rights lawyer; and Hicham Mansouri, a journalist in exile who had been imprisoned in 2015 on charges of adultery and sexual exploitation, which Amnesty describes as trumped-up. The report draws on interviews with a whistleblower using the pseudonym Safir, a former employee of Morocco’s General Directorate for Territorial Surveillance (DGST). Amnesty said it corroborated key parts of Safir’s testimony with independent sources, technical evidence and interviews with 10 people identified as surveillance targets, including Radi. “The Amnesty report connected many dots as to what I was living and feeling while I was under tight surveillance,” Radi said. “It explains the extraordinary aspect of my police interrogations and my trial, where many of my rights weren’t respected, because even the judicial police and the judges were under monitoring,” he added. Amnesty identifies the DGST as the agency behind the deployment of Pegasus spyware in Morocco and documents what it describes as abuses of the spyware against activists and journalists between 2017 and 2021. Morocco has previously rejected Amnesty’s allegations that its authorities used Pegasus to target journalists, activists and other critics. In statements issued in 2020 and 2022, Moroccan authorities challenged Amnesty to provide material evidence supporting its claims. Amnesty said it wrote to Moroccan authorities four weeks before publishing its latest report and invited them to respond, but received no response. Al Jazeera also sought comment from Moroccan officials but had not received a response at the time of publication. Moroccan media have also challenged the latest report. Le360 cited arguments that the presence of a phone number in Pegasus targeting records does not, by itself, prove that a device was infected or establish who ordered an alleged attack. The outlet also argued that Amnesty had not provided the conclusive technical and material evidence Moroccan authorities had demanded. The report says Morocco’s Pegasus operations were fully active by October 2017, pointing to the case of human rights lawyer El Bouchattaoui, whose number was entered into the system in September 2017 and selected for targeting weeks before he received an infection link by text message. Amnesty said its analysis of Pegasus records matched 103 Moroccan phone numbers to individuals identified as potential targets between September and December 2017. Of those, 65 were identifiable as civil society members, including 34 human rights defenders, 22 journalists and media workers, five lawyers and four academics. According to Amnesty, Safir described a surveillance apparatus that combined digital and physical methods. Targeted individuals were secretly filmed and recorded in detention, offices, cars, cafes and even bedrooms, he said. Phone shops, he added, were coopted to sell targets devices infected with spyware. Neighbours of human rights defenders, he said, were recruited as informants to file daily reports on their movements. Safir also described the use of remote control systems (RCS) at internet cafes. Field agents would identify which cafe a target was visiting, he said, giving the DGST access to activity on machines it had already infected and allowing an operator to track calls, read messages, access photographs and record audio. The report says similar tactics were used against activist Abdelmoumni, who was secretly filmed at home with his fiancee in 2021. Abdelmoumni said he believed the footage was captured through a hidden camera in an air-conditioning unit, based on the recording’s angle.
