events.title: The 13 artists with the most No. 1 singles on the Billboard Hot 100
events.summary: Taylor Swift. Matt Winkelmeyer/Getty Images for The Recording Academy There are only 13 artists in Billboard history who have topped the Hot 100 at least 10 times. Taylor Swift secured her 16th No. 1 hit in October 2026. The Beatles have the most No. 1 songs ever (20), followed closely by Mariah Carey (19). Throughout music history, there have been plenty of record-breaking songs , albums, and acts. These 13, however, have seen the most success on the Billboard Hot 100, which is widely considered to be the definitive ranking of best-selling songs in the US. Keep scrolling to see the elite tier of singles artists, listed from least to most No. 1 hits. 11 (tie). Bruno Mars — 10 Bruno Mars. Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for SelvaRey Mars earned his 10th No. 1 single — and his first song to debut at No. 1 — in January 2026 with "I Just Might." This comes 16 years after his first chart-topper, "Nothin' on You," in May 2016. Then came: "Just the Way You Are" also in 2010, "Grenade" in 2011, "Locked Out of Heaven" in 2012, "When I Was Your Man" in 2013, "Uptown Funk!" in 2015, "That's What I Like" in 2017, "Leave the Door Open" in 2021, and "Die With a Smile" in 2025. 11 (tie). Stevie Wonder — 10 Stevie Wonder performing at the 32nd Annual Grammy Awards. CBS/Getty Images In 1963, at just 13 years old, Stevie Wonder earned his first No. 1 song with "Fingertips." He was the youngest artist ever to top the chart. Throughout his illustrious career, Wonder has added nine more hits to the list: "Superstition" in 1972, "You Are the Sunshine of My Life" in 1973, "You Haven't Done Nothin'" in 1974, "I Wish" in 1976, "Sir Duke" in 1977, "Ebony and Ivory" in 1982, "I Just Called to Say I Love You" in 1984, and both "Part-Time Lover" and "That's What Friends Are For" in 1985. 11 (tie). Janet Jackson — 10 Janet Jackson performs at the 2009 MTV Video Music Awards. Christopher Polk/Getty Images Janet Jackson's reign on the Hot 100 began with 1986's "When I Think of You," which topped the chart when she was 20 years old. Next came 1989's "Miss You Much," 1990's "Escapade," "Black Cat," and "Love Will Never Do (Without You)," 1993's "That's the Way Love Goes" and "Again," 1997's "Together Again," 2000's "Doesn't Really Matter," and 2001's "All for You." Jackson is the rare artist to claim the No. 1 spot in three different decades, like Stevie Wonder. 10. Whitney Houston — 11 Kevork Djansezian/Getty Images Whitney Houston had no shortage of iconic songs, but she earned her first No. 1 with "Saving All My Love for You" in 1985. That same year, she also put "How Will I Know" in the top spot. Over the next decade, Houston collected nine more chart-toppers: "The Greatest Love of All" in 1986; "I Wanna Dance with Somebody (Who Loves Me)," "Didn't We Almost Have It All," and "So Emotional" in 1987; "Where Do Broken Hearts Go" in 1988; "I'm Your Baby Tonight" and "All the Man That I Need" in 1990; " I Will Always Love You " in 1992; and "Exhale (Shoop Shoop)" in 1995. 8 (tie). Madonna — 12 Christopher Polk / Getty Images Madonna has been topping the charts for decades, and it all began with "Like a Virgin" in 1984. She followed up with "Crazy for You" in 1985 before she scored three No. 1 hits in 1986 alone: "Live to Tell," "Papa Don't Preach," and "Open Your Heart."  The so-called "Queen of Pop" added to her collection with "Who's That Girl" in 1987, "Like a Prayer" in 1989, "Vogue" and "Justify My Love" in 1990, "This Used to Be My Playground" in 1992, "Take a Bow" in 1994, and "Music" in 2000. 8 (tie). The Supremes — 12 AP The Supremes are known as one of the best-selling girl groups of all time, earning 12 No. 1 hits in half as many years. In the mid-'60s, the trio released a string of five singles that all went to No. 1 on the chart: "Where Did Our Love Go," "Baby Love," and "Come See About Me" in 1964, then "Stop! In the Name of Love" and "Back in My Arms Again" in 1965. They continued to dominate the decade with a flood of hits: "I Hear a Symphony," also in 1965; "You Can't Hurry Love" and "You Keep Me Hangin' On" in 1966; "Love Is Here and Now You're Gone" and "The Happening" in 1967; "Love Child" in 1968; and "Someday We'll Be Together" in 1969. 7. Michael Jackson — 13 JUNE 25: Michael Jackson performs in concert circa 1986. Kevin Mazur/WireImage via Getty Images Michael Jackson began appearing on the charts as a child with The Jackson 5, but after he struck out on his own, the so-called "King of Pop" racked up more hits than any solo artist at the time. Perhaps most impressively, five out of his 13 No. 1 songs came from the same album ("Bad"), setting a record that remains unbroken. (It was tied in 2011 by Katy Perry's "Teenage Dream.") Jackson's first chart-topper was "Ben" in 1972 when he was 14 years old. "Don't Stop 'Til You Get Enough" and "Rock With You" both took the top spot in 1979, followed by "Billie Jean," "Beat It," and "Say Say Say" in 1983; "I Just Can't Stop Loving You," "Bad," and "The Way You Make Me Feel" in 1987; "Man in the Mirror" and "Dirty Diana" in 1988; and "Black or White" in 1993. He capped his collection with "You Are Not Alone" in 1995, which also became the first song in history to debut at No. 1 on the Hot 100. 5 (tie). Drake — 14 Drake performs in 2017. Ross Gilmore/Getty Images Drake is one of the most dominant artists of the streaming era, racking up 14 chart-topping singles to date — the vast majority of them at breakneck speed over a seven-year period. The rapper notched his first No. 1 hit thanks to Rihanna when their collaboration, "What's My Name," reigned atop the chart in 2010. In 2016, Drake topped the chart again as a featured artist on Rihanna's song "Work." Later that year, "One Dance" became his first solo hit to ascend to first place. He notched three No. 1 hits in 2018 with "God's Plan," "Nice for What," and "In My Feelings," followed by "Toosie Slide" in 2020; "What's Next" and "Way 2 Sexy" in 2021; "Wait for U" and "Jimmy Cooks" in 2022; "Slime You Out" and "First Person Shooter" in 2023; and "Janice STFU" in 2026. Ten of those songs arrived in the chart's top spot, making Drake the artist with the most No. 1 song debuts in history. 5 (tie). Rihanna — 14 Ezra Shaw/Getty Images In the span of just 14 years, Rihanna earned 14 No. 1 songs , starting with "SOS" in 2006 when she was still a teenager. Next came "Umbrella" in 2007; "Take a Bow," "Live Your Life," and "Disturbia" in 2008; "Rude Boy," "Love the Way You Lie," "Only Girl (In the World)," and "What's My Name" in 2010; "S&M" and "We Found Love" in 2011; "Diamonds" in 2012; "The Monster" in 2013; and finally "Work" in 2016, the lead single from her most recent album, "Anti." 4. events.title: Lucid's Q3 deliveries fall 6.7% as EV maker cuts production to align with demand
events.summary: Lucid Group reported a 6.7% decrease in year-over-year vehicle deliveries during the third quarter. The automaker on Monday said it delivered 3,806 EVs and produced 2,954 vehicles from July through September. The third quarter of this year was the first since Lucid cut production at its plant in Arizona amid an "operational reset" under new CEO Silvio Napoli. Lucid Group reported a 6.7% decrease in year-over-year vehicle deliveries during the third quarter, after the embattled all-electric vehicle maker cut production to better align with slower customer demand. The U.S. automaker, which is heavily backed by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, on Monday said it delivered 3,806 EVs and produced 2,954 vehicles from July through September. Those results compare with deliveries of 4,078 EVs on production of 3,891 vehicles in the year-ago quarter. Deliveries of Lucid vehicles are 3.4% higher through the third quarter than a year earlier. Production has climbed 33%, as Lucid ramped up vehicle production through early this year. Lucid's highest quarterly production of nearly 7,900 units occurred during the fourth quarter of last year, followed by 5,500 during the first quarter of this year. The third quarter of this year was the first since Lucid cut production at its plant in Arizona from two shifts to one amid an "operational reset" under new CEO Silvio Napoli, who started leading the automaker in June. The turnaround plan includes identifying $1.4 billion in cash flow improvement opportunities this year. They include approximately $600 million to $800 million in vehicle inventory, $500 million in capital expenditures, and $200 million in operating expenses, the company said when reporting its second-quarter results in August. Lucid said Monday it would report its third-quarter results on Nov. 9 after markets close.

events.title: Bird flu adds to fears for threatened species at proposed wind farm site
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Bird flu and wind farm spark fears for threatened species at Ramsar-listed wetlands The endangered Australasian bittern inhabits the Glenelg Estuary and Discovery Bay Wetlands. ( Supplied: Simone Carmichael/DPE ) The combined impact of bird flu and a proposed wind farm in Victoria's south-west poses risks to threatened bird and bat species, ecologists say. Developer HMC Capital says the project has undertaken extensive measures to mitigate the risks. A decision is expected on the future of the Kentbruck wind farm next month. Expertly camouflaged amid reed beds and sedgeland, the elusive Australasian bittern is a highly revered sight among birdwatchers. Across Australia, fewer than 1,500 birds are estimated to remain in the wild. In south-west Victoria, a small population of the endangered birds inhabit the Glenelg Estuary and Discovery Bay Wetlands all year round. Mark Bachmann is worried about the threatened bird and bat species inhabiting the wetlands. ( Supplied: Mark Bachmann/Nature Glenelg Trust ) In winter, the population at the Ramsar-listed site grows when more birds fly hundreds of kilometres south after breeding on the inland rice fields of the New South Wales Riverina. The Ramsar Convention was a treaty signed in 1971 in the city of Ramsar, in Iran, to conserve the world's most important wetlands. In Australia, nominations for Ramsar sites to the federal government must come from the relevant state or territory government and must meet at least one of nine criteria for possible listing. It is illegal to damage a Ramsar site's ecological character without ministerial approval. The bittern, along with the endangered fairy tern, hooded plover and the brolga, which is also at risk from habitat loss in Victoria, are among the species ecologist and managing director of the Nature Glenelg Trust Mark Bachmann holds concerns for amid nearby mass bird flu mortality events and a proposed 105-turbine wind farm. Brolga inhabit the Ramsar-listed Discovery Bay Wetlands. ( Supplied: Mark Bachmann/Nature Glenelg Trust ) In August, hundreds of dead and dying birds were found to have contracted H5N1 avian influenza at Portland and the Glenelg River Estuary at Nelson. Mr Bachmann said the "compounding threat" associated with bird flu "presents too much risk for the wind farm project to go ahead". Decision on nation's tallest turbines looms Seven years ago, renewable energy developer HMC Capital put forward plans for the wind farm — including turbines up to 270 metres tall — in commercial pine plantation land between Nelson and Portland. A final decision on the 600-megawatt Kentbruck Green Power Hub project is expected on November 10. A spokesperson for the developer said the project's approach was "highly sensitive to the impact on birds" and had undertaken "extensive research" and independent expert investigations to mitigate the risk to birdlife and bat species inhabiting the nearby wetlands. An image produced by Neoen showing how its Kentbruck Green Power Hub wind turbines could look among pine plantations near Nelson. ( Supplied: Neoen ) Among measures taken to placate dissent from community members and environment groups, the developer reduced the number of wind turbines by 33 per cent and agreed to set up a $30 million ecology fund to sponsor ecological studies, protection activities and species recovery projects. The spokesperson added that the wind farm project was "critical for the transition to clean energy and will power hundreds of thousands of homes, as well as provide power to the nearby Port of Portland and Portland Aluminium Smelter". A 'litmus test' for renewables projects Back in Nelson, Mr Bachmann said the federal government's looming decision on the wind farm would be "critical" to the intersection of environment, community and future renewables development. A map of the Kentbruck Green Energy Hub from its public consultation documents. ( Supplied: Neoen Australia ) He said the project would see turbines situated about 300 metres from the Ramsar site boundary and 500 metres from the edge of the wetland, "potentially disrupting flight paths of birds and bats". Mr Bachmann argued the additional proximity to coastal areas experiencing "more frequent" bird flu cases heightened uncertainty. He said the impending decision on the wind farm would set a national precedent. "It could either deter development in inappropriate locations, or it could signal that you can pretty much put a wind farm anywhere.

events.title: 'We had a threat': Trump explains U.S. moving long-range bombers from UK
events.summary: President Donald Trump said the U.S. moved its long-range bombers out of the United Kingdom in response to "a threat." "They would be linked to Iran," Trump said when asked who had made the threat. The Associated Press on Sunday reported that the U.S. Air Force withdrew all of its B-1 bombers stationed at an air base in southern England after a probe uncovered a planned terror attack. President Donald Trump said Monday that the United States moved all of its long-range bombers out of the United Kingdom in response to "a threat." Trump, when asked who made the threat, replied, "They would be linked to Iran ." "Why would I leave them there?" Trump told reporters at the White House . "It costs very little money to move them." The Associated Press on Sunday reported that the U.S. Air Force withdrew all of its B-1 bombers stationed at an air base in southern England, RAF Fairford, after a probe uncovered a planned terror attack. Those aircraft have been used in strikes on Iran. The AP reported that the bombers were redeployed to their home bases in the United States.

events.title: Brazilian stocks jump as Bolsonaro now seen as heavy favorite to win presidency
events.summary: Flávio Bolsonaro and Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva will face off in a runoff on Oct. 25 for Brazil's presidency, after both received the most votes in a first-round result on Sunday. Neither candidate received a majority of the votes. Bolsonaro is now seen as the overwhelming favorite to win the presidency, following a better-than-expected performance for him in the first round compared to what polls expected. Brazilian stocks jumped on the news, as investors broadly see the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro as more favorable to markets than incumbent Lula. Brazilians will decide in just under three weeks whether to reelect incumbent president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva or oust him in favor of Flávio Bolsonaro — the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro — as both advanced to a runoff after receiving the most votes in the first-round vote on Sunday. But the results of the first round are recalibrating how investors are pricing what the final decision will be. Speculators on prediction market platform Kalshi now give Bolsonaro a more than 80% chance of winning the presidency. Before Sunday's first-round results came in, he had about a 60% chance to win. On Polymarket , Bolsonaro's odds are now 85%, jumping from 63% before the first-round count. While Bolsonaro was seen as a narrow favorite to win the presidency before Sunday's first round, he was widely expected to trail the incumbent Lula in that initial tally, according to polls before the Sunday vote . This was the case even as Bolsonaro was favored to win a runoff. However, Bolsonaro secured more than 47% of the votes, beating Lula's first-round total by nearly 2 percentage points. If no candidate receives a majority of the votes in the first round of a Brazilian presidential election, the two who get the most votes advance to a runoff. Brazilian assets were on the rise following the result. The iShares MSCI Brazil ETF (EWZ) was up more than 12% on Monday. U.S.-listed shares of Itau Unibanco gained 15%, and shares of Banco Bradesco surged 19%. Brazil's local Bovespa index was up 8%. Investors broadly saw Bolsonaro as more favorable to markets , as the candidate is promising greater fiscal discipline. In June, Brazil's deficit-to-GDP ratio was almost 10%. Lula is running for a fourth term as president. He won back the presidency in 2022 — after a 12-year stint out of the office — when he defeated then-incumbent Jair Bolsonaro. Lula's campaign has tried to tie Flávio Bolsonaro to his father's efforts to contest his 2022 loss and brand the son as corrupt . The runoff in Brazil will take place on Oct. 25. Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

events.title: ASX rises for third straight day, Nasdaq hits new record high — as it happened
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts ASX rises for third straight day, tech rally drives Nasdaq to record high — as it happened The Australian share market ended its day higher, driven by gains across banks, miners and real estate stocks. The Nasdaq hit a record high after Wall Street's tech stocks surged, while the euro has fallen to a 22-month low against the Australian dollar. Follow the day's financial news and insights from our specialist business reporters on our live blog. Disclaimer: this blog is not intended as investment advice. Australian dollar: flat at 69.7 US cents, +0.1% to 62.1 euro cents Wall Street: Dow (+0.2%), S & P 500 (+0.7%), Nasdaq Composite (+1.1%) Europe: DAX (+0.1%), FTSE (+0.3%), Stoxx 600 (+0.4%) Asia : Nikkei (+1.1%), Hang Seng (+0.7%), KOSPI (-1%) Oil (Brent futures): +0.4% at $US100.68/barrel 10-year bonds: US 5.32%, Australia 5.41% Prices current at around 4:50pm AEDT Choose what information you see below by using filters And that's all we've got for you today. We'll be back with you tomorrow morning for another exciting day on the markets. ASX finishes higher with real estate in the lead The Australian share market's benchmark ASX 200 index has closed 0.6% higher at 8,736 points . The real estate sub-index led the way, up 1.2% . Utilities (+0.9%), industrials (+0.7%), financials (+0.7%) and miners (+0.7%) also posted strong rises. However, the Australian tech sector was dumped (-1.1%) , despite New York's tech-heavy Nasdaq climbing to a fresh record high overnight. Surging US interest rates 'a bigger problem for others' The usual optimism from Rabobank global strategist Michael Every in his daily note. "Monday saw Treasuries slump again, 10s up to 5.31% and 30s to 5.67% , the highest since early 2002," he observes. "If we keep going like we have since February, we'll soon have 20th century yields again, a shock for the generation who weren't born in it and for elders who kept telling themselves "lower for longer" would hold after the geopolitical consensus couldn't. "That's obviously a huge problem for the US but, as usual, it's proving a bigger problem for others." Every cites civil unrest over the potential for austerity in France, but we can see the local dissatisfaction brewing over the RBA's string of rate rises, the latest of which had a strong flavour of response to rising US rates. "Meanwhile, the US Nasdaq just hit a new record high, again taking us back to the turn of the century and its dotcom bubble ," Every continues. "That's another reason we can't expect yields to fall back easily — at least not until the miraculous deflationary impact of AI and SI (also referred to as AGI). "Either way, SI is now the national security equivalent of the 20th century Manhattan Project and the 19th century investment surge into railways and steel. It won't stop easily. "Neither will national security spending in general as wars rage on." So, inflation is back and, in his view, not going away for a fair while, therefore meaning we'll have higher interest rates for longer and all the fallout that comes with that. Euro sinks, largely due to France's record debt and political uncertainty The euro has dropped to a 17-month low against the US dollar. It's also near a 22-month low against the Australian dollar. Essentially, concerns about France's ability to rein in its budget deficit and a sharp bond market sell-off last week stirred fears of a return of sovereign debt crisis dynamics in the euro zone. French government bonds have been sold off as expectations of higher policy rates and rising political uncertainty cast doubt on the ability of the euro area's second-largest economy to put its public finances on a more sustainable footing. “Latest bond market dynamics are increasingly concerning and somewhat reminiscent of a sovereign debt crisis," Hauke Siemssen, strategist at Commerzbank, said. The French government is seeking to enact an unpopular 2027 budget to lower its deficit and contain its record-high debt load, a tall order in a deeply divided ‌parliament as political factions position ahead of next year's presidential election. "We're pretty pessimistic about the euro. We think it's going to go down to under $US1.10," said Joseph Capurso, a currency strategist at Commonwealth Bank. "We're not surprised that we've seen this weakness... For the euro to rise, you'd need a big decrease in oil prices... a big increase in expectations for European monetary policy tightening. "Another one would be them starting to get their act together on reining in the budget deficit, though I think there's no chance of that happening anytime soon.

events.title: OpenAI will start watermarking ChatGPT’s text in the EU
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. OpenAI will start adding an invisible watermark to text generated by ChatGPT and Codex in the European Union to comply with the EU AI Act, the company said Monday in a blog post . The EU AI Act’s transparency rules , which took effect on August 2, require AI companies to mark AI-generated content in a way other systems can identify. OpenAI said the watermark will roll out over the coming weeks to eligible ChatGPT and Codex users on all plans, but only in the EU. Developers using OpenAI’s API anywhere in the world can turn it on for select models starting today; it’s off by default. OpenAI said it is not making text watermarking a global default at launch. The watermark is not an actual symbol, but works by subtly shaping the model’s word choices, leaving a pattern readers can’t see, but a detector can pick up. Because it lives in the words themselves, it travels with the text when it’s copied and pasted. OpenAI said the watermark doesn’t identify the user, and that it saw no meaningful change in its models’ performance with it switched on. OpenAI also published a technical report for its method, called textGrain, alongside the announcement. Co-written with researchers from the University of Pennsylvania and Yale, it walks through an example of using a secret key to sort next-word predictions to finish the sentence. Add hundreds of these nudges together, and the detector can spot AI-generated content using only the text and the key. Can the watermark be removed by editing? OpenAI’s tests suggest yes. In one test, replacing 10% of words with synonyms dropped detection from about 92% to 66%. The company also said short passages, math answers, and translated text are harder to detect. “These limitations contribute to our decision to provide initial detector access only to approved researchers and expert organizations, who can help us evaluate reliability and responsible uses,” said the company. OpenAI also cautioned that a missing watermark “does not prove human authorship.” The text could be too short or too heavily edited, or it could come from another company’s AI. “[Watermarks] can indicate that an OpenAI system generated or processed part of a passage, but not how much human judgment, editing, or creativity went into it,” the company said. The announcement comes two months after Anthropic said it would watermark text generated by Claude, a move it’s applying worldwide. That decision drew backlash from some Claude users , who argued they had supplied “the instructions, context, decisions” while Claude was just “the tool.” OpenAI had built a text watermark before but held off on releasing it, partly over concerns that users would switch to rivals that didn’t watermark, The Wall Street Journal reported in 2024. Anthropic, Google, Meta, Microsoft, and OpenAI are among the companies that have committed to following the EU’s code of practice on AI-generated content. events.title: Meta's Muse is already pulling one CEO's purchases away from Amazon
events.summary: Meta is betting that its AI agent can help consumers find better product listings. A CEO said that's already changed how he shops with Amazon. Bloomberg/Getty Images Leif Abraham, Public's co-CEO, wants vintage wines and fancy Levi's jeans. Meta's Muse AI agent buys them for him. Because Amazon blocks Muse from making purchases, Abraham said he's noticed more of his orders being processed by Shopify. Meta's AI agent, Muse, has been going shopping for Leif Abraham. With Amazon blocking the AI agent from placing orders, Abraham says that means fewer purchases from Amazon. Abraham, the cofounder and co-CEO of investing platform Public, told Business Insider he's turned to Muse to purchase mostly niche, hard-to-find products — skincare, vintage wines, a German creatine product, discontinued Levi's jeans. "Since the thing came out, I've been buying so much stuff," he said. "I literally just have to approve the payment, and that's it." Muse is Meta's bet that customers will entrust AI agents to handle internet errands, like booking a restaurant reservation for friends or finding their next outfit. It's an early hit, rocketing to the top of the App Store charts shortly after its launch last month. On Sunday, Abraham posted about his Muse experience on X, calling Meta and Shopify's recent integration a "win for Shopify." "The amount of purchases I've made with Muse that I used to have gone to Amazon for," he wrote. "Now buying from the brands directly…" he added, along with a screenshot of him directing the agent to buy products "from a reputable store." The amount of purchases I’ve made with Muse that I used to have gone to Amazon for … now buying from the brands directly … win for Shopify https://t.co/w2axEYQMiT — Leif Abraham (@leifthunder) October 4, 2026 Public, Abraham's company, offers a Muse connector that lets customers link their brokerage accounts to the agent. Abraham said he has connected his own account and also uses Muse for daily brokerage updates and calorie tracking. Abraham's story is one person's experience and doesn't mean that Amazon has an impending sales problem. AI agent shopping has yet to catch on with the general public. But Amazon's decision to block Muse from making purchases on behalf of users — Amazon raised concerns about how Muse accessed or stored customer credentials and sensitive data, along with account data scraping — risks leaving money on the table, especially if Muse shopping takes off. Shopify, meanwhile, has taken the opposite approach. The payment processing platform announced a partnership with Meta that lets Muse users check out at Shopify merchants through Shop Pay. Abraham still labels himself an "Amazon mega user," but says some recent purchases weren't up to snuff. Now, instead of turning to Amazon for all his purchases, he uses the marketplace only for items that don't require as much research, like toilet paper. After Abraham wrote on X about the shift in his shopping habits, Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke reshared the post and added that he's "hearing so many of these stories." Not everyone's experience with Muse has gone according to plan . Abraham said several of his techie friends are also using Muse to find niche products, but results have varied. One friend, he said, is still searching for tickets to Christopher Nolan's "The Odyssey" in IMAX 70mm — a task he said that Muse hasn't accomplished. (Granted, whether that's a Muse problem or a supply problem is a whole other conversation.) Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Trump: U.S. willing to help Russia with potential pneumonic plague outbreak
events.summary: President Trump said Monday that the United States will help Russia amid a potential case of pneumonic plague , though he hasn't spoken with Russian President Vladimir Putin about it. Why it matters: International concern spiked over the weekend over the news that a Russian lab worker had died from a possible case of pneumonic plague, reminding some of how the COVID-19 epidemic began. Trump's comments came after a question about the reported death of Darya Shipilova, who was potentially exposed to plague bacteria while working at the Research Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia. There has been no official confirmation that Shipilova's death was due to pneumonic plague, but five hospitals in the area and dozens of institute workers have been quarantined out of precaution. Russian health authorities say Shipilova died from "pneumonia of unknown etiology" and that testing showed no pathogen tied to her work. No additional deaths or sicknesses tied to the incident have been reported. What they're saying: "We just heard about it," Trump told reporters Monday. "We'll help them," Trump said. "We'll help them as much as we can." Trump said the disease used to be more controllable, but "microbes and the germs have gotten stronger." The president appeared to be referring to antimicrobial resistance , but pneumonic plague itself remains treatable with antibiotics when diagnosed early Between the lines: The White House is monitoring the outbreak, Axios scooped, with the Department of Health and Human Services and State Department also on alert. The European Commission is also "very closely" monitoring the suspected outbreak. Go deeper: How pneumonic plague spreads, and how it is and isn't like COVID

events.title: Etched fields funding offers at $40B+ valuation, sources say
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Although it’s only been a couple of months since Etched raised $700 million at a $21 billion valuation , the AI chip startup is already being plied with investment offers at double or more its value, according to people familiar with the company. Etched is reviewing incoming bids that range from $40 billion from top-tier investors to $50 billion from lesser-known backers, one person said. These fundraising talks are early, so terms of any deal, should one happen, may change. Etched declined to comment. While this may seem like a fast timetable to raise another mega round, Etched is pursuing a particularly expensive segment of the AI industry: building full AI hardware systems powered by its own proprietary chips. The person familiar with these offers said that if it raises as much as its last round, this could give Etched a cushion of as much as 3.5 years of runway. There are reasons why VCs are hot to own a piece of Etched. The four-year-old startup shows promise of challenging Nvidia. Not only did quant trading firm Jane Street lead the last $700 million round, it is also a customer that took delivery of an early system. Etched said in July that it had already secured $1 billion in customer orders, including the one from Jane Street, after manufacturing its test chip at a TSMC factory this summer. Co-founder and COO Robert Wachen previously told TechCrunch that investors are so enthusiastic because Etched has designed two new components from scratch to speed up inference — the computing process that happens after a user submits a prompt. The company claims its chips can process more tokens faster and at a lower cost than Nvidia’s. That’s the reason its processors have been so attractive to Jane Street, for whom a microscopic advantage in speed can yield massive profits. The startup has also impressed investors with its ability to attract engineers from Nvidia, with roughly 15% of Etched’s 400-person workforce having previously worked at the chip giant, according to The Wall Street Journal. Etched also operates a new 10-megawatt data center in Silicon Valley and established a facility in Taiwan to coordinate production near TSMC. Co-founders Gavin Uberti and Chris Zhu famously met in an advanced math course at Harvard, while Wachen was Uberti’s roommate and they dropped out to pursue the company. In terms of fast rounds at big leaps in valuations, Etched already has a history of them. The startup announced a $300 million round at a $10.3 billion valuation led by Sequoia in July. It announced the $700 million round at a $21 billion valuation in September. Back-to-back funding rounds, which essentially act as a single financing split into two tranches with separate valuations, are increasingly common among the buzziest startups. events.title: SpaceX stock climbs to highest since June, returning Musk to trillionaire status
events.summary: SpaceX shares rose almost 8% on Monday, lifting CEO Elon Musk back to trillionaire status. Last week, SpaceX successfully launched a crewed NASA mission, and separately sent Google's AI chips into orbit. The stock has rebounded since bottoming in August. SpaceX shares rose almost 8% on Monday, reaching their highest since mid-June, shortly after Elon Musk's company held its record initial public offering . With the rally, Musk is once again a trillionaire. The jump followed a Sunday note from Morgan Stanley analysts, who called SpaceX "cheap" at today's prices, and highlighted "future AI product releases, Starship progress, and additional neocloud contracts." They recommend buying the stock and have a $300 price target, representing an increase of about 75% from Monday's $171.09 close. Late last week SpaceX conducted multiple historic flights in a single day, including sending a crewed mission for NASA to the International Space Station, and a separate launch of Google AI chips into orbit. The Morgan Stanley analysts suggested investors buy SpaceX shares before the company's next planned test flight for its massive Starship rocket, and ahead of its third-quarter earnings report expected in late October. Starship is SpaceX's next-generation spacecraft, the largest rocket ever built, and is designed to be fully reusable with both its upper stage and booster able to land safely back on Earth. The system is expected to supercharge SpaceX's business, bringing the company's Starlink satellites into orbit, as well as cargo and crews from other companies and agencies. Should SpaceX attempt a Starship upper stage ship catch in its next test flight, that could be "the biggest positive catalyst since the IPO," the analysts wrote. In prior test flights, the Starship upper stage has made splash downs in the ocean, but hasn't been proven reusable. SpaceX is also getting a boost from its artificial intelligence business, which it gained through the acquisition of Musk's xAI last year and expanded through the recent acquisition of Cursor. While the company's homegrown Grok model hasn't taken off compared to leading models from OpenAI and Anthropic, SpaceX is generating hefty revenue by renting out capacity to the likes of Google and Anthropic. Musk has the benefit of close ties to the Trump administration. On Wednesday, the Pentagon appointed Musk as co-lead of Project Meridian , an initiative that involves identifying weapons, technologies and military capabilities the U.S. may need in future wars. SpaceX makes a large chunk of its revenue from the U.S. government and increasingly from defense contracts, earning over $12.7 billion to date from its work with the Defense Department, according to FedScout. Musk said over the weekend he will be renaming SpaceX's AI division, known as SpaceXAI, as SpaceXSI, embracing President Donald Trump's new branding. As his company's stock soared on Monday, Musk was notably absent from a New York City Council hearing , where city officials grilled AI leaders and researchers about how the technology should be regulated. Representatives from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta were in attendance to testify. Councilmember Shekar Krishnan noted, "AI has taken over our economy, inflated valuations, stealing our public land for data centers, and increasing the net worth of AI CEOs like Elon Musk, who became our first ever trillionaire." According to Forbes' real-time billionaires list , Musk is currently worth $1.03 trillion, factoring in his holdings in Tesla and SpaceX. SpaceX went public on June 12, and jumped to a record close of $201.80 on June 16. The shares started trending lower soon thereafter, bottoming in early August. They've since climbed about 58%. events.title: Private-credit worries spur Fed review
events.summary: The Scoop The Federal Reserve Bank of New York has been visiting big banks to review their loans to private credit firms and understand their exposure to a financial industry that has unnerved investors and global policymakers. Fed officials have gone into JPMorgan, Wells Fargo, Barclays, and Morgan Stanley since the spring with questions about overall exposure, risk-management, and collateral quality, people familiar with the matter said. The Fed, JPMorgan, Barclays, Wells Fargo and Morgan Stanley declined to comment. The review was prompted in part by JPMorgan’s move in March to mark down large swaths of loans in private credit portfolios, particularly those to software companies threatened by AI, the people said. The Fed has concluded its review of some of the banks, including JPM, said the people. It’s not uncommon for the Fed to go into banks to review their holdings, particularly when there are frequent headlines about potential risks. The Fed also does regular on-site evaluations and continually surveys for banks’ risks. Know More Private-credit firms are one of the fastest-growing borrower sets for banks, which were chased out of risky lending after the 2008 crisis but have since found their way back into the trade by lending to the firms that replaced them. Loans to nonbank institutions have risen from $300 billion in 2016 to more than $1.5 trillion according to FDIC data, and now account for 11% of all bank loans outstanding. Those loans are backed by private-credit firms’ own loans, a debt pile that has unnerved regulators. The European Central Bank also recently expanded a probe into private credit, looking at banks with exposures to the market. Last week, the Securities and Exchange Commission released a rare statement about fair value in private assets, serving as a reminder to lenders that they should be rigorous in their valuations and disclosures. The Bank of England, during its September Financial Policy Committee meeting, said that private credit could be vulnerable to worsening financial conditions after testing the resilience of private markets. The private credit market got slammed earlier this year when investors panicked about funds’ exposures to software companies, which suddenly seemed obsolete amid developments in AI. The concerns caused investors in certain types of funds to pull out their money at record rates — sometimes requesting nearly 40% of a single fund in a quarter, but most funds have capped at 5%. Private credit lenders have long been criticized for the way they value their loans, or mark them, in particular when there is disparity between where different lenders value the same loan and when a company’s underperformance fails to translate to their marks. But lenders utilize third-party evaluators to create the marks and say they are making careful investments. Redemption rates have declined at many of the private-credit firms and some investors have warmed to software deals again , as more of them find avenues to finance themselves both in and out of the private credit market. Notable JPMorgan was early to reassess its valuations for loans to private credit companies.

events.title: The US Army created a new robotics job for special operations. Now, the service wants to go bigger.
events.summary: "These technical experts will help command teams understand integration across the force," Army Gen. Christopher LaNeve, vice chief of staff, said. US Army photo by Staff Sgt. John Bae The US Army wants to expand a new robotics role pioneered by special operations. The specialty, alongside another effort, is focused on building, modifying, and integrating robotics and new technologies. The first soldiers graduated from the course last week. The US Army wants to expand a new robotics specialty pioneered by special operations across the conventional force after graduating its first robotics technicians. The new specialty and expected expansion reflect the Army's growing belief that future wars will demand specialists who can keep pace with rapidly evolving battlefield technology. The war in Ukraine has shown how quickly innovative solutions can become obsolete, forcing soldiers to adapt in the field. US Army Special Operations Command is expected to provide Army officials with feedback for expanding the new specialty — officially robotics technician — beyond special operations in the coming weeks, Lt. Gen. Lawrence Ferguson, head of US Army Special Operations Command, said last month at an Army conference. "These technical experts will help command teams understand integration across the force," said Gen. Christopher LaNeve, acting Army chief of staff, at the same event. "We are scaling this across the Army," he said. Rather than simply flying drones, the Army is training these new robotic specialists to integrate drones, ground robots, artificial intelligence, and other autonomous systems across military operations. They'll serve as technical advisors for commanders while rapidly designing, modifying, and troubleshooting custom robotic hardware and software. That new specialty complements a second new role, the "Robotics Technology Integrators Course" graduate, whose job is to understand new technologies. The Army said the need for the specialized role became clear from lessons from recent global conflicts. "To maintain battlefield overmatch, the Army requires a two-tiered structure: highly specialized technical architects (MOS 390A) who engineer and secure the systems, working in tandem with tactical employment specialists (RTIC) who operate them in the dirt," explained an Army document on the two separate but related career paths shared with Business Insider. The first 10 soldiers graduated as robotics technicians on October 2 at the Army's John F. Kennedy Special Warfare Center and School at Fort Bragg, North Carolina Sgt. 1st Class Alexis Washburn/United States Army John F. Kennedy Special Warfare Center and School It compared the Army's approach to a racing team. "If the Army Special Operations wants to build a Formula 1 racing team, the RTIC Graduate is our high-performance racing driver," the document said. "They know how to push the car to its limits, read the track, and win the tactical race." Meanwhile, the robotics technician is the racecar's crew chief. "They design the engine, write the telemetry software, rebuild the transmission when it breaks, and formulate the team's strategy," the document added. Special operations isn't keeping that robotics expertise to itself, though. Army leaders want to spread this capability across the broader force. The first 10 soldiers graduated as robotics technicians on October 2 at the Army's John F. Kennedy Special Warfare Center and School at Fort Bragg, North Carolina. The program is considered a pilot for the Army at large, with the Special Operations Center of Excellence involved to avoid duplicative efforts. The course will be updated as technologies like drones and AI evolve, employing a flexible framework that allows instructors to update lesson plans. The new specialties come as the Army examines which  technological skill sets soldiers will need for future conflicts. The service has established various courses and schools on uncrewed systems, AI, and machine learning, with a focus on disseminating expertise across formations. "We are experiencing a SOF Renaissance as technological advancements are swiftly transforming the character of war," said Chief Warrant Officer 5 Gary Ostrander, Command Chief Warrant for the Army's special warfare school, in an Army news release this summer. "There will no longer be a time when a formation does not employ robotics technology on the battlefield to gain an advantage over an adversary," he said. events.title: US supreme court hears big oil’s bid to block climate damage lawsuits
events.summary: How the court will lean is unclear amid Suncor Energy and ExxonMobil’s attempt to stop lawsuits at state level The US supreme court began its new nine-month term hearing arguments on Monday in a major case in which big oil companies attempted to strike a fatal blow against lawsuits that seek to hold them accountable for the climate crisis . After the almost two-hour hearing, while it was not yet clear which way the justices were leaning, experts said the court may find it challenging to write a majority decision siding with industry. In Suncor Energy Inc v County Commissioners of Boulder County , local officials in Boulder are suing Suncor Energy and ExxonMobil in state court to force the companies to share a portion of the costs that the climate crisis has imposed on local taxpayers. However, Exxon and Canada-based Suncor are arguing that federal law prevents state courts from hearing Boulder’s climate change lawsuit. If the supreme court justices side with Boulder or decide that the case is not in their jurisdiction, then it would continue in state court. But if the fossil fuel industry convinces the justices, the decision could apply not only to the Boulder case, but also to dozens of other climate cases brought by state and local governments around the US. As a result of Justice Samuel Alito’s recusal from the case, there are only five conservative justices weighing in, so Boulder county must only convince one conservative justice to win, assuming the three liberal justices back Boulder. Some noted that the justices focused their questions primarily on the merits of the case rather than asking if the court had jurisdiction to hear it, suggesting they will make a decision on the question of whether federal law pre-empts Boulder’s state climate case. Kannon Shanmugam, a lawyer for the fossil fuel companies, told the justices that climate change was a pressing issue, but state cases such as the one filed by Boulder were the wrong way to resolve it, and the issue should be left to lawmakers. He argued that if the cases were heard in state courts, it would allow a high number of lawsuits to be filed. “The breadth of Boulder’s argument is astonishing,” he said. Shanmugam argued that climate change is different from other interstate pollution cases “because the claim runs through global climate change” and involves anyone who uses fossil fuels worldwide. Kirti Datla, the director of Earthjustice’s strategic legal advocacy program, said the industry lawyer needed five justices to agree with him. “Some of the justices seemed to be persuaded by the idea that climate change is different, or the sheer number of these suits creates a problem of a different kind,” Datla said. But she added that the justices were struggling to come up with reasons based in law that would support the industry arguments. “It’s always been Suncor’s task to provide them with clear answers to those questions, and I didn’t hear clear answers to those questions in argument.” Dennis Fan, the founder and director of the Appellate Litigation Clinic at Columbia Law School who wrote an amicus brief in the case, said it was too close to call, but he was concerned for the future of the climate cases. “They focused more on the merits,” he said. “That had me much more worried for Boulder.” Fan said the industry hopes this case is going to be the “death blow” to this type of lawsuit. “The industry is going for the home run … They’re thinking, ‘If we win this argument, there will never, ever be climate change litigation again.’” Boulder officials filed a lawsuit in Colorado court in 2018 arguing that Exxon and Suncor concealed and misrepresented to the public what they knew about the damage that burning fossil fuels would do to the climate, and that they should pay for the resulting costs of disasters. Initially, the firms sought to have the case moved to federal court. Then when the Colorado supreme court allowed Boulder’s case to make its way toward trial in state court, Exxon and Suncor appealed that ruling up to the supreme court, arguing it should be dismissed on grounds of federal pre-emption. Typically, cases must be decided by lower courts before reaching the supreme court, but the justices agreed to hear this case while the state case is ongoing. “That’s an incredibly weird thing to have happen,” Fan said. The supreme court considered whether it had proper jurisdiction to hear Boulder’s case right now, and whether federal law pre-empted Boulder’s case from being heard in state court. Congress has the power to pass federal laws that invalidate state laws, but the question is whether there are any federal laws that invalidate state climate cases. “They’ve had a little bit of difficulty identifying exactly what that source of federal law is,” Fan said.

events.title: Sam Altman says the world should accept some ‘bad things’ happening with AI as the industry signs on to Trump’s voluntary safety pact
events.summary: Following a controversy-filled summer in which OpenAI’s models executed more than one unauthorized hack, CEO Sam Altman said the world should accept some “bad things” happening with AI for the sake of all the good the technology will bring. During Politico’s Decoded podcast , he was asked where his and OpenAI’s view of new AI rules differed from that of Anthropic and its CEO, Dario Amodei. “We believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency,” Altman replied.  The comments come as debate intensifies over how much regulation and what safeguards should be applied to AI while Congress has yet to pass a law dealing with the technology. Fears over the tech recently increased after an Anthropic researcher resigned last month and warned AI companies are “ gambling with our lives ” by rushing AI development toward potentially self-improving systems that could threaten humanity. Anthropic has advocated for AI regulation, and Amodei last month called for a global slowdown in AI development to address the tech’s risks. Altman and other AI executives agreed with him on slowing down .  In August, OpenAI also backed a California law requiring AI companies to publish a public safety framework and a plan for mitigating catastrophic risks, as well as to report any loss of control of an AI model. It even asked for that law to go beyond reporting to include monitoring of AI models during their development.  OpenAI president Greg Brockman also joined other AI executives in signing an agreement at the White House last week to establish voluntary standards for the industry. Still, that falls short of calls for tougher regulation coming from other AI leaders like Amodei, who has proposed an FAA-style regulator that could require testing and auditing of AI models or block or reverse their release if they don’t meet the bar for public safety. In the interview with Politico, Altman said it would be impossible to avoid every bad thing that AI could be used for. The alternative would be to severely restrict access to the technology, which he said would be unacceptable. “I wouldn’t take a trade of saying, like, we’ll make sure there’s no major hacks, there’s no kind of, like, misuse of this technology, there’s zero scams, there’s zero all the other bad things that will happen, because I think people will do tremendously, orders of magnitude, more good stuff than bad stuff,” he added. Altman said AI companies should tread carefully, though, and draw a line when it comes to “catastrophic risks,” which have recently taken on renewed significance given recent hacks by AI models on third parties. OpenAI did not immediately respond to Fortune ’s request for comment. Concerns over the possibility of AI escaping human control have recently accelerated following hacks executed by OpenAI’s models on open-source AI platform Hugging Face and the Australian government . Anthropic last month also said it had discovered four incidents in which its AI models had gained unauthorized access to third-party systems during cybersecurity evaluations. While much of the AI safety debate has centered on losing control of AI, Altman said restricting access to AI too severely in the name of safety could be harmful too. “That also is a way that this can go horribly wrong because people are shut out of the kind of power and benefits and control and agency over the future they should have,” he added. The CEO said AI developers should strike a middle ground instead. “Accept bounded risks, accept risks that we understand in exchange for the benefits, and liberty, agency, all those things,” he said. “But don’t accept, like, the really catastrophic risk.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: How states are tackling midterm pump pain
events.summary: States are taking on the stubbornly high fuel prices squeezing Americans ahead of the midterm elections , pushing through tax holidays and other tactics to offer relief while federal efforts have stalled. Why it matters: With November 3 less than 30 days away, the political stakes of those price-lowering levers — even if the relief is only modest — are surging amid sky-high costs. While several lawmakers have introduced legislation aimed at or pressed for suspending the federal gas tax, which is 18.4 cents per gallon for gas and 24.4 for diesel, Washington hasn't coalesced around a solution. Driving the news: That's left states seeking ways to give their residents relief. Case in point: Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine (R) signed a bill last week that suspends Ohio's gas tax for 90 days, an effort that earned bipartisan backing. There's an underlying election story: The state's Democratic gubernatorial candidate, Amy Acton, had called for a gas tax holiday, followed by her rival, Vivek Ramaswamy, announcing a plan with GOP leaders. Flashback: Georgia was the first state to suspend its fuel taxes amid the war in Iran, with Republican Gov. Brian Kemp approving a 60-day pause back in March. Since then, at least five other states (including Ohio), have suspended, lowered or stopped increases in their fuel taxes. Kemp declared a state of emergency in late September and suspended the excise tax again for 30 days. Utah cut its gas tax by some 15% through the end of the year. Gov. Andy Beshear (D-Ky.) froze an expected increase in the gas and diesel taxes in May. Illinois suspended its set increase this summer for six months. Indiana Gov. Mike Braun (R) also suspended Indiana's gas tax in April. He renewed the suspension in late September and lifted restrictions on dyed diesel for farmers and timber harvesters. Friction point: The Trump administration signaled openness to a gas tax holiday this spring, but Congress must suspend the levy. While the idea has been floated before, lawmakers have never done so. Suspending the taxes can bring some relief to consumers, but it wouldn't offset the spikes they've felt at the pump since the start of the war. Plus, critics note doing so could increase the deficit and hurt the Highway Trust Fund it fuels. But as Axios' Ben Geman noted back in May, political winds aren't always predictable — especially with drivers and truckers still feeling the strain months later, and as political messages cluster around cost-of-living concerns. Zoom out: Other states have taken a similar approach to Braun by waiving seasonal and traditional restrictions for strained industries. For example, Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey (R) directed state law enforcement to stop enforcing rules against dyed diesel, usually reserved for off-road machinery and exempt from taxes, "to relieve the state's agricultural and timber communities." Louisiana , Nebraska , North Carolina , Oklahoma and Texas took similar action. Still, other states pursued different avenues for relief: California recently took action to permit cheaper, winter-blend gas to be sold earlier than usual, while Michigan allowed gas stations to sell lower-cost gasoline earlier this spring. The bottom line: Even if a federal gas tax holiday remains unlikely, pump pain — and perhaps, the possibility of future political pain — is fueling state action. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Like OpenClaw but with access control Schneider Electric drops $22.6B on PTC as datacenter boom rains money on infra companies 8 hours ago Altman-backed Volantis reveals plan to vault the memory wall by baking photonics into AI accelerators 14 hours ago Anthropic's super bug-hunting model Mythos is hardcore good at math, as latest vuln under attack shows 2 days ago OpenAI's wandering AI agents earn it a California subpoena 3 days ago Power approval set to delay Oracle's Wisconsin AI datacenter 3 days ago While OpenAI and Anthropic stoke fears over rogue agents, Canadian model dev Cohere promises enterprises a safer and more consistent experience. On Monday, the company said it revamped its North agent harness, which launched early last year, to improve collaboration, access control, token spend, and overall security of the platform. As you'd expect from an enterprise focused agent framework, Cohere's North 2 is designed to tie into existing knowledge bases and SaaS apps in order to automate various business processes. North 2 introduces a variety of features and functions that should be familiar to anyone who's used Claude Code or OpenClaw. Among them is the concept of skills, libraries, and automations. Skills are arguably the simplest, and are essentially standard operating procedures documenting how the agent harness should complete tasks. The skills are often generated by working with the agent to complete a task and then documenting which steps achieved the best results. With North 2, Cohere says that it has made it easier for these skills to be shared so that users aren't wasting time reinventing the wheel. Presumably, this should improve consistency by avoiding having the agent take different routes to achieving its goal, something that might miss key information or nuance. To facilitate the creation of new skills, North 2 also introduces the concept of automations, generic templates that can be customized using a drag-and-drop graphical interface, not unlike LangFlow, which we looked at earlier this year. Alongside skills and automations, Cohere's North 2 does something similar for shared knowledge and assets, which it calls libraries, to ensure that agents are working off of the same datasets. Finally, North 2 adds memory, a core feature of most modern agent harnesses, to ensure that agents can maintain context across multiple sessions. In some sense, these features are a bit like self-generating macros, but rather than being limited to Excel, they work across multiple applications and data sources. Sovereign AI remains a major talking point for Cohere, which says enterprises can deploy North 2 where they like and use their preferred models. If enterprises want to deploy the harness on-prem in an air-gapped environment, they can. If they prefer to run it in the cloud, that's also an option. Along with new features aimed at collaboration and automation, North 2 implements new guardrails designed to help enterprises get a handle on their token spend and access controls. Flow control functionality, meanwhile, promises greater visibility into which departments are hogging all the tokens, while access control functionality offers admins the ability to assign access control lists to various libraries and skills so that interns can't get their hands on proprietary data just because they asked for it. North 2 is only the latest in a slew of enterprise focused agentic AI platforms which have been rolled out over the last year. Essentially every major and minor cloud provider has introduced some kind of agent harness tailored to enterprise needs. The competition has only gotten hotter over the last few weeks as OpenAI , Meta and others have set their sights on the enterprise.

events.title: TNT Sports head Luis Silberwasser to depart Skydance as CBS Sports chief David Berson takes over combined global sports group
events.summary: TNT Sports chief Luis Silberwasser is departing the soon-to-be merged Paramount Skydance-Warner Bros. Discovery, sources tell CNBC. Silberwasser informed his team he's leaving on Monday. CBS Sports president and CEO David Berson will lead a newly formed combined global sports division. Luis Silberwasser, chairman and CEO of TNT Sports, is departing the soon-to-be merged Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery, according to people familiar with the matter. Silberwasser informed his team of the news Monday in an e-mailed note, said the people, who asked not to be named because the communication was private. "I am writing to let you know that, with the closing of the Paramount–WBD merger, I will be departing the company as TNT Sports and CBS Sports come together under new leadership," Silberwasser said in his note, which CNBC has obtained. David Berson, president and chief executive officer of CBS Sports, will lead a newly formed global sports group that will oversee all networks, platforms and territories. The CBS Sports, TNT Sports and WBD Sports brands will roll up into the new group. Sources familiar with the matter say Skydance is expected to make a formal announcement about Berson's move soon. A CBS spokesperson declined to comment. The combined company, which last week announced it will be named Skydance, will own a large swath of sports rights, including NFL Sunday afternoon games, all of March Madness, college football, NHL, MLB, The Masters, and many others. The Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery merger is expected to close tomorrow, Oct. 6. Silberwasser joined TNT Sports in 2022 from Univision. Warner Bros. Discovery lost NBA live rights in 2025, concluding a 40-year relationship with the league. Still, Silberwasser struck new multiyear deals to sublicense College Football Playoff games and air events such as All Elite Wrestling (AEW), the French Open and NASCAR races. That helped Warner Bros. Discovery reach distribution deals with pay TV providers and maintain distribution fees even without the NBA. Berson must now look at his entire portfolio and decide which sports are worth keeping and which can be shed as Skydance looks to pay down nearly $80 billion in debt in the coming years. events.title: How Greg Jackson runs Octopus Energy with no HR, no bonuses, and no succession plan
events.summary: The Signal Interview In a little more than a decade, Octopus Energy has grown from an outlandish idea into Britain’s largest energy provider. It now powers 12 million homes in eight countries, manages wind and solar farms from Scotland to South Korea, manufactures heat pumps, installs smart meters, leases out 50,000 electric vehicles, and supplies technology to utilities around the world. The tentacles of this “Octoverse” all lead back to Greg Jackson, a founder-CEO who has built his 13,000-person company without bonuses, HR or IT teams, or a succession plan. Beyond the walls of the company’s London headquarters, which is filled with thousands of its plushy pink octopus mascots, Jackson’s empire may look like an unwieldy one. It is not, he insists: “The thing that’s connecting it all is the underlying insight: that the technologies of electrification can deliver tremendous cost savings, but only if you build a new system.” And building that new system requires using every tool at his disposal. “There’s a scene in the movie where the astronauts are stranded and they’re going to die unless the solution is found. And on the ground, Mission Control assembles … everything there is on the space station, like duct tape and bits of piping, and they say, this is all we’ve got to save their lives,” he explains. “In any business, you choose your constraints, and then how you assemble the stuff you have to create the outcome you want.” Octopus’ job is “to take all these ingredients and say, how can we outcompete the old world of energy with better products and services with better value?” Jackson says, before reaching back to the beginning of that old world for another analogy. “When [Thomas] Edison first started building electricity businesses, he didn’t just have to innovate, fund, and build centralized electricity generation, which he did. He also had to invent the grid and distribution model. He also had to invent or sell the products that use electricity, from lightbulbs to music players. And if I look at what we’re doing, it’s almost trivial in comparison.” How to run a 13,000-person company with no HR department The growth of Octopus, which had revenues of £13.7 billion last year and a valuation of $9 billion at its last fundraising, poses a challenge for its irrepressible founder: how to transmit to thousands of employees the energy that has powered him since he dropped out of school at 16 to write video games. Jackson no longer knows each staff member by name, but he still runs his company by the same rhythms with which he started it. Each Monday starts with a gathering of senior executives to review performance data from the previous week. That helps maintain “pace and alignment,” Jackson says. Each week ends with “family dinner,” a Friday afternoon all-hands event at which the company recaps its latest innovations, achievements, and challenges. The Friday sessions began over beers with a small founding team, and Jackson “discovered that it was the best way of reminding you how great your colleagues were, and re-energizing you on the big picture.” Livestreams have since replaced in-person drinks. But the gatherings help Octopus “start the week left-brain, end it right-brain,” Jackson says, and help him explain to staff what they need to do next “and maintain the energy to feel great about it.” The company has no intranet or staff newsletters, he adds, so if people don’t tune in to “family dinner,” they won’t know what’s happening. Less is more in internal communications, he says: “The more information you put out there, the less it gets read. What you want to do is make sure the stuff that goes out there is canonical and consumed.” Octopus also has no central human resources department, devolving people management responsibilities to individual teams unless legal staff need to step in. Still a private company, it gives equity to every employee, but it pays no bonuses outside a few sales roles. Jackson says this is because he’s determined to focus people on the company’s success, rather than their own individual advancement. Similarly, Octopus sets no divisional performance targets, to keep each division from promoting whatever will make them look best at the expense of others, he adds. “The most important thing for us is to build trust among our team, so they wake up every morning thinking, ‘How do I drive the company’s mission?’ Not, ‘How do I get myself promoted?’” Hands-on leadership, from the cockpit to the customers Even as Octopus has grown to span industries as diverse as renewable power generation and software licensing, Jackson says his job has barely changed. The CEO’s role is still to understand customers and industry economics; set the vision for where the company needs to go; and build a team with the expertise and innovative impulses to get it there. For a pilot, the view from the cockpit window of a small Cessna is not that different from that of an Airbus A380, he says: “The difference comes when you look back.” If Octopus became a more complex organization, “then I’d get drawn more into wandering down the aisle of the plane than looking forward out the window,” he reasons. “The bit that really matters for me is being in the cockpit, looking forward, however many people we’ve got behind us.” So Jackson is constantly checking that his headcount is not growing faster than Octopus is adding new customers, as he looks to avoid diseconomies of scale and guards against the spread of bureaucracy. Yet he is equally anxious about ensuring that he is not losing touch with customers as their numbers run into the millions. Octopus was built on a proprietary technology platform called Kraken, which it spun off as a standalone company after a fundraising that valued the former subsidiary at $8.7 billion. Kraken gives Jackson and every member of his staff a “single view” of everything that is happening in the company, from customer service to pricing, energy trading to finance. Despite that tech-driven transparency, Jackson has maintained a habit of regularly meeting customers face-to-face. In the two weeks before our interview, he met roughly 1,000 customers at three different events, he estimates. “I stand on stage and talk to them, and then I get off the stage and have beers with them and understand their real experiences. They tell me not what our reports say, but what their real experience of dealing with our team is.” Everyone who signs up for an Octopus service is given Jackson’s email address. He used to answer each message himself, until Octopus reached 1.2 million customers and he found himself falling asleep at his keyboard at 2 am. Now his chief of staff and a team of five people farm out customers’ complaints and observations to the relevant executives, but he thinks the system still builds a “magic connectivity” with customers. “We’re not crazy hippies,” he says. “If we genuinely love our customers, they reciprocate.” How a CEO replaces themself when ther

events.title: After Factory’s public spat with Khosla, Menlo proudly invests
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Menlo Ventures partner Matt Murphy and his team announced Monday in a blog post that the firm has invested in AI coding startup Factory. Menlo declined to comment on how much it invested but said the deal was part of Factory’s latest funding round announced last month at a $5 billion valuation. A source familiar with the deal told us the investment was significant to Menlo — not a token gesture — and that Menlo would have invested more had there been room on the cap table. Ordinarily, something like this wouldn’t necessarily be news; startups often extend previous rounds to add new investors. But last week, Factory co-founder and CEO Matan Grinberg was embroiled in a very public airing of dirty laundry when he alleged that he had fired investor Chris Degnan of firm RPT Partners from his role as board advisor. Grinberg said he feared Degnan may have shared confidential information with Factory’s biggest competitor, Cognition. The accusation followed Degnan’s move to Cognition as its chief revenue officer. A who’s who of the tech industry came out of the woodwork either to support Degnan and condemn Factory, or vice versa, but none was more surprising than Vinod Khosla. Khosla’s firm is an investor in both Factory and Cognition. But that didn’t stop the venerable VC from calling Factory a desperate “struggling second tier competitor,” and accusing Grinberg of lying about firing Degnan and impugning his character. Degnan disputed Grinberg’s story, saying he resigned and that he’d rebuffed a competing job offer from Grinberg. So Menlo’s full-throated endorsement of Factory, which praised its founders, its tech, and its relationship with its customers, is more than a feather in Factory’s cap. It’s a statement that Factory is not in the state that Khosla implied it was. Murphy famously bet his firm on Anthropic back when it appeared to be an also-ran to OpenAI and has been on a hot streak ever since, landing deals with Lovable and Legora, for instance. So now some VCs are calling Factory “the next Anthropic. “ Sequoia’s Shaun Maguire, also a Factory backer who came out on X in support of Grinberg last week, appears thrilled with Menlo’s endorsement, saying the firm is “on a tear.” Notably, Menlo is not an investor in competitor Cognition. events.title: Reflection debuts Beam, an open-weight AI model to rival Chinese models at lower compute cost
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Reflection AI is officially unveiling Beam, its first frontier, open-weight AI model. The two-year-old, Brooklyn-based startup claims Beam matches the performance of leading Chinese open models on advanced reasoning benchmarks at dramatically lower costs, a claim that could heat up the race to build a Western answer to DeepSeek, Qwen, and Z.ai. Reflection’s announcement confirms reporting from Axios over the weekend that the startup was close to a launch. The company shared new details in a lengthy blog post Monday , which described Beam as a text-only mixture-of-experts model trained on high-compute reinforcement learning to be effective at reasoning, coding, and agentic tasks at “a fraction of the token cost and inference time compute” of rivals. Beam is a 501-billion-parameter model with 23 billion active parameters. It was pretrained on 23.8 trillion tokens and has a 1 million token context window. To compare, Z.ai’s GLM-5.2 has roughly 744 billion total parameters with 40 billion active. Reflection’s performance claims haven’t been independently verified, but on advanced reasoning benchmarks, the company says Beam scores on par with Z.ai’s GLM-5.2 and outperforms today’s leading Western open models while using “3-4x less inference compute.” Reflection calls it a “workhorse model” for enterprises, the public sector, and developers. Reflection is positioning itself against closed labs like Anthropic and OpenAI, against popular open models from Chinese developers, and against Western players like Mistral, Meta, and Cohere. Its most direct U.S. rival might be Inkling , the open model from Mira Murati’s Thinking Machines Lab released in July. Reflection’s own benchmarks show that Beam outscores Inkling on four coding tests where both report results, but Inkling is a multimodal model and Beam is text-only. Reflection was founded in 2024 by two former Google DeepMind researchers and has raised roughly $4.7 billion from backers, including Nvidia, Sequoia Capital, and Lightspeed Venture Partners, per PitchBook. Its last round valued the company at a $25 billion pre-money valuation . The startup has also been locking up compute — a key ingredient needed to train frontier models capable of luring customers away from Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s closed models, as well as the cheaper open-weight models from Chinese labs. This summer, Reflection signed deals collectively worth more than $7 billion with SpaceX and Nebius to secure access to Nvidia’s GB300 chips through 2029. Reflection is aiming Beam and future models at enterprises and sovereign nations. The pitch is to build “AI factories,” a product that would let institutions build their own customized, local AI system by training Reflection’s AI models on their own proprietary data. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, whose company backs Reflection, has long championed the “AI factory” idea and pushed to strengthen the open AI ecosystem — a vision that would also benefit Nvidia, whose GPUs would power those systems. Axios reported that hedge funds and trading firms are among those eager to build such systems. Reflection has already begun testing the concept of a sovereign AI factory partnership with Shinsegae Group in South Korea . Reflection says it will release Beam’s weights and full technical details this month, with distribution through hyperscalers and neoclouds and integrations across open source libraries at launch. Reflection did not respond in time to TechCrunch’s requests for more information. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission .
