events.title: Gatorade maker recalls 122,000 cases of popular sports drink across 37 US states
events.summary: PepsiCo initiated class II recall of 28oz bottles last month over ‘undeclared’ yellow dyes, FDA notice says About 122,000 cases of the popular sports drink Gatorade have been voluntarily recalled across 37 US states due to their having “undeclared” food dye, according to an official federal notice . The varieties of the drink involved in the notice include 28oz bottles of Gatorade Lemon Lime, Lime Zero, Orange and Gatorade Orange Zero, the notice said. Gatorade’s manufacturer – the soda giant PepsiCo – initiated its recall on 25 September, said the advisory, which was posted on the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA)’s website. The notice said the recall was considered class II, implying “a situation in which use of, or exposure to, a violative product may cause temporary or medically reversible adverse health consequences or where the probability of serious adverse health consequences is remote”, according to the FDA. “Undeclared Yellow No 6 and/or Yellow No 5” dyes were listed in the FDA notice as the “reason for recall” for people who are potentially sensitive to them. PepsiCo did not immediately respond to a request for comment from the Guardian. The states listed for the recall are: Alaska, Alabama, Arkansas, Arizona, California, Colorado, Florida, Georgia, Hawaii, Iowa, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, Mississippi, North Carolina, North Dakota, Nebraska, New Jersey, New Mexico, Nevada, New York, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, Washington and Wisconsin. CBS News reported that it was not known whether refunds were available for people who purchased the recalled Gatorade drinks. The FDA has come under fire during Donald Trump ’s second presidency, including after the agency implemented layoffs , slashing its staff by almost 20%.

events.title: Imposter recruiters taking over the job market
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Jobseekers exploited by recruitment scammers on LinkedIn Job seekers are noticing an increase in recruitment scams on LinkedIn. ( REUTERS/Robert Galbraith ) Tony Young is one of many Australians who have applied for work using websites like LinkedIn, only to realise afterwards it was a scam. The former tech executive has sent out applications for more than 400 jobs over the past three years. While responding to a job advertisement on LinkedIn, Tony was contacted by someone claiming to be a consultant who could help improve his resume. When he refused, the "consultant" quickly lowered their offer and asked Tony whether he would "do it for $50". The ABC has observed an uptick in fraud targeting jobseekers as soon as they update their online status to indicate they are looking for work. Sophisticated employment fraudsters target jobseekers as soon as they announce their unemployment. ( ABC News ) It includes fake job ads, fraudsters posing as recruiters with "cloned" profiles and people taking advantage of desperate jobseekers by offering to help with CV writing for significant sums of money. Australian jobseekers are being warned about this pervasive, sophisticated employment fraud as recruiters voiced concerns to the ABC and in online forums about fake advertisements flooding recruitment websites. The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) said in just two months, July and August 2026, it received 138 scam reports relating to LinkedIn with reported losses of up to $254,449. Tony said he often received emails or comments on his online posts that seemed to be from companies purporting to be "hiring" on LinkedIn. In June, he received an email from a so-called "career and talent leader" at engineering consultancy Aurecon who wanted to have a "senior leadership discussion" with him. Tony says he often receives targeted emails and comments. ( ABC News ) The ABC can confirm that no-one from Aurecon actually contacted Tony. In addition, the person who emailed Tony had cloned a LinkedIn profile belonging to a real employee from the engineering firm. Aurecon said it was aware that fraudsters sometimes misused its brand name to deceive jobseekers through fake job emails, fraudulent websites or unsolicited job offers. The company stressed that it conducts formal virtual or in-person interviews before making offers and would never ask candidates to make any up-front payments. LinkedIn's latest Job Search Safety Pulse report has found Australians are more vulnerable to recruitment scams than ever. Nearly half of the people surveyed for that report said they would take risks when applying for jobs due to ongoing cost-of-living pressures. More than a third said they would be more likely to let their guard down. Questioning whether a job is "actually real" has also become a routine part of the job search, according to the LinkedIn report. The same report found 61 per cent of Australians had seen a job ad that they suspected was fraudulent and 27 per cent have come close to falling for one. Around 16 per cent of the respondents said they had fallen victim to job scams. For younger gen Z jobseekers, born between 1997 and 2012, employment scam victim percentages rose to 25 per cent. Do you know more about job scams on LinkedIn? We would like to hear from you! Contact our journalist confidentially on li.yiying@abc.net.au or li.yiying@proton.me . "Recruitment scammers often pretend to represent large companies or recruitment firms and will contact people either directly through LinkedIn or via email with a job opportunity that is tailored to the information on their LinkedIn profile," an ACCC spokesperson said. They said "job scams may ask people to pay money to start a job" or participate in a "course or training". Trevor Churchley says scam activities on LinkedIn have become more noticeable in the past two years. ( LinkedIn: Trevor Churchley ) Tech recruiter Trevor Churchley said scam activities on LinkedIn had become more noticeable in the past two years. Mr Churchley said he was personally aware of several real profiles being "taken over or cloned". He said the fake profiles were then used to target jobseekers who publicly disclosed they were unemployed. "They're the perfect target to approach because … all of a sudden, they gain the attention of recruiters … hopefully leading to jobs," Mr Churchley said. Many applicants place the #opentowork banner on their LinkedIn profiles, hoping to become more visible to recruiters. Jobseekers attract attention from recruiters and scammers once they put an #opentowork banner on.

events.title: TikTok rolls out an AI shopping assistant and one-click checkout
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. TikTok announced Monday that it’s launching an AI shopping assistant and a new in-app checkout feature that lets users buy directly from brands. TikTok describes its new Shopping Assistant as a conversational AI agent designed to help users discover and purchase products. The company says the assistant understands context and remembers users’ preferences and needs throughout the conversation. It offers real-time, AI-powered shopping guidance, such as product details, shipping information, sizing, availability, and help completing a purchase. As for the new checkout feature, TikTok says users can buy directly from a brand from their For You feed (the app’s main, algorithm-driven video feed) with one click. The new features could allow TikTok to capture more of users’ shopping journeys, and potentially more transaction value, without sending them elsewhere. By pairing a shopping assistant with direct payments, TikTok is turning its impulse-driven discovery feed into a place where users can get answers to questions about a product and make a purchase on the spot. By building an AI assistant for shopping directly in its app, TikTok also appears to be hoping that users will stay within its platform when they have questions about a product, rather than turning to outside AI tools like OpenAI’s ChatGPT. The company says these new features are being built in partnership with commerce platforms and payment providers including Salesforce, Shopify, Shoplazza, and Stripe, among others. While TikTok Shop, the app’s in-house marketplace, has been the platform’s main engine for the company’s e-commerce ambitions, these new features broaden its approach beyond the existing shopping hub. Rather than relying on TikTok Shop to drive purchases, the social network is now integrating shopping tools more directly into the broader app, including the For You feed. The expansion comes as TikTok’s influence on shopping continues to grow. According to TikTok’s Economic Impact Report that was released last week, activity on the platform helped generate $81 billion in GDP for U.S. businesses, while 54 million Americans said they had purchased a product after watching a TikTok video. TikTok Shop launched in the U.S. in September 2023. The market research firm eMarketer estimates it generated about $15.8 billion in U.S. sales in 2025, representing roughly 18% of all U.S. social commerce. events.title: They built a multi-million-dollar empire cashing in on veterans
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts They built a business empire that cashes in on veterans. It's made millions The Veteran Benefits Australia empire is the brainchild of friends Nick Flanigan and Tom Bailey. ( Supplied ) From the outside, the only clues something was up in the industrial estate office building in Brisbane's south were the expensive cars with personalised plates clogging the driveway. Inside, the lavishly decorated office had gold accents in the bathroom and chandeliers in the kitchen where staff had Monday lunches. This was the heart of the Veteran Benefits Australia (VBA) empire — the brainchild of exercise physiologist Nick Flanigan and pharmacist Tom Bailey. The organisation appeared to simply connect veterans to the taxpayer-funded care they needed. But a Four Corners investigation has found that behind the scenes, the companies in the VBA network have made millions by turning veterans into valuable sales leads on an industrial scale. A Christmas staff lunch in VBA's headquarters. ( Supplied ) Veterans lured in by freebies and competitions on social media would end up on VBA's books, passed from one entity to another, each billing the Department of Veterans' Affairs (DVA) for their services. An internal email shows staff were told veterans should be told to sign over their DVA-funded GP care plans, worth thousands of dollars, to VBA, in order to access other forms of care like medicinal cannabis or "free" medication packs. In other cases, veterans' DVA details were used for billing by multiple allied health practitioners they had never even spoken to. Four Corners spoke to more than 50 current and former staff and clients and reviewed hundreds of pages of internal emails, company documents and corporate filings to piece together a system that enriched those at the top. While dozens of individual practitioners working for companies in the ecosystem have been accused by the DVA of overservicing and incorrect billing, the companies and the individuals running them have escaped scrutiny. Nick and Tom open their office in Algester, in Brisbane's south. ( Supplied ) After the Royal Commission into Defence and Veteran Suicide found veterans were struggling to get the compensation and care they needed, the government responded by pumping more than half a billion dollars into the complex system to clear a backlog of claims and improve services. The influx of money created an opportunity for a range of for-profit companies to cash in on connecting veterans to the care they needed. Veteran Benefits Australia started as a "blog" that says it connects veterans to "independent" services. But VBA itself is really a marketing funnel that feeds into what they referred to internally as "the Veteran Benefits Australia Ecosystem", a network of more than 70 companies, dozens providing services to veterans. An internal diagram shows how companies in the VBA ecosystem worked together to bill the DVA for different services for veterans, while other companies serviced the entities themselves, including a marketing company that billed the rest of the entities for "leads". An internal document from 2025 shows just some of the entities in the VBA ecosystem. ( Supplied ) Here's how it worked. Veterans would see a targeted ad offering anything from free headphones, backpacks and smartwatches to dream holiday competitions. To enter or sign up they had to provide their DVA details. Facebook ads targeting veterans from companies within the VBA network. ( Facebook ) Next, veterans would get a call asking if they wanted a range of "free" DVA-funded services. "If you say yes, then you've really opened the door for multiple calls. They're going to try to find every procedure, every process that they can put you through," Jon Hays, a former manager at one of the companies, Medibase Health, said. "There was veterans calling saying, 'I'm being called every day of the week. I don't need that service. Why do they call me all the time?'" he said. In some cases, veterans had no idea who was calling them or what was being billed against their DVA number by practitioners they had never even spoken to. The VBA marketing machine was working. An internal email shows, as early as 2022, Nick Flanigan boasting that a business he and Tom Bailey co-owned had amassed a database with 180,000 veterans' details in it. Nick (above) and Tom (below) seen here in a video promoting one of their other businesses, a car raffle. ( Supplied ) The next year he emailed some of the entities to suggest a marketing campaign to "hit more aggressive KPIs and grow the database even more".

events.title: The college with the highest first-year retention rate in every state
events.summary: The Massachusetts Institute of Technology had a first-year retention rate of 99%. Erica Denhoff/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Massachusetts Institute of Technology has a reputation for producing famous tech dropouts. But in reality, 99% of first-year students return — the highest rate in Massachusetts. Here is the college with the highest first-year retention rate in every state. Getting a student to choose a college is one thing. Getting them to come back for another year is just as important. Ranging from Ivy League universities to military academies , Business Insider calculated the college with the highest retention rate in each state. The first-year retention rate shows the proportion of students who return to their studies in the fall for their sophomore year. It's a metric colleges care about because it can indicate higher student satisfaction and strong academic support. Business Insider compiled each state's winner using provisional fall 2024 data from the Department of Education's Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System (IPEDS). The retention rate covers full-time, first-time bachelor-seeking students who entered in fall 2023 and measures whether they returned for fall 2024. The cohort size is adjusted to account for any permitted exclusions, such as a student's death. Business Insider also limited the data to degree-granting institutions only and set a minimum cohort size of 100 to avoid very small cohorts inflating retention rates. Because the data is provisional, the figures could be revised and should not be considered final counts. Here are the colleges with the highest retention rate in every state. events.title: Sam Altman says Elon Musk is a ‘bully’ who only respects people who punch him back
events.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman Heather Diehl/Getty Images OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said a little drama may grease the gears for talks with Elon Musk. "I think once in a while you've got to punch a bully back in the nose," Altman told Vanity Fair. Altman said that Musk "only respects people" who take such an approach. Sam Altman says you need to accept some level of drama if you want him and Elon Musk to work together. "I think once in a while you've got to punch a bully back in the nose," Altman told Vanity Fair during a wide-ranging interview. "And I also think Elon, like many bullies, only respects people who do." Altman and Musk had a famous falling-out that has since been recounted and is at the center of multiple legal battles. Their drama, which is far from the only simmering beef in the AI world , is now also the backdrop to efforts among the world's largest AI companies to reach a consensus on how to steer their technology. The OpenAI CEO said he would work with Musk, who has taken to calling his one-time ally "Scam Altman ," as the industry grapples with renewed concerns over AI safety. "If you want me to be able to work with him, maybe you should be happy I hit back once in a while, but I will work with Elon, of course," he said. For his part, Altman said that he "won't call myself a saint." At the same time, he doesn't view himself as the biggest problem. "I'm not sure if I'm the one that you're supposed to come after between Elon and me," he said. In July, Musk lashed out at Altman when another account said that he had "warned the world about Scam Altman." Musk quoted that post and added, "He takes scamming to a whole new level." In response, Altman took a shot at Musk's advocacy for orbital data centers , something the OpenAI CEO has repeatedly expressed skepticism about. "Homeboy you're the one selling public market investors on short-term space datacenters," Altman wrote. Despite the drama, AI companies have taken more steps toward cooperation. Leaders of OpenAI, Anthropic, SpaceXAI, Google, and Nvidia signed a White House-driven agreement in which the companies agreed to some self-imposed safety measures. Altman told Politico's Decoded Podcast that there's no single group chat, but officials at frontier labs have multiple avenues to continue talking. "There's no like big WhatsApp that everybody's in," Altman said, "but there's like lots of, you know, people are running into each other at the same conference. There's calls, occasional meetings, stuff like that." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: At 19, founder raises $11M for Ghost, maker of a $3,499 computer for personal AI
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. For much of his life, Zain Javaid, 19, wanted to be a quant who uses math and data to guide his investment decisions. And for a while, he was one. But he got bored. Then, in 2022, ChatGPT was released, and he told TechCrunch, “I felt fundamentally excited in a way that I never had been before.” He became interested in personal AI, and that interest led him to start Ghost, which announced Monday that it has emerged from stealth after a year of building, along with an $11 million seed round led by Andreessen Horowitz. Other investors in the round include Abstract, Audacious Ventures, SV Angel, and Nova. His founding team includes Nicholas Chua, 19, Yifei Chen, 24, and Gautam Sharda, 23. Ghost’s first product is Core, a personal computer designed specifically for AI agents that can take actions on a person’s behalf. According to Javaid, the idea is to centralize a person’s data, from what’s on their desktop to apps to smart home devices, into one piece of hardware designed to continuously run AI agents that can act as an assistant, perform tasks, and understand a person’s life. “You can run models on existing hardware, but it’s a terrible experience on many levels,” said Javaid, who is also Core’s CEO. Core includes an Nvidia RTX Pro 4000 SFF Blackwell GPU (a type of chip commonly used to run AI models), said Javaid, adding that the GPU is bundled into the device’s price, so customers don’t need to buy one separately. He said it also has its own software layer, browser, and filing system and can continuously process information and tasks without constant prompting. Core costs $3,499. Preorders for the first batch open Monday, and shipping is scheduled for the last week of October. Javaid described Core as a “brain in a box” without a screen, which users access through a phone or app. Voice mode is also available, but users must speak into the Core app rather than the box itself. Core comes with three models preinstalled: Qwen-3.8-Next, Qwen-3.8-27B, and Gemma-4-31B. Javaid said users can also install other models from Hugging Face, where developers share AI models, or load their own trained models. Asked how Core differs from a Mac Mini, Apple’s small desktop computer that some people set up to run AI tools, Javaid said Core’s hardware and software were built specifically for running AI agents, with models already installed, while the Mac Mini is a general-purpose computer that can be configured for AI. “As new models or improvements to existing models come out, we can push out over-the-air updates, similar to how Tesla works,” Javaid said of Core, adding that if a new generation of models comes out, the company asks users whether they want to switch. “Users can also turn on auto-updates so they’re always running the latest generation of a given model.” The team currently builds the units at its San Francisco facility. Javaid said the goal is to sell a fully functioning computer that doesn’t require complex setup or configuration. He said the models and personal memory run locally, and that all personal information is encrypted so that no cloud provider or third party, including Ghost, can meaningfully access it. He also said users can control how much autonomy they give their Core agents, and that the device is programmed to keep working if Ghost shuts down. “All of the source code, logic, and model weights live on the device, not the services,” he said. “We build this device to not be dependent on having an outside entity maintaining the service.” He said the team is also building a firewall to limit how the agent can use its credentials, such as logins and passwords. The firewall “monitors every outgoing network request on the computer and if it sees the agent performing a sanctioned action or exfiltrating data it shouldn’t, it rejects the request and flags it for user review.” “The user owns all of it,” he said of the device, memory, and data. “Once you buy the hardware, everything is stored, run, and processed on the device.” He said he is not too worried about the competition, including from established tech companies. “People sometimes give incumbents credit for having already built the product because they have the ingredients,” he said. He credited Apple with good hardware and disruption, but said much of what Core is aiming to tackle is software: “The model reasons over your life, how it remembers, how it takes action, how it knows when to reach out,” he continued. Javaid offered an example of how Core is meant to work: “Core proactively sends you a notification that you might be getting sick because it sees your resting heart rate is elevated, sees from computer history that you were up late working on a project, and has seasonal context that it is flu season in San Francisco.

Why it matters: It's the latest example of President Trump's allies targeting Amodei. Moreno's letter comes ahead of Anthropic's expected historic IPO , with valuation estimates as high as nearly $2 trillion. "I do not understand how you can ask them to invest their hard-earned savings in Anthropic's continued development while warning those same Americans that your product could ultimately lead to their extinction," Moreno wrote, referencing the expected IPO. Zoom in: "With great power comes great responsibility," Moreno wrote, "and in this case, I am concerned that you are failing to meet the moment." Moreno adopted Trump's new terminology, replacing artificial intelligence (AI) with super intelligence (SI). He said Amodei's own words agreeing with "doomer" views about the potential for AI to kill humans, "indicate that your instinct is to wreak havoc on the public SI discourse." Moreno urged more emphasis on how AI can also be used to protect against the very safety threats being warned about as well as how how it can strengthen national security and ensure the U.S. stays ahead of China. Zoom out: Public concern over AI advancement and data centers has become a focus of the midterm election. Moreno's fellow Ohio Republican, Sen. Jon Husted, has faced an onslaught of ads accusing him of being pro-data centers as he seeks re-election.

events.title: 6 Guidelines for Governing AI
events.summary: For the first 10 years of my career, I worked in product management and data analytics by myself. I wrote database queries that pulled numbers out of corporate systems, built statistical models to predict what customers would buy, and shipped data pipelines that moved information between business systems. I built and scaled analytics teams at Best Buy and Target , studying how customers shop and what stores should stock. Today I lead enterprise AI transformation at Lowe’s , the Fortune 100 home improvement retailer. The goal is not to sell artificial intelligence ; it is to use it to deliver useful expertise at the moment a customer needs it. In retail and other customer-facing industries, virtual assistants can help people address everyday questions—such as how to repair a leaky faucet—while guiding them toward relevant products, services, or next steps. As these capabilities become more common, technology roles are changing. The work is no longer limited to building AI systems ; it also includes defining how they operate: which decisions they can make autonomously, when they must escalate to a person, and which actions must remain off-limits. That shift—from building AI systems to governing them —is coming for anyone who is accountable for what such systems produce. Not the casual user typing into a chatbot but the engineers, product managers, analysts, and business operators who sign off on work a machine drafted. It is the subject of the book I recently coauthored, The Enterprise Brain . I call the change the “governor shift,” from executing tasks yourself to setting the intent, principles, and boundaries within systems that execute them for you. Business operators might not write code; they will decide which pricing exceptions an agent may approve and which it must escalate. That is governing. A 2025 report from MIT Media Lab’s Project NANDA found that, despite an estimated US $30 billion to $40 billion in enterprise generative-AI investment, the vast majority of organizations in its dataset had not yet demonstrated measurable profit-and-loss impact. The report estimated that only about 5 percent of integrated pilots were generating substantial value, underscoring how difficult it remains to move from experimentation to scaled business outcomes. Researchers named the pattern the GenAI Divide , the term I adopted for the book. The companies rarely lack technology; they use the same models as the 5 percent that are winners. But they lack people who can direct the systems and stand behind the results. Guidelines to follow Here are six guidelines. Recognize when you have become “human middleware.” In software, “middleware” is the code that sits between two systems and passes information back and forth. Many of us have become its human version. Take an honest look at your week. How much time is spent pulling data out of one tool, reformatting it, and routing it to another team? I call this the “administrator trap,” which is set by the architecture, not by the people caught in it. Relaying is what AI agents now do well. But they cannot judge which numbers deserve attention, which risks are real, or which compromises are worth making. Trade rules for principles. For many years, workers used rules to manage their work. Refunds for a product over a certain amount needed a signature from upper management, for example. Writing code needed two reviewers. Rules work at human speed. But rules break when a system makes thousands of decisions per hour and meets situations no rulebook anticipated, such as a complaint covered by three different policies. A rule says to do exactly this specific thing; a principle says to achieve the outcome without crossing certain lines. Governing AI means writing those principles in priority order so the system settles its own conflicts the way a well-led team does when the manager is not available. Never harm the customer. Tell the truth even if the company loses a sale. Protect the economics, and then move quickly. Underneath sits a question of decision rights: the formal authority over who or what may make a given call. Writing down the answers in what I call a “library of principles” is now core leadership work, whether you’re a technologist or a business owner. Write your culture into your code. Many companies have turned their values into posters that hang on office walls. But an AI agent cannot read the posters. Instead, write your governance as code. Include your values and policies as machine-readable instructions that the AI agent will follow automatically. Do so in three layers. The top is the constitution, which states the rules an agent may never break, and never state a fact it cannot support. The second layer is the doctrine: how the business competes and the acceptable trade-offs to get there, such as protecting a long-term relationship over a short-term sale. At the bottom sits the playbook, which has the tactics used for one task. Install a trust thermostat, not a trust switch. The question that stalls nearly every company’s AI deployment is some version of: “What if it tells our biggest customer something wrong, or quotes a price we will not honor?” It might. Treating trust as a switch leaves two bad options: an unsupervised system or a human reviewing every transaction—which would cost more than the automation would save. The alternative is a thermostat. Every decision an agent makes carries a confidence score measured against the principles set. Above an agreed threshold, it proceeds alone; below it, a human decides. That person’s answer is fed back into the learning loop so the next similar case clears the threshold on its own. Every decision stays transparent, auditable, and explainable—which is what I call a glass box. Fix context before you govern. You cannot govern a system that cannot see the whole picture. Ask your best employee about a project, and they will pull together the budget, the contract clause, and the customer’s last complaint because they know it all by heart. Most enterprise AI fails that test, because the information sits scattered across applications that store it in incompatible formats. I describe the full loop as Connections, Context, Reasoning, Actions, and Governance (CCRAG). Connections feed in raw information such as transactions and service records. Context weaves it into a context graph, which is a single connected picture of the business that gives agents something close to memory. Reasoning makes the decisions. Actions carry them back into the business systems. Governance keeps things aligned with the company’s intent. Most organizations obsess over the reasoning in the middle and underinvest in context and governance, which is exactly where humans play a role. Context compounds: Every interaction makes the graph richer and harder to reproduce. Learn to lead by exception. The most important change in habit comes last. Anastasia Sevriukova When she was 25, Anastasia Sevriukova experienced a few colon cancer symptoms . Because she had no family history, she thought she had hemorrhoids and was just tired from her job. She was diagnosed with stage 4 colon cancer. When Anastasia Sevriukova first noticed blood in her stool at age 25, she didn't tell anyone at first — not her then-boyfriend or her mom. Her Google search narrowed the cause down to either colon cancer — which seemed extremely unlikely due to her lack of family history — or hemorrhoids. "I Googled 'I had oysters. Did the shell cut my intestine?'" Sevriukova, now 27, told Business Insider. She tried hemorrhoid creams that didn't work. When the bleeding persisted for months, she saw a primary care physician in September 2024, who put her on a four-month waitlist to see a GI. In the meantime, Sevriukova kept living her life in St. Louis, Missouri. She worked as an engineer for Boeing's military branch . In her free time, she learned to watercolor and had one of her paintings displayed at a local exhibition. Sevriukova was passionate about her work as an aerospace engineer. Anastasia Sevriukova Even at the end of 2024, when she was told that she'd be laid off from Boeing in mid-January 2025, things were looking up. Shortly after, Sevriukova, who is Ukrainian, was offered a position at a San Francisco startup developing drones to be used by Ukraine in the ongoing war — a dream job. Weeks later, she got engaged. "The whole month was a rollercoaster," she said. Between plans to start the new job, move to a new city, and eventually build a family with her now-fiancé, Sevriukova was excited about the future. Then, four days after the engagement, she was diagnosed with stage 4 colon cancer . "Everything had to pretty much stop because I was very, very sick," she said. "It was really difficult to accept that I need to take a break for now." She thought she was tired because of work Sevriukova's ongoing fatigue ended up being a sign of anemia, a common side effect of colon cancer. Anastasia Sevriukova In the months leading up to her scheduled GI appointment in January 2025, Sevriukova frequently felt very fatigued. "I was like 'I'm just tired from work, I have to do a lot,'" she said. Then there was the date night a week before the doctor's visit. She and her fiancé went to a wine-and-pizza bar. Suddenly, Sevriukova felt drunk from one glass. After her diagnosis, she learned that she had anemia , a common symptom of colon cancer. She had a hemoglobin level of 8 g/dL (a normal range for women is 12 to 15.5 g/dL). A CT scan revealed her stage 4 colon cancer diagnosis, and explained her feeling drunk off one drink: It was a sign of her liver not functioning properly, because the cancer had spread to it. Given her diagnosis, Sevriukova declined her job offer. The couple moved to Rochester, Minnesota, where Sevriukova's mother lives. Upon seeing her new oncologist, she was put on an iron infusion before starting cancer treatment. She also underwent genetic testing and learned she had no predisposition for cancer, such as Lynch syndrome . "It was a stroke of bad luck," she said. A breakneck decision about her future fertility Sevriukova (pictured with her fiancé, Pradeep), was given two weeks to extract and freeze Sevriukova's eggs before starting chemotherapy. Anastasia Sevriukova Sevriukova's oncologist told her that she would most likely lose her ability to have kids after side effects from chemotherapy. Because he wanted to start her treatment right away, he gave her two weeks to retrieve and freeze her eggs . Sevriukova was referred to the Mayo Clinic and decided to go through with the procedure. "It was very physically and emotionally demanding," Sevriukova said. "I was also trying to process at the same time, the fact that whatever eggs they can get, that's all they got." She had her egg extraction in March 2025. Two days later, she started chemotherapy and antibody therapy, which her doctors selected after a liver biopsy identified features of her tumor relevant to treatment. By that point, she was exhausted from two weeks of hormone therapy to produce as many eggs as possible, plus the frequent bloodwork and ultrasound appointments during the monitoring phase. The egg retrieval itself was also painful and led to spotting by the time she began cancer treatment. "Yet, I do not regret it at all," Sevriukova said. "It was the best decision I've made." She took a break from both treatments in June 2025, when she was prepped for surgery on her colon and the installation of a hepatic artery infusion (HAI) pump, which channels chemotherapy medication directly into the liver. Sevriukova dealt with unexpected and painful complications during her treatment. Anastasia Sevriukova There were complications with the surgery. She had a rare bowel leak because the incision in her colon was not sealed properly, leading to an infection in her abdomen. "That is probably the most pain I have experienced in my life," she said, spending 20 days in the hospital. The resulting surgery left Sevriukova with scars and a stoma bag, a waste collection pouch outside of her abdomen. "I could not stop crying for days, and the nurses didn't even know what to do, how to console me," she said. "My body doesn't look like what it used to look like a year ago, and body image is a huge, huge aspect of a young woman's life." She needed a liver transplant After her liver transplant, Sevriukova was briefly cancer-free for 3 months. Anastasia Sevriukova From the beginning, Sevriukova had "too many tumors to count" on her liver . Even when her scans were clear, the tumors would quickly resurface the moment she stopped chemo. "I never know when the cancer decides to mutate and take over," she said. Sevriukova was eventually able to get a liver transplant in June 2026, which left her cancer-free for three months. Then, in August 2026, a CT scan revealed a few small tumors on her lungs. She will soon resume chemotherapy and antibody therapy. Sevriukova has gradually adjusted to her new normal. She said that when she's in treatment, her mom, sister, and fiancé take turns staying with her at the hospital and talking to doctors on her behalf. The side effects of treatment have been so debilitating that Sevriukova can't work — something she found devastating at the start of treatment. Instead, she's taking a full semester of computer science courses from a local community college, with the aim of getting her master's and advancing her career. events.title: Business class seemed out of reach for my family of 4 — until we found an easier way to find the right deals
events.summary: I didn't think my family of four would be able to get business-class seats or other upgrades using our credit-card points. Then, we found a better way to review point deals. Blythe Chadim We wanted to use points to get business-class seats for our family of four, but felt overwhelmed. To help, we used a tool to find deals that work with our credit-card points and our family's needs. Ultimately, it helped us find four business-class and four economy-plus seats that worked for us. Two years ago, when my family of four flew from Dallas to Scotland via London, our young children barely slept on the 10-hour economy flight, leading to meltdowns and frustration. So, when we planned our trip to Europe earlier this year, my husband and I wanted to do anything we could to avoid this travel chaos. Ideally, that meant booking upgraded seats to make our long flights more comfortable. Our main goal was business class, but we couldn't justify spending over $10,000 on upgrades, so we planned to use credit-card points . We had a lot to work with because we use primarily use just one Capital One card to earn points on everything we spend. Unfortunately, finding flights that worked with our schedule, points, and family wasn't so easy. For one, credit-card travel portals usually don't show every flight available with points. Airlines also limit the number of tickets available for points, making it difficult to find deals that work for a group. After spending hours opening dozens of tabs across different travel websites and scrolling through all sorts of deals, we decided to see if an online search tool might help. We had luck using a search tool to set travel alerts and find the right deal For the first time, we tried a searchable tool that helps people find deals that work with their needs and credit-card points. Blythe Chadim There are several different search engines and tools out there that help people find the best ways to optimize their credit-card points, whether they're booking hotels or flights. My husband did some research online, and we ended up trying PointsYeah to find upgraded flights that worked for us. On this searchable tool, we were able to enter details like how much we wanted to spend and with which carrier, the specific dates we wanted to travel, and our departure and arrival cities. From there, when flights that met our criteria appeared, we could receive an alert via email. PointsYeah's free version felt quite robust, especially for real-time searches, but we upgraded to a yearly plan for about $120 because it allowed us to set up to 32 point alerts, versus only four with the free version. We used the extra alerts to search by country rather than just by a specific airport, which gave us more flexibility and proved extremely useful. Departure city can be a major factor in international-flight prices , so we kept ours open to anywhere in the US. We were OK with booking separate tickets to travel from Denver to the official starting point of the international leg of our trip, provided the price was right. We also kept our arrival airport flexible between Krakow and Warsaw, and looked for specific ticket types (preferably business, but we were open to premium economy) for four people. After a few weeks and point transfers, our upgraded tickets were ready to go Business-class seats were worth using points for the added comfort, but without points, I couldn't justify the expense. Blythe Chadim Within a few days of setting up our alerts, we found our return flights. It was a bit strange booking the return first, but the deal was too good to pass up. It took us several more weeks to find an outbound flight we liked, and that meant sorting through alerts daily. Eventually, we found a points deal that we were happy with, and the alerts helped us act quickly. Once we decided to move forward with a flight, the process became a little more complex. After PointsYeah found me an option I liked, that process was in my hands. For this step, I had to visit each airline's website — in this case, KLM for a flight operated by Air France , and Air Canada for a flight operated by SWISS — set up an account, transfer our points from Capital One, and then purchase through the airline. I've found it can be tricky to convert credit-card points to miles on different airlines, so this part wasn't my favorite. Notably, some competitors, like Points.me, offer concierge services that will transfer points and book flights for you for an added fee (about $200 a person). The best flight deal we found from the United States to Poland had us flying from Chicago to Warsaw through Paris. To reach our international starting point, we bought separate tickets from our home airport in Denver to Chicago for $217.40 per person. From Chicago, we secured premium-economy seats on Air France for 75,500 points per adult and 56,625 points per child, plus $249.30 per person in fees. We enjoyed the extra legroom of premium economy. Blythe Chadim Though premium economy wasn't what we were hoping for, the extra legroom was well worth it. We even had enough room to place inflatable footrests in front of the kids after takeoff, letting them stretch out and sleep. On our return flight, we flew out of Zurich in business class on Swiss Air to Washington Dulles and connected to Denver, costing us 70,000 points per person and $165 in additional fees. We could lie completely flat, and we had plenty of legroom and access to a larger bathroom, which was very helpful with young kids. Now that I've successfully used points for upgraded seats, I can't wait to do it again We found deals that worked for our trip, and we will do it again. Blythe Chadim For our family of four, the outbound leg of our trip cost $1,866.80 and 264,250 points, and the inbound leg cost $660 and 280,000 points, for a total of $2,526.80 and 544,250 points. Had we purchased upgraded premium economy and business-class seats for cash on similar flights, it would have cost over $17,000 — an expense we definitely could not justify. Ultimately, we loved getting to skip the overwhelming, time-consuming process of sifting through page after page of points deals across different airlines. Being able to explore all our options in one spot and set alerts to only be notified of what works for us was really helpful. Although parts of the process were more complicated than we expected — we still had to transfer points and book our own tickets — PointsYeah helped us snag upgraded flights for our family that actually worked with our budget. The best tool for you will depend on your needs and preferences, but it's nice to know services like this exist, and we'll absolutely be using them again. events.title: Norway temporarily bans Meta glasses in public spaces
events.summary: The latest styles of Meta Ray-Bans won't be so popular in Norway after a temporary ban in certain public spaces. Bloomberg/Getty Images Norway is issuing a temporary ban on camera glasses in certain public spaces. Meta glasses can still be sold, and they're not banned for private use. The government plans on making a decision about regulation after more investigation. Bad news if you planned on capturing photos of the majestic fjords in your Meta Ray-Bans. Norway is issuing a temporary ban on camera glasses in public spaces like parks, schools, and beaches. This ban doesn't prohibit the sale of Meta glasses, and it only applies to their use in certain areas, like changing rooms or beaches. It also points to the need for extra privacy around places for children, like schools and daycares. Norway's Minister of Digitalization, Torgeir Micaelsen, expressed concern that new, powerful technology is being introduced where people risk being photographed, filmed or audio recorded without their knowledge, according to a translated press release . Micaelsen just started as Minister of Digitalization in September, but his predecessor had started floating the idea of looking into regulation on Meta glasses in August. Representatives for Minister Micaelsen did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Meta's CTO, Andrew Bosworth, has said that only a few "bad actors" are responsible for disabling the glasses' LED indicator lights, which has given the glasses a bad reputation as "pervert glasses ". Meta recently rolled out a software update in which the camera won't work if the light is covered or  tampered with . The government also said it will form an expert group to investigate the challenges posed by wearable technology and provide advice on permanent regulation. Norway's temporary ban follows unease about camera glasses in other European countries. In the last few weeks, a debate about smart glasses has  been brewing in the Netherlands , following media reports and advocacy group concerns. An official from the country's data privacy group told Parliament they want to wait for findings from a broader European Union report on the matter before taking any action. Meanwhile, Hans Anders, a large eyewear retailer in the Netherlands and Belgium, has paused selling Meta glasses in its stores. "We're excited that our glasses continue to be very popular for listening to music, making calls, or getting live translations, so we're continuing to expand styles and features around the world," a Meta spokesperson told Business Insider in response to the Norway ban. "Every pair with a camera has a bright light on the front that blinks when you take a photo or video," they said. " It can't be turned off, and the camera is disabled if someone covers or tampers with it -- something smartphones and other cameras don't have." Read the original article on Business Insider

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Legacy sign-on service comes back to bite school software provider Bromcom 21 hours ago Anthropic's super bug-hunting model Mythos is hardcore good at math, as latest vuln under attack shows 2 days ago OpenAI alerts 100+ orgs that its 'misaligned models' attempted to break in - or worse 3 days ago OpenAI's wandering AI agents earn it a California subpoena 3 days ago Teen suspected of running KillSec ransomware group as cops seize servers, arrest three 3 days ago The FBI and law enforcement partners have arrested “multiple” suspects as part of an investigation into a September hack allegedly involving data-theft-and-extortion group ShinyHunters, the bureau told The Register . “The bureau continues to aggressively investigate the recent cyber incident allegedly involving ShinyHunters, having already worked with partners to arrest multiple subjects and we will spare no resource in bringing each of the responsible individuals to justice,” an FBI spokesperson told us in an email on Monday. The FBI declined to comment on the specific arrests, including that of Saif al-Din Khader, a suspected ShinyHunters member who has reportedly been detained in Jordan, according to Reuters. Khader, who goes by the alias Rey, was reportedly brought into custody on September 29, and is said to be cooperating with the FBI to identify other members of the group. ShinyHunters did not respond to The Register’ s inquiries about the arrest and Khader’s alleged involvement with the criminal group. Rey confirmed his real identity - Khader - to security journalist Brian Krebs last year. Krebs described Khader as the “technical operator and public face” of Scattered LAPSUS$ Hunters . “Rey got picked up finally,” said security sleuth Kevin Beaumont following news of the arrest. According to Beaumont, Rey was “one of the kids who got into JLR.” The Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) breach , which occurred in late August 2025, affected the company's IT systems and halted manufacturing operations. Dealer systems also went down, and suppliers faced canceled or delayed orders. In addition to crippling the carmaker’s business operations for months, the digital thieves stole personal payroll data belonging to thousands of JLR employees. The cyberattack, one of the most costly in UK history , was attributed to Scattered LAPSUS$ Hunters. Khader’s detention came two weeks after the Dutch National Police arrested a 24-year-old whom the FBI described as “one of the alleged leaders of ShinyHunters.” While Dutch cops have not named the suspect, Krebs and other reports say he is Pepijn van der Stap , who was convicted in 2023 for hacking and extorting numerous organizations and was on supervised release after three years in prison. Van der Stap also worked as a software engineer at the Amsterdam-based cybersecurity startup Hadrian and volunteered as a security researcher at the Dutch Institute for Vulnerability Disclosure (DIVD). In a video message following the arrest , Brett Leatherman, assistant director of the FBI's Cyber Division, had some advice for the “remaining members” of the data theft and extortion gang. “Arrests have a way of changing who is willing to talk, and seized infrastructure has a way of showing us who's left,” Leatherman said last week. “The longer you stay in this, the more we learn about you. You know how to find us, and we know how to find you. I suggest you reach out first while the choice is still yours.” At the time, the FBI declined to answer The Register ’s questions about the video message, including whether it had seized any of the cybercrime group’s infrastructure, and whether any of ShinyHunters’ members had taken Leatherman up on his offer to “reach out first.” In late September, ShinyHunters hacked the FBIJobs.gov portal and claimed it stole sensitive personal details about current, former, and prospective FBI employees.

events.title: The Guardian view on Tory economics: Britain’s future needs more than Thatcher’s past | Editorial
events.summary: The Guardian view on Tory economics: Britain’s future needs more than Thatcher’s past The Conservatives blame their failures on abandoning their 1976 principles. But the country needs investment and resilience rather than another round of spending cuts T he Conservative party wants to go back to the future under Kemi Badenoch. In her foundational text, The Right Way , released at the weekend, the Tory party leader makes its intellectual lineage explicit, repeatedly invoking Margaret Thatcher’s 1976 policy statement The Right Approach . The 2026 economic framework is familiar: only private enterprise creates wealth; taxes, regulation and spending can obstruct growth and competition; markets make the country stronger. The speech by her shadow chancellor, Andrew Griffith, made it clear that Conservative failures over its 14-year spell in charge were the result of the party straying from Thatcherite principles. One might argue that, on the contrary, errors were because the party slavishly followed such a creed. When Rough, a depleted North Sea gasfield that once provided around 70% of the UK’s gas-storage capacity, was judged uneconomic by its private owner, a Conservative government in 2017 accepted that international markets could provide the UK with adequate energy security. That proved to be a big mistake when Russia invaded Ukraine, sending fossil fuel prices upwards. Britain was particularly exposed as a net energy importer and highly dependent on gas. Tory ministers had to bring back Rough into operation in 2022. Mrs Badenoch puts its closure down to “ false economies ”. But what was wrong was putting private profitability ahead of the country’s needs. In his speech to conference, Mr Griffith attempted to distance himself and his party from the chaotic Liz Truss administration, although he was a member of its disastrous Treasury team . But his diagnosis today appears similar. Britain, in his telling, is supposedly more of a command economy than a market‑based one. To kickstart it, he argued, will require lower taxes, welfare reform and deregulation. The difference, Mr Griffith was keen to stress, is that tax cuts will now come through spending cuts rather than additional borrowing. Why shrinking the state would strengthen growth enough to offset its effect on demand and productive capacity is unanswered. Just how big those cuts might be was revealed by the Guardian. Mr Griffiths admitted when he was the shadow business secretary that the Tories were planning to make sweeping cuts beyond the £47bn that the party had announced if it won the next election. This might be seen as the kind of clear blue water that the Tories need to put between themselves and Labour. But the real enemy is further right. As the pollster John Curtice told a Demos fringe event, the voters most dissatisfied with high rates of immigration, the performance of the economy and the NHS are disproportionately moving to Reform UK. The perceived failures of Labour are not automatically benefiting the Conservatives. Prof Curtice said that either the party was “still getting the blame” for its record in government, or Reform was “simply speaking a language” that appeals more to those voters. It is hard to see how restoring Thatcherite principles will help the party here. Mrs Badenoch recognises that the world has changed. She acknowledges that insecure supply chains and economic coercion may require the state to step in. But public investment must remain a special case, and, she says, “help to an individual firm should be exceptional and, where possible, temporary”. The real problem with her prospectus is Britain’s future requiring permission from 1976. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? events.title: Amazon hires Microsoft's former Copilot CTO
events.summary: AWS logo Noah Berger/Getty Images for Amazon Web Services AWS hired Microsoft executive Pedram Rezaei as a distinguished engineer. He is joining AWS's Agentic AI and Emerging Technologies group. Rezaei's move is the latest in a series of leadership departures from Microsoft. Amazon hired former Microsoft Copilot CTO Pedram Rezaei to help the e-commerce and cloud giant build out its agentic AI business. Rezaei joined AWS as a distinguished engineer in its Agentic AI and Emerging Technologies group, according to an email announcement on Monday. He spent two decades at Microsoft, most recently training foundation models on the company's Superintelligence team. Rezaei served as Copilot's CTO until June and previously held senior technical roles in key product areas including search engine Bing and business software suite Dynamics 365. At Amazon, Rezaei will initially work on Quick and Kiro, two products Amazon sees as central to its AI agent strategy, according to the email by Swami Sivasubramanian, the company's VP of agentic AI. An Amazon spokesperson shared the memo with Business Insider. Pedram Rezaei Amazon Quick is AWS's AI assistant and productivity app, while Kiro is an AI-powered coding tool. Quick's monthly AI users grew fourfold from the first to second quarter, while Kiro's user base doubled over the same period, Sivasubramanian noted in the email. "Pedram joins at an exciting time for our organization as we continue to build out our technical leadership team to help take on the ambitious work we have planned," he wrote in the memo. The hire gives Amazon an experienced builder from one of its biggest rivals at a moment when the company is trying to turn its AI investments into widely used products. Microsoft has made Copilot a centerpiece of its AI strategy. Amazon, meanwhile, has been building its own portfolio of AI tools, from its Bedrock model platform to coding assistants and agentic software. Rezaei's arrival also suggests Amazon is making a stronger push in the AI agent space. The market is growing quickly, with new agent offerings such as OpenAI's Dots, Meta's Muse and Instinct gaining traction. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has been shaking up leadership to accelerate its AI strategy. Two more high-profile executives are on the way out. Peter Lee, a Microsoft veteran influential in the company's AI research, on Wednesday announced plans to leave. The next day, Microsoft Office boss Ryan Roslansky said he'll be gone at the end of the year. Roslansky's departure was especially surprising as he was seen as a successor to longtime veteran Rajesh Jha, who retired in July. Roslansky was also a key part of Nadella's new inner circle and was one of three executives who made up Microsoft's new Copilot leadership team . Here's the full email from Amazon's Sivasubramanian: Team, I'm happy to share that Pedram Rezaei is joining Agentic AI and Emerging Technologies as a Distinguished Engineer , effective today. Pedram joins us after more than 20 years at Microsoft, most recently working on training foundation models and, before that, in senior architecture and CTO roles across Copilot, Power BI, and other products. He is a hands-on engineer who is still in the code every day, and he plans to keep it that way here. He lives in Seattle with his wife and their two young sons. Please join me in welcoming him. As many of you know, we have a major opportunity with Quick and Kiro to transform how work gets done. The number of users for Kiro doubled from Q1 to Q2, while monthly AI users for Quick grew 4x. Initially, Pedram will help work to bolster these product areas. His plan for the first few months is straightforward: meet people, learn how things work here, and ship something real. Pedram joins at an exciting time for our organization as we continue to build out our technical leadership team to help take on the ambitious work we have planned. In addition, I want to take this opportunity to share some news with the wider team. As many of you know, we see our investments in Neurosymbolic AI and automated reasoning as one of our biggest bets for the future, and to help execute that vision, we've brought back Marvin Theimer and Reto Kramer . They've already been back for a little while now, and it's great to have them in the fold again. Thanks for the warm welcome I know you'll extend to all three. Swami Have a tip? events.title: OpenAI PR tells journalist to ‘move on’ while asking Sam Altman about a ChatGPT user’s suicide
events.summary: An OpenAI publicist tried to change the topic of CEO Sam Altman's interview with Vanity Fair 's Mark Guiducci after the editor brought up a ChatGPT user's suicide. events.title: Hot Girl Hotline is like ‘Dear Abby’ for the AI era
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Women throughout history have always sought out relationship advice, whether from newspaper columnists like “Dear Abby,” letters to Cosmo, or just chatting with girlfriends. In the social media era, you can instead post anonymously on Reddit relationship forums or look to social media creators who discuss the topic. Now, two sisters are launching a startup for young women, Hot Girl Hotline , which focuses on bringing AI into these conversations. I know what you may be thinking: With all the advances in AI technology, founders are building something for women to talk about their dating woes? Well … yes! The reality is that people have already been turning to large language models (LLMs) via apps like ChatGPT for this type of advice, and the team believes this type of activity should be handled more carefully. Unfortunately, as we’ve seen, chatting with a general-purpose chatbot about personal topics can sometimes lead to disastrous effects — especially for those who were already mentally fragile. ChatGPT, for example, has faced a wave of lawsuits over its alleged manipulative conversation tactics that plaintiffs say contributed to negative mental health effects, including, in some cases, suicide. The idea behind Hot Girl Hotline is to reach young women who are looking to have these sorts of private conversations while navigating dating life and relationships, but in a safer way. “We’re not trying to be an AI companion,” explained Baila Mudgil , formerly a social media consultant, who co-founded the startup with her sister Sumrin (“Sumi”), who studied computer science at Stanford. “A companion is really going after solving loneliness, escapism, boredom — and you can rely on a lot of emotional dependency from that AI companion.” Baila says the startup’s approach is to focus on offering quality advice grounded in behavioral science, but in a way that makes it feel like you’re chatting with a trusted friend or big sister. The conversation is often Socratic, with the AI asking you questions to help you arrive at the answer yourself. “This is not to replace speaking to a human. This is not clinical advice, and we have a lot of safeguards in place … we take safety really seriously,” Baila said. If conversations raise flags, for instance, the user is referred to resources such as the crisis hotline 988. “We believe the key to quality advice is not just knowing what to do next; it’s understanding why you’re doing it. So that’s a big piece of it,” added Sumi. Notably, the AI also knows when to end the conversation; it doesn’t keep asking follow-up questions to drag you further down a rabbit hole. Instead, it pushes users to go take action out in the real world rather than ruminate on the problem. The sisters believe there’s room for an app like this because not everyone wants to post on the web for advice, and there are times when you don’t want to bring up a personal, dating, or relationship-focused issue with a friend. Friends can bring their own biases into the conversation, or the user may not want to put their partner on blast for something they did before they determine whether they’re going to work through it or end the relationship. “It doesn’t mean you’re replacing your friend — you’re just trying to get another perspective,” says Baila of the hotline. The app also personalizes its advice for each user to reflect their values, goals, identity, and tastes. Under the hood, the startup relies on a mix of AI models and encrypts users’ data in transit and at rest. It doesn’t sell or train on the data, either. When it uses a third-party AI model, it follows a zero-data-retention policy there as well. Hot Girl Hotline plans to monetize through a $9.99 per month subscription, which hundreds of its most active users are already paying for. Later, it may incorporate ads, too. Relationship advice is just the beginning of how the company wants to cater to young women. It also plans to expand into other areas, like beauty and lifestyle. New York-based Hot Girl Hotline is currently bootstrapped and will be participating in the Startup Battlefield 200 at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 , taking place October 13-15 in San Francisco. events.title: 5 startups that caught VCs’ attention at the latest PearX demo day
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. There isn’t a shortage of accelerators for startups, but one of the few that investors watch closely is PearX, a 12-week program that caps its cohorts at a mere 20 startups and is run by Pear VC, a pre-seed and seed-focused venture firm. PearX’s biannual demo day is consistently attended by top venture capitalists, reflecting the historically strong caliber of companies in each batch. Some of the startups that came out of recent cohorts include Known , which uses voice AI to match people for dates and secured funding from Forerunner Ventures. Another is Andera , a startup that automates corporate audit and compliance tasks and raised a $37 million Series A from Lightspeed this summer. The PearX program distinguishes itself from Y Combinator, the OG of startup accelerators, in several ways. Besides being much smaller, it doesn’t offer companies standard terms. Its investments can be as high as $2 million. Moreover, unlike YC, where some of the buzziest startups raise funding before the program ends, PearX claims to keep its participants under wraps until demo day. TechCrunch attended Pear’s latest demo day, which took place in San Francisco last week, and then stuck around to ask some of the VCs about which companies stood out to them out of the 16 startups in the batch. Below are five of the companies that seemed to have generated the most buzz. What it does: Spatial foundational models for powering robotics, gaming, and special effects. Why it stood out: While Speridlabs is certainly not the only startup developing world models to do for 3D space what LLMs did for language, it argues that its more established competitors, including Runway, Odyssey, and Google’s Genie, cannot be queried or modified. To solve this, Speridlabs built Mundus, which it calls a 3D Midjourney because it keeps its geometry persistent when a part is changed. What it does: Builds a fast, cost-efficient chip that runs inference directly on device. Why it stood out: Nvidia’s GPUs and Google’s TPUs require expensive, power-hungry memory that is currently in short supply. Saia claims to have designed a chip that bypasses traditional memory by running AI directly out of flash storage. The startup claims its chip delivers vastly superior speeds and eight times the capacity while using four times less power than Nvidia’s Jetson, a leading local AI chip and board. Saia says it’s already in discussions with Samsung regarding memory integration, plans to start fabricating test chips next year, and aims to launch mass production by 2028. Developing hardware is notoriously brutal, but 20-year-old founder Ayaan Govil managed to convince Pear VC co-founder Mar Hershenson, a semiconductor engineer with a PhD in circuit design, to take a chance on his vision. What it does: A more secure AI personal assistant. Why it stood out: Ren claims to offer functionality similar to Muse and Instinct, but with a heavy focus on security and privacy. The startup says it keeps data on-device where possible or uses a secure private cloud, checking actions against strict user-set guardrails. Furthermore, Ren distinguishes itself from competitors that rely on human operators to place phone calls by using a fully automated voice system, keeping human involvement entirely out of the loop to protect user privacy. What it does: AI native trust and estate planner. Why it stood out: Setting up a trust is expensive and time-consuming. Veros wants to simplify the work normally done by attorneys, wealth managers, and trust administrators by employing AI to recommend structures and manage assets over their lifetime. Already managing $250 million in AUM, the startup is also in the process of securing a trust charter so it can operate as a regulated trust company itself. What it does: AI engineer for industrial design. Why it stood out: Datum wants to expedite physical product development by helping engineers find and use what they built previously. The startup indexes a company’s library of 3D designs. Using proprietary Geometric Fingerprint technology, Datum identifies parts based on their shape, helping streamline and automate engineering across a massive physical design market. events.title: How Microsoft helped deliver clean water during Indonesia’s drought emergency
events.summary: Supporting communities through drought: Providing clean water in Karawang and Bekasi Working with Yayasan Rumah Energi and local disaster agencies, Microsoft helped deliver clean water to villages across two regencies during a declared drought emergency . In August 2026, due to the dry season, declining river levels and reduced irrigation flows disrupted access to water in parts of Karawang and Bekasi regencies. Irrigation channels serving rice fields began to run low, while river levels continued to fall. For families in Karawang and Bekasi, everyday activities such as washing, cooking, and bathing became increasingly difficult because access to clean water was limited. The regional disaster management agencies (BPBD) of Kabupaten Karawang and Bekasi declared a drought emergency. Fourteen villages in Kabupaten Karawang and thirty-two villages in Kabupaten Bekasi were affected, part of a wider El Nino-driven extended dry season that placed pressure on agricultural land and household water access across the region. Responding where the need was immediate Microsoft responded to the emergency by partnering with Yayasan Rumah Energi (YRE) to deliver clean water to affected communities in Kabupaten Bekasi and Kabupaten Karawang, coordinating closely with BPBD Kabupaten Bekasi and BPBD Kabupaten Karawang to identify where support was needed most. Soon afterwards, 28 water storage tanks, each with a capacity of 5,000 litres, arrived. The tanks were installed in accessible locations where households could easily reach them and filled with clean drinking water, in coordination with local officials who understood which neighbourhoods were under the most strain and village leaders who guided their placement. In total, 140,000 litres of clean water were delivered to 12 villages across the two regencies. “Thirteen districts in our area have been affected by the drought; the provision of these water storage tanks is very helpful for storing clean water, optimizing its distribution, and ensuring the tanks remain filled.” Dodi Supriadi, Kepala Bidang Kedaruratan dan Logistik, BPBD Kabupaten Bekasi. Before the tanks arrived, many families spent time searching for water that could be used for daily needs. As traditional water sources became less reliable during the dry season, access to clean water became an increasing challenge. The arrival of a filled tank within walking distance eased that pressure for many households. “It feels like a dream come true to have water in my home in this time of drought season,” said villager in Serang Village, Karawang, West Java. It is a simple statement that carries a great deal. Having clean water close to home means less time spent collecting it, reduced exposure to unsafe sources, and a welcome return to everyday routines navigating a crisis beyond their control. Local priorities, shared responsibility Emergency drought response is most effective when informed by local knowledge and a coordinated response. Before requesting support, BPBD teams in both regencies had already mapped the affected villages and identified priority locations. Yayasan Rumah Energi contributed delivery experience and established community relationships, while village leaders coordinated access so the tanks could be installed where residents could reach them. “Access to water is an essential need during the dry season. Microsoft’s support is making a direct difference while drought conditions continue. The tanks have been distributed according to community needs and made available for shared use.” Said Sumanda Tondang, Executive Director Yayasan Rumah Energi. Since 2025, Microsoft has partnered with Yayasan Rumah Energi to help address water access challenges in communities across Karawang and Cikarang. Following a comprehensive feasibility study, Yayasan Rumah Energi constructed 68 rainwater harvesting tanks in Desa Pasirranji and Desa Cicau in Cikarang, as well as Desa Wanakerta and Desa Wanajaya in Karawang. These systems enable residents to collect, filter, and store rainwater as a reliable source of clean water, particularly during the dry season when water scarcity becomes a significant challenge. The initiative is especially important in Cikarang and Karawang, where the soil is predominantly clay-based and has poor water absorption capacity, resulting in limited groundwater availability. By capturing and storing rainwater, the harvesting tanks provide communities with a sustainable and affordable source of water, improving household resilience during prolonged dry periods and improving water security for local residents. Building on this work, Microsoft and Yayasan Rumah Energi plan to continue their partnership next year, expanding access to improved water and renewable energy solutions such as biogas and solar power. ThroAugh investing in sustainable infrastructure and community well-being, the partnership aims to help local communities thrive and become more resilient. This work forms part of Microsoft’s Datacenter Community Pledge and reflects its commitment to sustainability, community prosperity, and responsible operations. “Microsoft and Rumah Energi’s support of water tanks is very impactful to residents facing a clean water crisis. We have installed the tanks across three districts, distributed according to need. We hope this assistance will help meet the community’s clean water requirements.” Said Ferry Muhammad – Kepala Bidang Kedaruratan dan Logistik, BPBD Kabupaten Karawang. Emergency support cannot prevent the dry season from returning, but it can make an immediate difference when water becomes difficult to access. In Kabupaten Karawang and Kabupaten Bekasi, collaboration between local agencies, community organisations, and private-sector partners helped bring clean water closer to families when they needed it most. The response demonstrated how partnerships built on local knowledge and shared commitment can mobilise quickly to support communities during times of need. Learn more * Yayasan Rumah Energi ### Main image: Residents can once again access water amidst the drought, with the help of Microsoft and the Rumah Energi Foundation.

So are these codec updates 3 days ago What eldritch horror lurks behind Heathrow's information screens? 6 days ago Decades-old file security flaws found in Android, Linux, macOS, and Windows 11 days ago Windows CLOSEDQUORUM malware uses AI models to autonomously select post-compromise actions 13 days ago Microsoft Windows 11 26H2 has arrived, and, unfortunately, it's already picked up a known audio issue within weeks of release. The glitch also affects Windows 11 25H2 and 24H2, which share the same code branch. It relates to decoding AC-3 (Dolby Digital) audio and can cause the application using the decoder to crash abruptly or fail to start at all. Identified after the September 22 Windows update, the issue mostly impacts older applications, according to Microsoft. "Many modern applications do not use Windows for this type of encoding and therefore will not encounter this issue. "The code component involved in this issue is most commonly used in legacy applications that still rely on Windows built-in audio decoding." In summary – if your app has the temerity to use Windows built-in audio decoding for AC-3, you might have a problem. If it includes its own audio decoding component, you should be okay. "Affected applications may vary," explained Microsoft, "and can include games, media players, and certain productivity applications." There's also no fix as yet, so uninstalling is the only way to address it for now. To be clear, the AC-3 malfunction is not specific to Windows 11 26H2; the update preceded the release of the operating system's latest version by a week. It joins other known issues in 26H2, including other ongoing audio woes that have lingered in the list despite workarounds being available from Microsoft Support for Business. Microsoft currently has no mitigation for the AC-3 bug and offers little comfort to affected users: "We are working on releasing a resolution for this issue in a future Windows update." Acknowledging the latest trouble continues a run of misfortune for Microsoft. September's Patch Tuesday resulted in an out-of-band update to deal with RDP and Hyper-V issues. The update did not, however, fix all the audio problems it introduced, and the September 22 preview update has compounded the situation.
