events.title: I turned my passion for the outdoors into a community for startup founders. It's become a side hustle that makes me $10K in revenue.
events.summary: Alena Beliauskaya turned her community outings into a fun side hustle. Kevin Mei Alena Beliauskaya turned her weekends into free community meetups for founders. The group goes hiking, dirtbiking, and does other fun group activities. She now offers paid membership and has earned $10,000 a month in revenue since the summer. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Alena Beliauskaya, a 37-year-old product director based in San Francisco. The following has been edited for length and clarity. Here in San Francisco , it seems like everyone is a startup founder. I'm the director of product management at Wolf Games, an AI narrative games company, where I work part-time. On the side, I run 12 Scrappy Founders, a founders community in the Bay Area with paid memberships and sponsored events. When I first moved here for my job in March 2025, I wanted to make friends, so I started going to founder events, but the interactions were so transactional. The first question everyone asks you is, 'What's your goal at this event?' So, I started hosting my own events . I'm an outdoorsy person and love extreme sports, so I'd plan a weekend hike, a backpacking trip, or dirt biking in Tahoe and invite other founders to join me. Now, I make over $10,000 in revenue each month and take home $2,000 to $3,000 in profit. I've worked in startups for about 15 years and am a founder It was natural to build my network around other founders. These are the people whose lives and problems I understand best. Finding like-minded people who understand startups and also want to spend Saturday riding dirt bikes in Tahoe is worth more to me than another 100 LinkedIn connections. At our events, there's no formal networking , and nobody pitches. People got to know each other by spending eight hours on a trail or learning to ride a motorcycle together. I started my community group charging $0 and now earn $10,000 in monthly revenue I didn't charge at first because we started with hiking, which doesn't cost anything. But when we started dirt biking, I usually paid out of my pocket and then asked people to reimburse me. Beliauskaya shares her outdoor hobbies with a community of founders. Kevin Mei This hobby was starting to take up a lot of my free time, and I thought about monetizing it, but I debated at first because I thought that if I turned it into a business, I might stop enjoying myself. I started thinking about monetization around spring this year, after so many members told me I needed to because they were getting so much value. I started rolling out memberships at the beginning of this summer. We have over 600 founders in our community To join, the person's startup needs to be at the seed, Series A, or Series B stage. Most members have AI startups , because that's what is happening right now. You also have to be based in the Bay Area, since events are in person. We're all connected on Slack, and there are about 20 paid members. There are two tiers right now. General membership is $99 a month, which includes free members-only events, priority access, personalized introductions to founders and investors, and access to the private member platform and Slack community. Our core membership, which is full, costs $3,000 a year, and core members get to work with me on where the community goes next. We also monetize working with brands that sponsor many of our events. Recently, we partnered with Red Bull. I run paid experiences like hard hikes, overnight camps, dirt-biking, go-karting, pickleball, poker nights, and roundtables. I'm not planning to make my side hustle a full-time job I just want to figure out how to grow and nurture this community well and have something joyful in my free time. I invest much of my free time in this side hustle. Almost every Saturday, I spend the full day outdoors with the founders. Besides that, I spend about three to four hours a day organizing. My advice to those wanting to start a side hustle is to find something you love. You already spend the whole day at your full-time job, and often don't have much energy left. Your side hustle should bring you joy, which will motivate you to keep going. Do you have an interesting side hustle to share with Business Insider? events.title: Shadow chancellor vows to cut at least one tax in every Tory budget
events.summary: Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said he hopes to scrap at least one tax every budget if the Conservatives return to power, with the so-called "mansion tax" in his sights. Speaking at the party's conference in Birmingham, Griffith said "lower, simpler and fairer taxes" would be his "personal north star" although he noted his ambition for cuts would take place "only when we can afford to do so". He also said he would scrap the High Value Council Tax Surcharge (HVCTS), which takes effect from 2028 and introduces an extra levy for owners of properties in England valued at more than £2m. Labour said the Tories "completely failed at every turn" to grow the economy during their 14 years in power. Following their historic defeat in the 2024 general election, the Conservatives have been trying to rebuild and convince voters that they can be trusted again. The Tories have faced repeated attacks from their opponents for their record in government between 2010 and 2024. Speaking on the main stage, Griffith said: "No country in history has ever taxed its way to prosperity, so we will cut taxes, but only when we can afford to do so, and always saying clearly how we will fund that within our golden economic rule." The party's "golden economic rule" involves at least half of all savings identified going towards "deficit reduction, with the other half going to tax cuts and pro-growth measures". Griffith likened his approach to that of former Tory Chancellor Nigel Lawson, adding: "It's my ambition to scrap at least one tax every budget. What would we prioritise? There's a lot. "Tax cuts that help growth, tax cuts that improve incentives to work, tax cuts that make life simpler and fairer." The Extended Packaging Responsibility (EPR) scheme, which requires firms to cover the cost of collecting, recycling and disposing of packaging it produces, would be scrapped by the Conservatives. Griffith sought to signal a different approach under Kemi Badenoch's leadership, telling members that the EPR was the "sort of thing the old Conservative Party went along with". He also said Labour plans a "vindicative raid on family homes" in the form of the HVCTS, also dubbed the "mansion tax", which he would seek to scrap. The shadow chancellor said: "It's an anti-growth tax that will distort the housing market and remove the incentive to make home improvements." Ahead of his speech, Griffith was pressed on BBC Breakfast on whether he would keep the pensions triple lock, which Prime Minister Andy Burnham has proposed changing. Griffith said: "We are going to keep it." In 2021, then-backbencher Griffith wrote an article saying that the state pension triple lock was "unfair" as pensioners could "gain from the misfortune of others". Senior Conservatives including former chancellor Jeremy Hunt and shadow foreign secretary Tom Tugendhat have individually suggested the current triple lock is unsustainable. Properties worth more than £2m in England face mansion tax Published 3 December 2025 Tories committed to pension triple lock, deputy leader says Published 4 days ago Andy Burnham refuses to back third runway at Heathrow Published 27 September During a series of speeches on Monday, Griffith and other shadow ministers also announced further details on the policies they believe will help free up businesses and grow the economy. The proposals included ditching environmental and energy efficiency regulations, such as the future homes standard. Griffith said the next Conservative government would support a third runway at Heathrow Airport. Plans for expansion were scrapped by the Tory-led coalition government in 2010. The Conservatives also want to implement a single levy for developers in place of section 106 agreements and the Community Infrastructure Levy, which fund projects in the community when building plans are progressed. The party has been critical of the roles of Natural England and the Environment Agency in relation to house building and flood prevention work respectively, and wants to abolish both. Their functions would be looked after by the Department for the Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra). Prospect general secretary Mike Clancy, whose union represents members in Natural England and the Environment Agency, said: "Conservative budget cuts have left these regulators struggling to perform their vital functions with 'lack of resources' the most common reason for planning delays. "The solution is to restore their funding to adequate levels, not scrap vital safeguards." Liberal Democrat deputy leader Daisy Cooper said the Conservatives have "cemented their position as a pointless anti-growth, anti-business party" by rejecting closer ties with Europe. She added: "No-one can take anything the Conservatives say on the economy seriously given their litany of fantasy-land financial pledges.

events.title: Merz, Macron seek tougher EU measures against unfair trade
events.summary: Emmanuel Macron and Friedrich Merz have written to Ursula von der Leyen, calling for tougher EU mechanisms against unfair trade practices by other states. They name no names but seem to have China or the US in mind. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron sent a joint appeal to the European Commission on Monday, calling for tougher EU measures against unfair trade practices by other states. They said that the existing instruments at the EU's disposal were no longer sufficient. The appeal did not name any specific country but it seemed most clearly tied to Chinese trade policy , the EU's vast deficit with China , and its dependence on certain key raw materials. The other apparent candidate would be the US, not least under the current unpredictable trade policy stewardship of tariff-loving President Donald Trump. It also came just a few days before the EU's trade commissioner, Maros Sefcovic, is set to visit Beijing. How China is upping pressure on German businesses The joint letter to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called for two new measures to be introduced in Brussels. One would aim at ensuring diversification and preventing companies from becoming too dependent on suppliers from individual companies. The other would allow another country to be excluded from access to the European single market on an expedited basis if exceptional circumstances made this necessary. Merz and Macron wrote that this could be used in cases "where third countries deliberately seek to undermine the restoration of a level playing field and fair market conditions through political or economic means, leading to serious and systematic distortions of our single market." The French and German leaders, both struggling to balance economic growth and public spending, said the EU's struggles to maintain global competitiveness and its dependencies on certain suppliers of core materials led to "geoeconomic risks." "The open and rules-based trading system is being massively compromised by the instrumentalization of trade, systemic market-distorting practices and global macroeconomic imbalances," they wrote. "All this undermines the level competitive playing field for our companies, our position as a sovereign core industrial producer and our capacity for innovations, which leads to increasing dependencies and geoeconomic risks." Tungsten prices rally as China limits exports Appeal comes ahead of EU China visit, and EU leaders' summit Monday's letter is what's known in EU diplomatic circles as a "non-paper." These are nonbinding, informal documents shared between EU member states and institutions that are supposed to propose ideas and initiate discussions without officially committing to a position. It recommends authorizing the Commission to exclude a country from single market access in extreme situations if it sees the need — currently a complicated process that would take some time to arrange and requires approval from member states. It suggests reversing this process: allowing the Commission to take the step independently, but with member states then having the chance to block it with a qualified majority vote, which the EU currently defines as a vote by a minimum of 55% of member states that also represents a minimum of 65% of the bloc's total population. The EU's trade deficit with China is vast and growing. The EU put the figure at around €360 billion (roughly $400 billion) in 2025, though China's statisticians reached a more modest tally of $292 billion. The bloc is also particularly dependent on China for a number of raw materials, not least rare earths , and is increasingly reliant on both the US and China for high-tech imports and services, particularly in computing and the so-called AI sector. The EU's trade commissioner, Maros Sefcovic, visits China this week for talks, ahead of an EU leaders' summit next week, on October 15-16. Sefcovic said earlier this year that he hoped to see "tangible results by October" on the question of trade with China, although whether these will materialize is an open question. Beijing has warned that it could retaliate with changes of its own after learning of the EU's plans, if it perceives a need to. events.title: House GOP whip: Limit spending to districts with "biggest return"
events.summary: House Majority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) is scaling back expectations and zeroing in on a narrowed battlefield as Republicans' prospects of keeping their majority look increasingly bleak. Why it matters: Emmer, a former National Republican Congressional Committee chair who helped the GOP unexpectedly gain seats in 2020, argues his party can still defy historical headwinds in November. But with less than a month to go, Emmer acknowledges that some tough decisions are coming about where Republicans spend their money, including walking away from races they don't think they can salvage. "It really is a business, and you're looking at a balance sheet, and you're putting your money where you're gonna get your biggest return," he told Axios aboard a plane between campaign stops. Axios joined Emmer, who plans to visit 56 districts between September and Election Day, as he traveled from Charlotte to Richmond last week for stops with Reps. Mark Harris (R-N.C.) and Rob Wittman (R-Va.). Driving the news: It's a lesson Emmer says Republicans learned the hard way in 2022, when expectations of a "red wave" led the party to spread its resources too broadly. "We expanded the map when we should have kept it narrow," Emmer told donors in Charlotte. "We should have been conservative about what we were going after." This cycle, Emmer said Republicans have to identify "where you're not gonna be able to salvage this, and you've got to pick up something over there." Yes, but : That strategy is being tested by a difficult national environment for Republicans, with an unpopular president and voters focused on the cost of living and the war in Iran, which is driving up gas prices. Between the lines: Asked about embattled Rep. Max Miller's (R-Ohio) increasingly difficult race , Emmer immediately pointed up the ticket to the Senate and gubernatorial races, where Democrats are faring better than expected. "The problem is, when you got these statewide candidates that are not creating momentum, that's tough," he said. Emmer also pointed to the North Carolina Senate race, where Democrat Roy Cooper has opened up a lead in polls, as having a "large impact" on the 1st and 11th district races there. Miller has a path to victory, Emmer said, "but it's narrow." Still, he defended the NRCC's decision to spend money backing Miller. Zoom in: Emmer's instinct is to let members run the race that fits their district — within limits. He called Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar's (R-Fla.) campaign ad breaking with Trump on immigration a "huge mistake, adding, "I'm not sure why now was the time for that message" (although he later walked back those comments, saying Salazar "knows her district"). Salazar posited in the ad that Trump's immigration enforcement efforts have "gone too far" and that Hispanic voters who helped elect him in 2024 "feel betrayed."

events.title: Taylor Swift's 'The Life of a Showgirl' is one of her biggest albums on the Billboard 200. Here's how her others rank.
events.summary: Taylor Swift performs during The Eras Tour in Dublin. Charles McQuillan/TAS24/Getty Images for TAS Rights Management Taylor Swift's "The Life of a Showgirl" has spent 13 weeks at No. 1 on the Billboard 200. It's her second-longest reign atop the chart, surpassing "Fearless" and "1989." "The Tortured Poets Department" holds the record in Swift's catalog with 17 weeks at No. 1. Taylor Swift gave us fair warning in her newest album: "I'm married to the hustle." Swift's 12th studio album, " The Life of a Showgirl ," not only broke the record for the biggest debut sales week ever , but it also continued to amass sales and streams in the US for months after its release. After seven consecutive weeks at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 , "Showgirl" returned for another five atop the all-genre album chart, surpassing "Fearless" and "1989" as Swift's second-longest reign. The impressive tally came shortly after Swift set a personal-best chart record with " The Tortured Poets Department ." Keep reading for a ranking of her 16 studio albums (including both originals and rerecords) based on their Billboard 200 performances. 10. "Taylor Swift" Taylor Swift's debut album, "Taylor Swift," was released in 2006. Taylor Swift Billboard 200 peak: No. 5 Swift's self-titled debut is the only studio album in her catalog that hasn't reached No. 1 on the Billboard 200. "Taylor Swift" debuted at No. 19 and scaled the chart for more than a year, peaking at No. 5 in 2008. 9 (tie). "Lover" Taylor Swift's seventh album, "Lover," was released in 2019. Taylor Swift Billboard 200 peak: No. 1 for one week Swift's seventh studio album was the first one that she owned outright, thanks to her new label contract with UMG. "Lover" was promoted by several singles, including " You Need to Calm Down ," " The Archer ," and " The Man ." Four years later, after Swift kicked off the Eras Tour with "Cruel Summer" near the top of the set list , the fan-favorite song climbed to No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 and remained there for four weeks, becoming the album's biggest hit. 9 (tie). "Red (Taylor's Version)" The cover art for "Red (Taylor's Version)" was photographed by Beth Garrabrant. Taylor Swift/UMG Billboard 200 peak: No. 1 for one week The extended tracklist for " Red (Taylor's Version) " included the storied extended cut of "All Too Well," a longtime fan-favorite song in Swift's catalog. "All Too Well (10 Minute Version)" was released alongside a short film directed by Swift and promoted by a convention-breaking performance on "Saturday Night Live." It became the longest song to reach No. 1 in the history of the Hot 100. 8 (tie). "Fearless (Taylor's Version)" "Fearless (Taylor's Version)" was released in 2021. Taylor Swift/UMG Billboard 200 peak: No. 1 for two weeks "Fearless" was the first rerecorded album that Swift ever released. The "Taylor's Version" series was inspired by the sale of Swift's masters to Scooter Braun in 2019, which she described as her "worst case scenario" in a passionate open letter. Swift decided to remake and rerelease her first six albums in a bid to reclaim ownership of her life's work. (Braun later sold Swift's masters to a private-equity company.) In addition to faithfully recreating each tracklist , Swift decided to add never-before-heard songs "from the vault" that were written during the album's original creative process but cut from the final product. "I've spoken a lot about why I'm remaking my first six albums, but the way I've chosen to do this will hopefully help illuminate where I'm coming from," Swift explained. "Artists should own their own work for so many reasons, but the most screamingly obvious one is that the artist is the only one who really knows that body of work." "For example, only I know which songs I wrote that almost made the 'Fearless' album," she continued. "Songs I absolutely adored, but were held back for different reasons." Many were skeptical that the "Taylor's Version" project would be embraced by fans, let alone achieve commercial success . Those skeptics were forced to eat their words when "Fearless (Taylor's Version)" began to outpace the original on streaming platforms. According to Billboard , "Fearless (Taylor's Version)" earned more equivalent album sales in its first week of release than "Fearless" earned over the entire next year. Four years later, in May 2025, Swift announced that she bought back her masters from Shamrock Capital, giving her complete control over her musical catalog and rendering her "Taylor's Version" project moot. 8 (tie). "Speak Now (Taylor's Version)" "Speak Now (Taylor's Version)" was released in 2023. Taylor Swift/UMG Billboard 200 peak: No. 1 for two weeks The rerecorded version of Swift's third album featured six songs from the vault , including two duets with Fall Out Boy and Hayley Williams. 7 (tie). "Reputation" The album cover for "Reputation." Taylor Swift Billboard 200 peak: No. 1 for four weeks "Reputation" arrived after an extended period of silence. Swift's longtime feud with Ye (then known as Kanye West) and Kim Kardashian had reached a fever pitch; in response to a massive social media hate campaign, Swift decamped to London and withdrew from the public eye. She returned with a new snake-infested aesthetic and "Look What You Made Me Do," a cheeky lead single that poked fun at her own persona — and quickly rose to No. 1 on the Hot 100. Swift also declined to participate in interviews or media appearances while promoting her sixth album. Instead, she relied on a simple tagline: "There will be no further explanation. There will just be reputation." 7 (tie). "Evermore" Taylor Swift's ninth album, "Evermore," was released in 2020. Taylor Swift Billboard 200 peak: No. 1 for four weeks "Evermore" was surprise-released just five months after Swift's previous album, "Folklore." The two were billed as "sister albums," created under near-identical conditions with the same team of collaborators. "To put it plainly, we just couldn't stop writing songs," Swift explained on social media. "Evermore" was nominated for album of the year at the 2022 Grammys, but lost to Jon Batiste's "We Are." 6 (tie). "Speak Now" Taylor Swift's third album, "Speak Now," was released in 2010. Taylor Swift Billboard 200 peak: No. 1 for six weeks Swift's third album had a lot to live up to, following the blockbuster success of "Fearless." In response to skeptics — who questioned whether the teen phenom was relying too heavily on her collaborators — she decided to write "Speak Now" entirely by herself. Swift is the only songwriter credited on the standard tracklist. 6 (tie). "Midnights" Taylor Swift's 10th album, "Midnights," was released in 2022. events.title: Our family and friends are scattered across the globe, so my husband and I decided to elope. I have 1 regret.
events.summary: The author (right), shown on her wedding day, is happy with her decision to elope but regrets not having more photos to commemorate the day. Courtesy of Renate Flanagan. Our friends and family live around the world, and we didn't want them to travel for our wedding. We didn't need or want a big, elaborate wedding, and our families were fine with our decision. Our wedding was a beautiful start to our life together, with just the two of us. Growing up, my family has always been spread out. I grew up on the East Coast of the United States, but many of my relatives lived on the West Coast or in Europe. My high school friends and friends I made at work have also become scattered around the country. My friends and I were like a dandelion, we all started together, then we got dispersed by the wind. When I first started dating my husband, he was in a similar situation, except the wind had brought him to me from Belgium . When we got engaged, we faced the conundrum of choosing a location, not a venue, but a geographical region to tie the knot . There seemed to be no good answer, so we decided to forgo a wedding party altogether. We wanted to be considerate of our friends and family We live in Washington, DC, but most of my husband's family and friends live in Europe. My brother and his family live in the Middle East. My closest friends are spread out across New England, Florida, and the West Coast. There was no good option that wouldn't require at least half of our expected invitees to travel across the country , or across the Atlantic, or both. Any scenario we came up with would burden our friends and family with  significant expenses  for airfare, accommodations, and time, only to spend less than an hour with us to celebrate our wedding. I've also traveled for weddings before. I was happy to celebrate the people getting married, but the reality is that the time I actually spent with the couple was minimal. The couple always has a full agenda of things to do on top of spreading their time across all the guests attending. I knew I didn't want my guests to travel if I wasn't going to get to spend genuine time with them. We decided eloping made sense for us In addition to not wanting to burden our guests with travel for a wedding, we didn't want to spend a lot of money to throw a party. We had just purchased a house and were planning to start a family. We wanted to put our money towards those areas of our life. Neither of our families come from a background where having an elaborate wedding holds major significance in the culture. We were fortunate that our family supported our choice to elope. Our wedding day was simple but meaningful to us The day we got married was simple and beautiful and represented our relationship. DC allows you to officiate your own wedding, which we did. My husband and I were the only two people at our ceremony, which made it completely intimate. The only thing we had scheduled to do that day was our dinner reservation. The author said she and her husband exchanged vows in the park where they met. Courtesy of Renate Flanagan. In the morning, we went hiking near the weekend house we had purchased in the mountains. In the afternoon, we exchanged the vows we had each written at the park where we had our first date, and then had celebratory drinks. We ended the evening at a fine-dining restaurant. I have one small regret The only thing I have some regret about from our elopement was not hiring a photographer. The only pictures we have from that day are selfies we took and a picture the hostess took for us at the restaurant where we had dinner. On the flip side, not having a scheduled photographer allowed us to have the flexibility to change the date. Our original plan was to get married on a Friday, but we changed it to the following Monday because of rain. We only had to reschedule our dinner reservation and our days off from work. I've heard some people say getting married was the best day of their lives. To me, the day I got married was just the start to the beautiful life we continue to build together. events.title: Former Trump press secretary Karoline Leavitt is heading to Fox News. Here's what to know about her life, marriage, and career.
events.summary: White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt with her husband, Nicholas Riccio. Julia Demaree Nikhinson, File/AP Photo Karoline Leavitt, 28, was the youngest-ever White House press secretary. She worked for Kayleigh McEnany and Rep. Elise Stefanik before joining Donald Trump's 2024 campaign. She is married to 60-year-old real-estate developer Nicholas Riccio, and they have two children. Karoline Leavitt landed a White House internship as a college student during President Donald Trump 's first term. In his second term , she served as the youngest-ever White House press secretary before announcing her departure in August. A former college athlete who spent her summers scooping ice cream in New Hampshire, Leavitt, 28, quickly rose through the ranks of Republican politics through communications jobs with former White House press secretary Kayleigh McEnany and Republican Rep. Elise Stefanik. During her tenure as the 2024 Trump campaign 's national press secretary, she traveled the country while pregnant and returned to work four days after giving birth to her son. Leavitt has also acknowledged her "atypical love story" with husband Nicholas Riccio, a 60-year-old real-estate developer. The couple welcomed their second child, a daughter, in May. In August, Leavitt announced that she would be leaving her role as Trump's White House press secretary, writing on X, "Being a mother and welcoming a new baby while working in one of the most demanding jobs in the world has been the most rewarding yet challenging season of my life, to say the least." Here's what to know about Leavitt's background, family, and career. The White House Press Office did not respond to a request for comment. Karoline Leavitt grew up in Atkinson, New Hampshire, and went to a Catholic high school. New Hampshire Republican 1st Congressional District candidate Karoline Leavitt after a campaign event, Thursday, Sept. 29, 2022, in Manchester, N.H. Charles Krupa/AP Leavitt's parents owned an ice cream stand where she worked during the summers. She attended Central Catholic High School in Lawrence, Massachusetts. "Having a Catholic education really formed who I am," she said on an episode of The Catholic Current podcast in 2021. She continued, "It taught me discipline, it brought me closer in my own relationship with God, and it also taught me the importance of public service and giving back to your community." She graduated from Saint Anselm College in 2019 with a degree in politics and communication. In this Dec. 26, 2019, photo, the campus of Saint Anselm College is shown in Manchester, N.H. Monks at a Catholic college in New Hampshire have gone to court in a dispute with the school's board of trustees over an effort to limit their power. The two sides were in Hillsborough Superior Court on Monday, Jan. 6, 2020, over the lawsuit filed against the Saint Anselm College board last year. events.title: HackerRank’s AI interviewer offers a glimpse into what job interviews could become
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. What happens when AI moves from helping job candidates to evaluating them? HackerRank , a platform used by companies to assess and hire developers, is offering a glimpse at what that future of job interviews could look like with Chakra , an AI agent that conducts interviews, observes candidates as they work, and evaluates not just their answers but also how they got there. After around six months in beta, HackerRank is making Chakra generally available to its customers on Monday. The startup says the AI interviewer has already conducted more than 500,000 interviews during testing, with companies including Snowflake, Snorkel, and Capgemini among those that tried it, while HackerRank also tested the product internally. AI has been a staple in job interviews for some time , with companies using voice agents and other automated tools to screen candidates and make the hiring process more efficient. Job seekers, meanwhile, have increasingly gained their own AI tools to help them navigate interviews, sometimes without employers knowing. With Chakra, HackerRank is betting AI can change not only how interviews are conducted, but also what employers can measure. Beyond whether someone arrives at the right answer, the startup wants to assess harder-to-capture signals such as critical thinking and judgment, as well as what it calls “AI fluency” — how well a candidate frames a problem for AI, judges its output, and steers it toward a solution. “The previous modality of evaluation was evaluating the output,” HackerRank co-founder and CEO Vivek Ravisankar said in an interview. “Now, because of AI, anybody can produce an artifact.” The question for employers, he said, becomes whether they can understand the thinking and judgment that went into producing it. In practice, a Chakra interview is designed to look more like doing the job than taking a traditional coding test. A candidate gets a task involving a real-world code repository, and they work through it in a canvas that includes an AI assistant. As the candidate works, Chakra can use the context of what they are doing to ask follow-up questions, such as why they chose one approach over another, or how their solution would change if a new constraint were introduced. Ravisankar told TechCrunch that Chakra is changing the basic structure of the hiring process itself. What previously involved three separate rounds, comprising a recruiter screen, take-home assessment, and follow-up interview with an engineer, is now combined into a single Chakra interview, he said. Giving candidates access to AI during an interview might seem to make it easier to cheat. However, HackerRank says it found the opposite. Suspicious-activity flags, Ravisankar said, were 70% to 80% lower in Chakra interviews than in comparable traditional HackerRank assessments, though the rate varied depending on factors such as geography and seniority. Ravisankar told TechCrunch that giving candidates access to AI reduces the incentive to secretly use outside tools that can feed them answers during an interview. Launched at TechCrunch Disrupt in 2012, HackerRank built its business around coding challenges, eventually helping companies assess and hire developers based on their technical skills. The Y Combinator-backed startup now has more than 3,000 business customers, including Amazon, Nvidia, Clay, and Replit, and a community of over 30 million developers worldwide. Chakra represents a bet against the kind of technical assessment business HackerRank spent years building. Its traditional product largely tested whether developers could solve coding problems correctly. Nonetheless, Ravisankar believes AI has made HackerRank’s earlier model less useful to measure engineering ability. Ravisankar compared the transition internally to Apple moving from the iPod to the iPhone, as the old product still has value, but the new one represents where the startup believes the market is headed. “Chakra is going to be the headline,” he said. “It’s going to be the way that we’re going to move forward.” However, giving AI a deeper role in evaluating candidates raises a different set of questions, particularly around how much of a hiring decision companies should delegate to an algorithm. Ravisankar told TechCrunch that Chakra is designed to score candidates rather than make the final hiring decision, which remains with humans. AI, he said, can handle more structured parts of an interview by consistently applying criteria set by an employer, while human interviewers can spend more time determining whether they actually want to work with a candidate and answering questions about the company, team, and role.

events.title: BT’s purchase of TalkTalk is cosy – but probably politically sensible | Nils Pratley
events.summary: BT’s purchase of TalkTalk is cosy – but probably politically sensible For all the howls of a ‘stitch-up’, it’s hard to see what ministers were supposed to do, as the alternatives risked worse outcomes BT to buy broadband supplier TalkTalk in £400m rescue deal, saving 900 jobs “A ll the characteristics of a stitch-up masked as a rescue deal in the public interest,” thundered Virgin Media O2. It’s not an unreasonable view of BT’s hurried weekend acquisition of TalkTalk . Once upon a time, TalkTalk was seen as a plucky upstart performing the useful role of irritant to BT’s giant Openreach broadband operation. Now the challenger is being consumed by the dominant player via a pre-pack administration that minimises short-term political headaches. Here’s the problem, though, with the cosy stitch-up thesis. For all the howls of outrage, it’s hard to see what the culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, who gave her blessing by issuing a little-used public interest notice, was supposed to do differently. Alternative approaches, notably a chaotic collapse of TalkTalk without a rescue plan for the customers, risked worse outcomes. OK, perhaps the worst fears of GP surgeries and hospitals being disconnected at a stroke, and thousands of vulnerable customers losing their internet connection, were overdone. But, in Nandy’s shoes, you probably wouldn’t take the risk. TalkTalk, after all, had had months to find a buyer but failed to land a credible deal even when its retail division and its wholesale unit, PXC, were up for grabs separately. Disappointed would-be buyers blame the reluctance of BT, as the critical supplier to TalkTalk, to extend financial support to a new ownership vehicle. From BT’s point of view, however, one can see why another private equity backer for TalkTalk wouldn’t feel like an improvement on the last one . As it is, BT will be booking £100m as a non-payment of a debt even as it takes control. The deep problem here is that TalkTalk – Sir Charles Dunstone’s creation more than 20 years ago – hasn’t been doing much real challenging work of late. After going through the refinancing wringer more times than is healthy, it was a financially distressed company. At the last count, borrowings were in the region of £1.5bn, a staggering sum for a loss-making business with only 1.5 million retail customers and 1 million wholesale ones. Telephony, remember, tends to be a low-margin game even when things are going well. That is not to say the politicians get a free pass. Successive governments have been told many times by the regulator Ofcom that a “supplier of last resort” regime should be in place in the broadband market, just as it is in energy and water. The logic is simple: in extremis, there should be a way for a government-supported operation to step in to prevent sudden disconnections and look for an orderly permanent solution. The unavoidable fact, though, is that such a regime didn’t exist with TalkTalk. That glaring hole in the regulatory setup needs to be addressed for future cases. But a weekend arrangement with BT , however objectionable in theory, at least has the advantage of not drawing on a penny of public money. The medium-term regulatory test will be to ensure BT and Openreach can’t abuse the advantage of gobbling TalkTalk. There was a theatrical public exchange of letters between the BT chief executive, Allison Kirkby, and the Ofcom boss, Dame Melanie Dawes. The former pleaded for regulatory mercy, in effect, for removing a political problem; the latter replied that applying the regulatory framework was a statutory duty. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning It’s anyone’s guess how that will work out in practice since the wriggle room would seem to be enormous. But the guiding principle hasn’t changed – wholesale operators need to have access to Openreach’s network on reasonable commercial terms. TalkTalk couldn’t make it pay but that, in the end, seems primarily to be a story of its own perilous financing. Wrapping the business into BT is very far from being ideal – but it’s not the worst pragmatic fudge.

events.title: Altman-backed Volantis reveals plan to vault the memory wall by baking photonics into AI accelerators
events.summary: Sam Altman-backed AI chip startup Volantis has a plan to break through the memory wall using light, and this time it's not just an IP play. Founded in 2022, the San Francisco-based startup is developing an AI accelerator that will use a photonic interposer to dramatically increase memory bandwidth without compromising on capacity. Volantis believes it can pack upwards of 10 TB of memory at speeds up to 240 TB/s onto a single massive package. This, it claims, should be enough to serve a 20 trillion parameter model at 10,000 tok/s per user. To do this, Volantis is taking a somewhat unusual approach. Rather than developing some novel compute architecture or memory technology, the company is focusing its efforts on the optical interposer. Everything else it plans to license from IP providers. "The differentiation is primarily coming from the optical interposer. So why don't we license absolutely everything we possibly can, even if it's not the highest performance in the world, because we're already biting off a lot of risk with the interposer and the integration," CEO Tapa Ghosh tells El Reg. The basic idea behind the chip, which Volantis is calling A-1, is that by using optical wave guides rather than electrical interconnects it can dramatically increase the amount of high-bandwidth memory per package. Because of the speeds at which most AI accelerator memory, like HBM, operate, and the size and number of data pins used, it needs to be as close to the compute as possible to minimize power consumption and maximize signal integrity. As a result the maximum capacity and bandwidth of modern GPUs is limited by the compute die's shoreline. That's the physical perimeter around the chip. For now, that means the cap is right around 432 GB on AMD's MI455X. Photonic interconnects can extend that much farther. Instead of a few millimeters the memory can be located a few centimeters away, eliminating the shoreline as a bottleneck. While HBM is useful as an example, we'll note Volantis hasn't said what memory tech its chip will use just yet. Volantis aims to achieve this using optical waveguides integrated into an interposer. Compute and memory designed or supplied by its partners will be packaged on top. If any of this sounds familiar, Volantis isn't the first to propose using silicon photonic interposers in this manner. As our sister site Next Platform has previously reported, both Lightmatter and Celestial AI have toyed with the idea in the past. In fact, we strongly suspect the idea of HBM-at-a-distance contributed to Marvell's decision to acquire Celestial for $5.5 billion. However, unlike either Celestial or Lightmatter, Volantis isn't trying to license its tech to other chipmakers. At least not yet. Instead it aims to develop a fully fledged inference chip. "It is, at least on day one, a way easier problem to demonstrate a solution that ships," Ghosh says. Another differentiator is the technology on which the startup's interposer is based. Rather than relying on external lasers, Volantis' design uses micro vertical-cavity surface-emitting lasers — micro-VCSELs for short — and means the light source is integrated directly into the interposer. VCSELs aren't new by any means, but have faced criticism over their reliability. However, Volantis CTO Roy Meade tells us the technology has come a long way in recent years and by giving up some speed, significantly higher reliability can be achieved, a philosophy he describes as wide and efficient. "People are still constrained to this, what I would call a fat pipe point-to-point mentality, and naturally, if that's the case, you're going to go towards SerDes," he says. "If we were to go back and take a look at the benefits of a wide-and-efficient approach. HBM for example. Taking that same playbook makes a lot of sense." What Meade is getting at is that interconnects can achieve higher bandwidth in a couple different ways. The first is by increasing the link speed, and the second by using more links. For example an 800 Gbps link can be achieved using four 200 Gbps links or eight 100 Gbps links. In his example of HBM, higher bandwidth is achieved by using an extremely-wide bus but slower data rate per pin relative to other memory technologies. The same concept applies to Volantis' optical interposer-based accelerator. Power efficiency remains an open question that's dogged many photonics startups, but this may be less of a problem for Volantis because it's not trying to license its first-gen interposer tech. For its first product the company is targeting 1 picojoule per bit per 24 Gbps lane and a total system power of around 20kW. Volantis still has a ways to go before it tapes out its first production-ready chip, and will need to raise a fair bit more in venture capital to do that — far more than the $88 million it raised this week with the help of Lachy Groom, Abstract Ventures, and others. Ghosh is well aware of this. He says the funding will enable the company to scale from small-scale optical demonstrators to something more closely resembling the final product. The interposer alone is challenging enough, but then there is the complexity of actually integrating the IP they license. "Aggressively, we should aim for an MVP product in 12 to 18 months as our target," he tells us, noting that's to have a working prototype not volume production. ®

events.title: Row-Parallel DRAM Computing Cuts Data-Reorganization Overhead (Syracuse, FAU, TU Dresden)
events.summary: Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Technical Papers Home '; AI/ML/DL Architectures Automotive/ Aerospace Communication/Data Movement Design & Verification Lithography Manufacturing Materials Memory Optoelectronics / Photonics Packaging Power & Performance Quantum Security Test, Measurement, Analytics tech papers Transistors Z-End Applications Videos & Research Videos Industry Research Newsletters & Store Newsletters Store MENU Home Special Reports Systems & Design Low Power-High Performance Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Test, Measurement & Analytics Auto, Security and AI Knowledge Center Videos Startup Corner Business & Startups Jobs Technical Papers Events Webinars Industry Research Newsletters Store Special Reports Researchers at Syracuse University, Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg , and TU Dresden published a technical paper titled “RAPID: Row-Parallel Arithmetic Processing in DRAM.” Abstract Excerpt: “Processing-using-memory (PUM) architectures perform computation directly within DRAM to reduce costly data movement between memory and processors. Because charge-sharing operations are confined to individual bitlines, existing DRAM-PUM architectures reorganize data into column-oriented, bit-serial representations. This organization is fundamentally incompatible with the row-oriented, word-parallel layouts used by conventional processors and accelerators, requiring expensive data-layout transformations whenever computation transitions between PUM and conventional execution. In this paper, we present RAPID, a Row-parallel Arithmetic Processing-In-DRAM architecture. RAPID augments the DRAM subarray with two lightweight extensions: migration cells that enable localized horizontal data movement between neighboring bitlines and inversion cells that provide efficient in-array logical inversion. These primitives enable RAPID to operate directly on row-parallel, bit-parallel data, preserving CPU-compatible layouts while exploiting the massive parallelism of the DRAM subarray.” Find the technical paper here . events.title: Eurodrama in currency markets raises U.S. dollar's standing
events.summary: Data: FactSet; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios The euro fell to a 17-month low against the dollar on Monday as political and fiscal worries rattled European markets. Why it matters: Rising borrowing costs and political instability are reviving concerns about strains within the eurozone — and whether the European Central Bank may eventually have to step in. France is grappling with high deficits, rising long-term rates and political stalemate over how to address them, as our colleague Emily Peck noted . Spain's prime minister called a snap election for Nov. 29, which could strengthen Pedro Sánchez's position or open the door to a populist right government. By the numbers: The euro fell below $1.12, its lowest since May 2025 and down about 4% since Sept. 8. Between the lines: France's rising borrowing costs echo the eurozone crisis of the early 2010s, though the ECB now has more tools to contain market stress. What they're saying: In an opinion article Monday in the Financial Times, former ECB board member Lorenzo Bini Smaghi called for the central bank to suspend its quantitative tightening program in light of stress on long-term rates. Compared with the early 2010s, the ECB "is much better equipped to address tensions in financial markets that could endanger the integrity of the single currency," he wrote. "It has bond-buying tools and programmes that address spikes in yields." "However, one aspect that is more difficult to understand for observers and market participants is why, in the current stress, the ECB continues to implement its policy of quantitative tightening," he continues, or shrinking its balance sheet by not replacing government bonds as they mature. "This policy means that a larger share of the net supply of government bonds has to be absorbed by private investors, at a time when long-term rates are already under upward pressure," Bini Smaghi wrote.

events.title: Pentagon stops using Anthropic AI tools after blacklisting company, BBC told
events.summary: Defence secretary Pete Hegseth has publicly criticised Anthropic's boss Dario Amodei The US Department of Defence is no longer using Anthropic's AI tools, an official has told the BBC, months after it designated the company a supply chain risk on national security grounds. The Pentagon "has ceased the use of Anthropic products", the department official said in a statement on Monday. Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth labelled Anthropic a supply chain risk in February, and announced that the Pentagon would stop using it by late August. It is not clear why there has been a delay. Multiple people familiar with the matter told the BBC that as recently as last week Anthopic's Claude model was still being used by the department in research, analysis and intelligence gathering as well as in military operations against Iran. It was viewed as a critical tool for sorting through vast quantities of information, the people said. They include former US defence officials and contractors who have worked closely with the Pentagon specifically on AI. A spokesman for Anthropic declined to comment when asked about the Pentagon's statement. The details of the department stopping all use of Anthropic's tools have not been previously reported. The firm had been used by the US government and military since 2024 and was the first advanced AI company to have its tools deployed in government agencies doing classified work. But earlier this year, the Pentagon pressed it to remove its safety guardrails from Claude and give the military unfettered access to its AI products. When Anthropic refused, citing concerns of mass surveillance and autonomous weapons, Hegseth designated the company a "national security supply-chain risk" - a law typically reserved for companies based in countries that pose a threat to the US. Anthropic said the move was "unprecedented and unlawful" and has sued the Trump administration in an effort to overturn the designation. Trump administration illegally retaliated against Anthropic, judge rules Published 28 August Anthropic sues US government for calling it a risk Published 9 March Anthropic blocks possible attempt to use AI to make biological weapons Published 11 September Anthropic boss Dario Amodei calls for AI development to slow down Published 12 September As this legal fight has played out in the courts, the Pentagon has signed contracts with other major tech companies, including Google, xAI and OpenAI. OpenAI tools have been more widely adopted in recent months in some military departments, according to two people familiar with AI use in the defence department The Pentagon's statement on Monday came in response to a question from the BBC about its use of Anthropic, after multiple people said in interviews that Claude was still being widely used. It was embedded in a larger data platform used by the Pentagon called Maven Smart System, multiple sources said. Maven, which is operated by Palantir, is the Pentagon's primary platform for organising intelligence and other data. Lauren Kahn, a senior research analyst at Georgetown's Center for Security and Emerging Technology said that because Claude was deeply integrated into Maven it would have been difficult to remove it quickly from the system. "The fact that it took the Pentagon until now to remove all use of Claude from across the system is indicative that these things are not just plug and play," she said. "Once they become integrated it can be painful to remove them," added Kahn, a former US defence official. Trump recently met with Anthropic boss Dario Amodei at the White House The BBC spoke with defence contractors who specialise in AI and have worked closely with the Pentagon, as well as former US defence officials and others familiar with the Pentagon's use of artificial intelligence. Several spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to speak to the media. When Hegseth initially ordered Anthropic to be phased out of government, "there was concern with moving beyond Anthropic to OpenAI" and other tools, a former senior US defence official said. Hegseth set a six-month deadline to phase out Anthropic on 27 February, one day before the US and Israel attacked Iran. Pentagon employees continued to use Anthropic's Claude tools, including its powerful Mythos models, "throughout the whole period of the controversy" with the company, one of the people said. Claude was used in particular for intelligence gathering and analysis, including through Palantir's Maven system, several sources said. Palantir, a leading defence tech firm, was founded by the billionaire ally of President Donald Trump, Peter Thiel. 'There is a possibility of human extinction,' former Anthropic employee says about AI Sources familiar with the way the technology is used said analysts and other defence officials rely on Maven to access and organise visual data, including satellite imagery and drone footage.

events.title: Dennis Hastert, disgraced ex-House speaker, dies at 84
events.summary: Dennis Hastert, the longest-serving Republican House speaker in U.S. history who later admitted to sexually abusing several teenage boys, died Saturday at 84. The big picture: Hastert was the highest-ranking elected official in U.S. history to serve time in federal prison, and Congress still conducts business under an unwritten rule named after him. Driving the news: Hastert died at his home in Plano, Illinois, while under hospice care, the Kendall County Coroner's Office told Axios in an emailed statement. He is survived by his wife, Jean Kahl, and their two sons. Catch up quick: Hastert pleaded guilty to evading banking laws in 2015 after prosecutors investigated him for concealing large cash withdrawals. Court proceedings revealed he paid hush money to cover up his past sexual abuse of boys while working as a teacher and high school wrestling coach. Prosecutors alleged that Hastert molested at least four boys, some as young as 14. He faced no sexual abuse charges due to the statute of limitations. He was sentenced to 15 months in prison and released in 2017 after serving 13 months. Zoom out: While in Congress, Hastert became known for the unwritten Hastert Rule, under which the speaker will only bring a bill to the floor for a vote if a majority of the majority party supports it. Critics say the rule encouraged partisanship by keeping bipartisan bills off the floor if they lack support from most members of the majority party. Early life Hastert was born in Aurora, Kane County, Illinois, on Jan. 2, 1942. He attended Wheaton College and earned a master's degree from Northern Illinois University. He later worked as a high school teacher and athletic coach at Yorkville High School, where the abuse of at least four athletes took place. He left education for politics, winning a seat in the Illinois House of Representatives, where he served from 1980 to 1986. Hastert then won election to the U.S. House, serving from 1987 to 2007. Professional career Hastert has been dubbed the "accidental speaker" after he won the gavel in 1999 as a compromise candidate after Newt Gingrich resigned and the expected replacement, Bob Livingston , withdrew. Hastert led the House during the aftermath of the 9/11 terror attacks and for most of President George W. Bush's administration. After his resignation , he became a highly paid lobbyist until his indictment. The indictment Hastert pleaded guilty in 2015 to one count of illegally structuring cash withdrawals to evade federal reporting requirements. His plea agreement says Hastert paid an unnamed individual $1.7 million between 2010 and 2014 after the person confronted him about "past misconduct" Hastert committed against them decades earlier. Hastert had agreed to pay the individual $3.5 million to resolve the matter. From 2010 to 2012, he regularly withdrew roughly $50,000 in cash every six weeks to make the payments. After bank representatives questioned him about the large withdrawals, Hastert began taking out less than $10,000 at a time to evade federal reporting requirements. He ultimately withdrew $952,000 in those smaller increments. Hastert later stopped making payments before reaching the agreed-upon $3.5 million, prompting the individual to sue him for the remaining money. That lawsuit was ultimately settled out of court. After the indictment Hastert's state pensions from working as a teacher and in the state legislature were forfeited and revoked in the years after his indictment. His federal pension, worth more than $70,000 a year, was still in place. His name was also removed from Wheaton University's Center for Economics, Government, and Public Policy in 2015, and his official House Speaker portrait was removed from the Speaker's Lobby. events.title: Trump's economic tightrope messaging of strong economy, high prices
events.summary: President Trump's economic officials acknowledge that a strong economy alone will not persuade Americans that they are better off under this president. Why it matters: The administration is trying to avoid what it sees as a Biden-era mistake: touting strong economic data while Americans are still reeling from a historic run-up in prices to which Trump's policies have contributed. It is a high-wire messaging act just weeks before the midterms: The administration wants to promote strong growth without appearing to dismiss Americans' frustration over the cost of living. "If I say, 'Oh, people are wrong, the economy is great,' then it looks like I'm insensitive. And if I then go into why the economy is great, then it looks like I'm insensitive," top White House economist Kevin Hassett said on CNN's "State of the Union" on Sunday. What they're saying: "What we're not going to do is do what the Biden people did and tell the American people how good they had it," Bessent told Axios' Mike Allen on Friday in a wide-ranging interview on "The Axios Show." Bessent said that the economy remains strong despite the recent inflation surge. "Any of the numbers are quite strong, other than headline inflation," which includes energy prices driven up by the Middle East conflict. He predicted the energy shock would "fade away." He acknowledged that Americans are still dealing with the cumulative hit from higher prices: "Sometimes I feel like an emergency room doctor. ... The American people were backed over by the inflation Mack Truck." The Treasury secretary said that wages keeping pace with inflation now isn't enough to make up for the earlier erosion in purchasing power. "Breaking even after what happened during the Biden years is not our goal." Yes, but: The administration still wants credit for the strong economy on paper, even as the headline economic indicators obscure the financial strain Americans still feel. "There is the stated preference and revealed preference," Bessent said, referring to Americans' spending behavior versus their weak sentiment. The other side: "What we did was to say, 'hey, we know you're struggling and we're trying to help with prices, but look at this good GDP or jobs report!' That talked past people," Jared Bernstein, former White House top economist under Biden, told Axios in an email. "What they mostly say is 'You're not struggling! And the economy's booming.' That too talks past people." Bernstein argued that the administration has not only dismissed affordability concerns — Trump called the affordability crisis a "hoax" last year — but worsened them through tariffs, budget cuts and the war. The big picture: The bond market is complicating the administration's affordability push as long-term interest rates rise sharply and mortgage rates top 7%. Bessent has made lower Treasury yields a pillar of the administration's affordability push. A speech he gave last year had one section titled "Treasury Markets as a Barometer for Affordability." Speaking to Axios, Bessent played down the signal from the recent yield surge, pointing out that borrowing costs have climbed around the world. "I would be concerned if we were having some kind of idiosyncratic rise," he said. "It's been a global rise." What to watch: The Treasury secretary recognized the limits of his influence on the bond market after this summer's intervention . "I can't control the bond market," he said. "What I can do is try to get people to slow down and think." Bessent said he does not regret declaring last month that "I am the house now," a reference to his informational advantage over Wall Street. "The house doesn't win every hand. The house plays percentages." Go deeper: Watch the extended Scott Bessent interview on "The Axios Show"

events.title: The Iran war is hitting America's school buses — and kids are paying the price
events.summary: For millions of children, the school day starts on a diesel-powered bus with a driver behind the wheel. Now, school districts are struggling to afford both. Why it matters: The Iran War is sending diesel costs higher just as districts are grappling with a yearslong bus driver shortage — a double whammy that can ripple into missed breakfasts, late classes and fewer school activities. What they're saying: "We're a non-instructional expense for a district," Peter Mannella of the National Association for Pupil Transportation tells Axios. "The inclination is always going to be let's see what we can cut out of transportation costs because we don't want to affect the school library," he says, adding that districts would rather protect spending on teachers, aides, and special education. The big picture: Districts are consolidating routes, cutting trips and squeezing more efficiency out of their fleets. A May survey of 188 school officials found 40% had adjusted routes, 27% enforced anti-idling rules, 25% cut routes, 20% limited optional trips, 14% changed fuel purchasing and 8% made students walk farther to stops. Mannella said those changes result in more parents driving students to school activities or districts moving pickup points farther from students' homes. "It starts to affect kids and families, which you know you'd rather not do," he said. Case in point: Cherry Creek Public Schools outside Denver is short about 40 drivers, transportation director Mark Ingram tells Axios. "It's an all hands on deck thing," he said. "Every morning and afternoon, we're looking at running some routes 10 to 15 minutes late … we just don't have the people to cover the routes." For some students, that can mean missing the school-provided breakfast or arriving late to first period, he said. Ingram's district has about 611 vehicles, including 320 yellow buses, plus vehicles for students with special needs and other district operations. The district budgeted $1.5 million for fuel this year, up $300,000. It now expects to spend roughly $2 million to $2.3 million. Ingram said the district hasn't cut services but is being frugal. Zoom in: The driver shortage isn't just about wages. Nick Martini, a former school bus driver who is now an executive at a Minneapolis-area school bus contractor, said drivers must simultaneously manage children and traffic while meeting extensive training, licensing and safety requirements. Split shifts can keep drivers tied up for 10 to 12 hours while paying for only a fraction of that time, and districts compete with delivery and logistics companies for the same workers with commercial-driver's licenses . Between the lines: Rural districts have even fewer escape routes. Whereas kids in urban and suburban areas can sometimes walk to school, rural children may live miles from school, requiring longer bus routes, while districts struggle to match private-sector driver pay or hire third-party operators. Special-needs transportation can be similarly expensive because curb-to-curb routes may have long gaps between stops. Flashback: The Biden administration offered federal funding to electrify school bus fleets, but some of those programs have since slowed or ended, Association of School Business Officials International's Elleka Yost tells Axios. Electric buses aren't an immediate fix everywhere. Yost pointed to narrow or winding roads, small bridges, extreme temperatures and a lack of trained technicians. The bottom line: Districts will keep adapting, Mannella said. "We are inherently problem solvers," he said. "Transportation is too important to just let us say, 'Well, we're not going to be able to do that anymore.' We'll find a way." Go deeper: School bus tech drives classroom gains

events.title: Connecting AI agents to enterprise knowledge
events.summary: For all the data that AI systems continually amass and analyze, enterprise AI agents often suffer from a curious shortcoming: a lack of knowledge. More than data, knowledge is the understanding of what the data means in the context of individual organizations. AI agents need this understanding to reason about situations, make decisions, and ultimately take actions. Without sufficient knowledge, agents are prone to making flawed and unreliable decisions. A lack of knowledge, our research finds, is a major reason agentic AI use cases never make it to production. Competitive pressure is making it urgent to address this. Organizations need to deploy and scale more of their agentic projects to capture the efficiency gains AI promises. Falling short risks wasting the investment already sunk into these projects, and it cedes ground to rivals already putting their agents to work more effectively. DOWNLOAD THE REPORT The purpose of this report, which is based on a survey of 300 data, AI, and other technology executives, is threefold. First, it seeks to gauge organizations’ agentic knowledge capabilities (i.e., their ability to give AI agents a full contextual understanding of the data they ingest) across semantic knowledge, episodic memory, and procedural knowledge. Second, the report probes the challenges organizations face in improving access to knowledge and ultimately to getting more agent use cases into production. Third, it explores the measures organizations are taking to overcome these challenges. The key findings include the following: Data and knowledge weaknesses consistently stall AI agent progress. On average, only around a third (34%) of organizations’ agentic AI projects make it into production. Even high-tech firms struggle with this. Legacy data systems, security and privacy concerns, and a lack of knowledge and context are the key points of failure. Strong knowledge capabilities correlate with agent success. A small group of production leaders (organizations where on average 61% of agentic projects advance beyond pilot) have stronger knowledge capabilities than the rest, especially when it comes to semantics. This advantage tracks closely with their higher production rate. Fragmented data hugely complicates knowledge access. Data fragmentation (the inadequate sharing of data across systems) was most commonly cited as a top challenge to expanding agents’ access to knowledge (cited by 55%). Production leaders, by contrast, are more likely to see security and privacy concerns as a major concern (cited by 72% of this group). Most firms aim to strengthen the link between data and agents. Among steps that can yield higher quality agent decisions, executives expect the biggest impact to come from strengthening the structural foundation between the organization’s data and its AI agents. The experts we interviewed see a knowledge layer as a prime way to achieve this. Investment priorities to boost knowledge range from pipelines to knowledge graphs. To expand agent access to knowledge, organizations will prioritize investments in retrieval technologies, like ingestion pipelines, AI-ready APIs, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG); in AI evaluation agents; and in knowledge graphs. events.title: Preppers used to be ridiculed – but we’re all stockpiling now | Zoe Williams
events.summary: Preppers used to be ridiculed – but we’re all stockpiling now The UK government urging households to prepare for unknown threats with a three-day supply of food and water doesn’t feel like an overreaction. But is there a bigger plan to go with it? T here is no national food stockpile and there hasn’t been since it was wound up in the 1990s. It feels like a metaphor for the delusions of that era: nothing bad can possibly happen again; no two countries with a McDonald’s have gone to war with each other (according to the journalist Thomas L Friedman, also in the 90s ). Now, we all have a McDonald’s and wars regularly disrupt food supplies. The problem with metaphors is you can’t eat them – not even satisfying ones. For people who remember the second world war, or feel as if they do, there is always enough muscle memory to do topical household stockpiling. My mum kept a trunk of food that was mainly filled with condensed milk in case of a nuclear war, all the way through the 80s. When the Berlin Wall came down, we should have had a ceremonial toffee-sauce-making event where we ate it all, but we didn’t; in 1990, she was stockpiling again, to mark the Gulf war. The spectre of Y2K saw a large amount of bottled water enter the house, but by then I’d left home. When 9/11 happened, the water had gone off, but it was still fine for washing, apparently, so all she needed was a load of new water – and all that remained for the wider family was to call her mad and occasionally steal her anchovies. The 2008 financial crash may have brought almost 20 years of roiling turmoil to the world, but the period spent wondering whether the cash would stop coming out of the wall was only a couple of days, during which if you had got your arse into gear enough to buy beans, you would have been considered hysterical. It would be dispiriting to go through all the events since that have made stockpiling seem like a good idea and impossible to pinpoint the date on which having a three-day food stash went from “crazy prepper idea from someone who probably also keeps a crossbow” to “something any sensible person who reads the news and listens to the authorities would do”. The UK government’s resilience campaign , urging households to prepare for threats unknown, doesn’t feel like an overreaction. But nor does it feel realistic. A record number of households – one in eight , or one in six with children – experience food insecurity already, which is to say can’t be sure they have enough even without external events. The range of possible disasters is so wide that it’s hard to consider them practically without freaking out: are we planning for crop failures in the UK or for the collapse of the global food supply, which would mean us relying on our own crops? Are we anticipating a hostile foreign act such as a cyber-attack, or something more meat-world? Power outages, extreme weather, floods – they all seem possible, but none of them seem as if they’d be over in three days. You can see that having a torch would be better than no torch, but a stash of tinned pineapple wouldn’t meet the moment. The advice is to have three litres of drinking water a day for each person, but can you seriously imagine having that and not sharing it? There is no household solution that doesn’t hinge on the emergency being very short-lived and a collective response being ready to go within only a few hours. The more you think about emergencies, though, the less likely they seem to be short-lived. The chance of inoculating yourself household by household seems vanishingly small. The essence of old-school prepping – the reason people who did it were mocked and viewed with suspicion – was that it was implicitly off-grid, or rather planning for a world without a grid and without meaningful order. The modern preppers’ problem is that stockpiling for your own household – even having a workable first aid kit and some non-perishables – feels ridiculous unless you believe there’s a bigger plan under way. The government has the unenviable task of asking us to trust the future less while trusting its authority more. It’s enough to make you want to do something helpful – more helpful, even, than buying a gigantic bag of rice. Debian's latest Linux kernel security update comes with a formidable reading list of 1,313 CVE identifiers. The DSA-6528-1 Linux security advisory , published on September 29, covers kernel package version 6.12.111-1 for Debian 13, codenamed Trixie. Debian 13.7 was released on September 12 , before upstream kernel 6.12.111 arrived nine days later. The Debian security tracker links to descriptions of the individual issues. We have not examined every entry. If we had, this article would not appear until after Debian 13.8 (which is likely to appear later in October), or possibly at some point in 2027. Several checked at random also affect older kernel versions, so the list should not be read as a tally of bugs introduced in 6.12.111. The Linux kernel project became a CVE Numbering Authority (CNA) in February 2024 . Back in February this year, kernel maintainer Greg Kroah-Hartman described the Linux CVE assignment process in some detail. He said kernel development averages around nine changes an hour, with a feed of known bug fixes averaging about 30 changes a day providing the basis for the CNA team's review. The kernel team's policy is to assign CVEs automatically after fixes have reached a stable kernel tree. It takes a deliberately cautious approach because the security implications of a bug may not be apparent when it is fixed. A CVE identifier alone therefore says little about severity or exploitability. We strongly suspect that this number of CVEs is due to LLM bots doing the bug hunting, and quite possibly doing the bug fixing as well. Linux is not an anti-AI project , and neither is Debian . AI-assisted bug hunting is already swamping the Linux security mailing list , as The Register reported in May. Kroah-Hartman released kernel 6.12.112 on October 3. Its detailed changelog runs to more than 27,000 lines. With both the rates of change and the sizes of the changes getting so large, it is hard to deny that LLM bot assistance must be very useful to the hard-pressed maintainers. events.title: Sainsbury’s and Morrisons ‘held talks this year’ on multibillion-pound merger
events.summary: Deal would have created a supermarket with a market share of 23.6%, still well behind Tesco’s 27.8% Sainsbury’s held merger talks with rival Morrisons this year to discuss a multibillion-pound deal that would have been the biggest shake-up for UK supermarkets in decades, according to reports. The two companies held exploratory negotiations, according to the Financial Times and Sky. It is believed they are no longer in live discussions. Morrisons, which was once one of the big four UK grocers alongside Sainsbury’s, Tesco and Asda, was bought by the US private equity firm Clayton Dubilier & Rice in 2021. The deal loaded it with more than £7bn in debt on its balance sheet, and it has since struggled to grow as fast as its rivals. The German discounter Lidl overtook it in market share this year. A merger between Sainsbury’s and Morrisons would have created a business with a 23.6% market share, putting it still some way behind Britain’s biggest retailer, Tesco, which has 27.8% of the market, according to analysts at Worldpanel by Numerator. The last attempt to merge two of the big four supermarkets was in 2019, when Asda and Sainsbury’s almost joined forces. That £7bn deal was blocked by the Competition and Markets Authority on the basis that it would result in a loss of competition and higher prices for customers. The CMA would have almost certainly reviewed any merger between Sainsbury’s and Morrisons, and could have required the former to sell some of its stores to gain approval for any deal. Reducing competition in the grocery sector could also be politically sensitive, given that millions of households have grappled with persistent food inflation in recent years. Clayton Dubilier & Rice, however, is open to a tie-up between Morrisons and another major supermarket, according to Sky. It reported that Asda, which is majority owned by the private equity firm TDR Capital, could also be drawn into deal talks. Sainsbury’s, which employs about 140,000 people, is the second biggest grocer in the UK by market share at 15.2%. The company said pre-tax profits at its British arm rose by 30% to £245.5m in the year that ended in February as shoppers sought out cheaper fresh meat, fruit and vegetables, as well as its Deluxe upmarket food range.
