events.title: 'Debris field' found in search for missing medical flight from Bermuda
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts 'Debris field' found after 6-person medical flight goes missing over Atlantic The US Coast Guard is continuing the search. ( US Coast Guard via AP ) The US Coast Guard has found a "debris field' in its search for an air ambulance that went missing over the Atlantic. The Canadian-registered aircraft was carrying six people from Bermuda to Boston in the United States. The Coast Guard said the search would continue. Searchers have found debris from an air ambulance that was carrying six people when it went missing over the Atlantic during a flight from Bermuda to Boston. The "debris field" was found off the coast of Nantucket, in the US state of Massachusetts, following the disappearance on Saturday, the US Coast Guard said. Four Canadians and two Bermudian nationals were aboard, the Coast Guard said in a statement. It added that the next of kin of those missing had been notified and one of its cutters would keep searching the water overnight and into Sunday. According to the Coast Guard, the Federal Aviation Administration reported that the Gulfstream G100 aircraft lost contact very early on Saturday morning. Air traffic audio indicates that it may have been "coming in blind" when a storm loomed ahead shortly before it disappeared. The pilot reported electrical problems and declared an emergency as the jet approached the coast, according to air traffic control audio posted by LiveATC.net. "Roger, you said you're coming in blind. Is that what you said?" a controller can be heard asking the pilot. The plane may have lost its navigational instruments as a storm seen on radar moved across its path, former US Department of Transportation inspector-general Mary Schiavo said. The plane also descended sharply from its cruising altitude of around 7.3 kilometres to around three kilometres, according to preliminary data from flight tracking site FlightRadar24. "Something bad happened with this big drop, and they flew into this big storm," Ms Schiavo, an aviation attorney, said. "It's a terrible place to have a loss of your instruments and be flying blind. "It's very easy to get disoriented and not know if you're turning, climbing, descending, etc." The Canadian-registered air ambulance jet had four crew and two passengers aboard when it departed Bermuda's L.F. Wade International Airport for the night flight to Massachusetts, according to a statement from the Bermuda airport's operator, Skyport. Transport Canada was closely monitoring and working with authorities on search and rescue efforts, the country's Minister of Transport Steven MacKinnon said on X. The Bermuda government is in contact with US authorities and the families of the passengers, Bermuda Premier David Burt wrote in a statement posted on Instagram. "We are praying that all six people will be found safe," the statement said. The US National Transportation Safety Board said it was gathering information about the situation, but it did not say immediately if it would investigate. events.title: Syria 'pressing on accelerator' to attract US investors
events.summary: US investors see an opportunity to invest early in Syria as the transitional government races to establish a pro-business environment and attract foreign capital. “We see that the door is open, and we're coming early,” Steve Lutes, vice president of Middle East Affairs at the US Chamber of Commerce, said in an interview. “I think US companies made it very clear across a different range of sectors that they're looking to be strategically engaged, to be a long-term partner in helping Syria get back up on its feet and excel economically.” Mr Lutes spoke to The National after the Chamber of Commerce hosted a round-table with Syrian President Ahmad Al Shara and Foreign Minister Asaad Al Shibani on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly last month. He also recently led a delegation of more than 50 American businesses and 80 delegates to Damascus. The delegation – which included Baker Hughes , Caterpillar, Visa and dozens of other US firms – marked a significant step in re-establishing Washington's economic relationship with Syria after the 13-year civil war. It also came shortly after the US lifted its state sponsor of terrorism designation on Syria, which had been a prominent roadblock to the country’s reintegration into the international financial system. Syria’s government has moved quickly to attract investment since the fall of Bashar Al Assad's regime in 2024. The World Bank estimates it will cost $216 billion to rebuild the country. Some investment pledges from the Gulf have already moved towards implementation, including DP World's $800 million investment commitment to Tartus Port. At the same time, Syria has also courted foreign investors from Silicon Valley to Riyadh. “They're really pressing on the accelerator to try to move things forward,” Mr Lutes said. He added that the Chamber of Commerce was turning significant attention towards Syria's banking sector , which has undergone a rapid transformation under the current government. Mr Al Shara carried out the country’s first international Visa transaction in August. “It's so foundational to everything else,” Mr Lutes said. QNB and Mastercard issued the first internationally accepted payment card in Syria. The World Bank has also approved a $100 million grant to help establish a digitally enabled financial sector. Last Sunday, Central Bank of Syria Governor Mohammed Raslan told official news agency Sana that the government expected foreign investment in establishing new banks to surpass $1 billion in the coming period. The US Treasury Department on Thursday held a round-table in New York to support the country's financial sector and reconnection to the global financial system. Finance Minister Yisr Barnieh said in a LinkedIn post that discussions had focused on advancing anti-money laundering and counter-terrorism financing standards, among other reforms. Treasury Assistant Secretary for Terrorist Financing and Financial Crimes Jonathan Burke also stressed financial connectivity remains a vital component to combatting illicit finance and supporting Syria's reintegration into the global financial system, according to a readout. Public spending in Syria for first six months of the year totalled roughly $3.7 billion, compared to a public revenue of $2.7 billion, according to the finance ministry's first-half 2026 budget report. That leaves a fiscal deficit of about $1 billion. “The biggest challenge at the end of the day are the budgetary constraints and how are they going to finance and pay for it all,” Mr Lutes said. Damascus said it was implementing new measures to control public spending, including reviewing investment projects. Mr Barnieh wrote in a social media post on Monday that the measures would not affect salaries, wages or spending on essential needs such as health, education, water, energy, security, public safety and necessary operational maintenance. Gulf partnerships While the state sponsor of terrorism delisting removed the final pillar in the US sanctions architecture, investing in Syria continues to carry reputational risks. It remains on the Financial Action Task Force's grey list, and parties may have previous links to sanctioned actors. Mr Lutes described the Chamber of Commerce’s delegation to Damascus as an “exploratory” one to give US companies the chance to identify sectors for investment and re-establish trust with Syrian officials. Several US companies have already signed memorandums of understanding and other agreements with Syria including ConocoPhillips, Chevron, Baker Hughes, Hunt Energy and Ardent LNG. Gulf partners have joined some of these projects including Qatar's UCC Holding, which signed an agreement with Chevron and Syria's state-run petroleum company to develop the country's first offshore oil and gasfield. Mr Lutes anticipates more US companies could go down similar routes with Emirati, Saudi or Qatari partners who already have relationships with the country. Doing so could mitigate some risks and increase US investor confidence. He added that he hopes the delegation will become an annual occurrence. He also said the chamber is engaging with the Syrian government on addressing policy regulatory issues. “We're not going out of business any time soon. There's a lot of work for the chamber to support US companies that are interested in doing business in Syria, so we're going to be at this … for many years to come,” Mr Lutes said.

events.title: Regional audiences to lose Network 10, as licensee warns of TV's future
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Network 10 to disappear in parts of SA, NSW's Riverina, after no deal made Network 10 channels will disappear from Mount Gambier, Riverland and Griffith TV screens. ( ABC News: Jak Rowland ) Audiences in Mount Gambier and the Riverland in SA, and Griffith in NSW, will lose terrestrial Network 10 channels on Friday. Network 10 and license holders WIN failed to come to a new agreement after months of negotiating. WIN says it will be "challenging to maintain services", due to the economics of regional broadcasting. Viewers in parts of regional South Australia, and parts of the Riverina in New South Wales, will lose access to Network 10's terrestrial channels, after the network and license holder, WIN Network, failed to reach an agreement. WIN has announced it will stop broadcasting 10, 10 Drama and 10 Comedy in the Mount Gambier, Riverland, Griffith and Murrumbidgee Irrigation Area, with the final broadcasts to be on Friday, October 9. The network had flagged its agreement with Network 10 would expire in July, and that the channels would be pulled. However, local audiences were given a three-month reprieve , with Network 10 saying it would provide its feed "free of charge" to WIN while the parties worked on a deal that has not eventuated. WIN Network says the decision reflects the economics of regional broadcasting. ( ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters ) In a statement, a WIN Network spokesperson said providing Network 10 services to the impacted markets was "no longer viable". "This is a business decision that reflects the realities of regional broadcasting," they said. "Regional markets carry high transmission and infrastructure costs, while digital disruption continues to erode audiences and advertising revenue. "These economics will continue to make it challenging to maintain services across regional Australia. "WIN recognises this will be disappointing for viewers and thanks them for their understanding." The move follows a similar loss of Seven Network channels to the same markets, after Seven and WIN failed to reach an agreement before Seven's deal expired last year. The channels were eventually restored after a multi-day shutdown that saw the channels replaced with red screens advising they were "no longer available". Audiences in Mount Gambier, the Riverland and Griffith temporarily lost Seven Network channels last year. ( ABC South East SA: Eugene Boisvert ) Job cut fears at one of Australia's largest toilet roll manufacturers How a 'piece of rural propaganda' became 'compulsory listening' for Aussies Soccer player with broken leg endures 70km car trip between hospitals Regional women share postpartum journeys to create change A Network 10 spokesperson said audiences could continue to access the network's channels online and via its app. "WIN holds the broadcast licences in the Riverland, Mount Gambier and Griffith regions and although Network 10 has worked closely with WIN to explore options to maintain local access to its content, WIN has advised that continuing to operate them is no longer commercially viable," they said. The WIN Network holds the broadcast licenses in Mount Gambier, the Riverland and Griffith. ( ABC South East SA: Eugene Boisvert ) It is not the first time a regional market has lost Network 10 channels due to the financial challenges of regional broadcasting. In 2024, audiences in Mildura, Victoria, lost their Network 10 channels when Mildura Digital Television (MDT), which carried 10's signal to the market, was closed by co-owners Seven and WIN. The networks said "it did not make commercial sense" to keep MDT going, as it had been unprofitable throughout its existence. A government spokesperson said the decision was a "commercial matter" and that it was up to the networks to explain it to the community. "The government continues to support Australian broadcasters through a range of measures including the deferral of the Commercial Broadcasting Tax, which will deliver an estimated $111.3 million in savings for the sector," they said. "We know how important free-to-air TV is and are examining ways to ensure it continues to be delivered in a sustainable way in the future, with public consultation now underway.

events.title: Houthis target Saudi oil facility as hostilities escalate in Yemen
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Iran-backed Houthis target Saudi oil facility as hostilities escalate in Yemen Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis say they targeted a Saudi Arabian oil company in retaliation for Saudi attacks on Yemen. The fighting has worsened the already appalling humanitarian conditions in Yemen. Iraq's state-owned Oil Tanker Company says it has transported 2 million barrels of Iraqi crude aboard a large crude carrier through the Strait of Hormuz. Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis say a targeted attack on a Saudi Arabian oil company facility near the capital Riyadh is retaliation for Saudi attacks on Yemen. The foes have traded strikes since the Houthis seized all of Yemen's Red Sea coast and took control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait in a lightning offensive last month. Houthi-affiliated channel Al-Masirah TV reported that Saudi aircraft hit Sanaa with 26 strikes, after earlier reporting "Saudi aggression" against the Yemeni capital. Houthis say they targeted a Saudi oil facility, south of Riyadh. ( AP ) Two correspondents in Sanaa reported hearing loud explosions and seeing warplanes firing missiles at the city. In Saudi Arabia, flames and smoke were seen rising on Saturday afternoon from an Aramco facility south of Riyadh. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had targeted an oil facility in Riyadh with ballistic missiles and drones. They said the attack sparked fires at the targeted sites. Al-Masirah also reported missile strikes on the telecommunications network in Yemen's north-western governorate of Saada, one of the group's strongholds. After several years of calm, Yemen was plunged back into civil war in July, pitting the Iran-backed Houthis, who control most of north-west Yemen, including Sanaa, against Yemen's internationally recognised government. The government, based in the city of Aden, controls much of the country's south and east, a region that is larger but much less populated. A big, expensive, global excursion into hell What so many of the current major global conflicts have in common with the debacle in Iraq is their undefined, or sometimes not truthfully defined, missions. Hostilities were reignited after four years of a fragile truce when Iran sent a plane to Sanaa carrying a Houthi delegation. The flight did not seek authorisation from Saudi Arabia, contravening a decade-old practice. Riyadh retaliated with strikes on Sanaa airport, and in response the Houthis attacked Saudi territory for the first time since 2022. Since then, fighting has intensified, with the Houthis launching a lightning offensive in which they seized control of coastal regions along the Bab al-Mandab Strait. Houthi fighters took over the Red Sea port of Sanaa in Yemen. ( AP ) They have also struck multiple Saudi targets, including oil infrastructure and Riyadh, while also announcing a naval blockade on Saudi shipping in the Red Sea. The renewed fighting has worsened the already appalling humanitarian conditions in Yemen, one of the world's poorest countries, with the World Food Programme warning on Friday that three-quarters of the population was unable to meet its basic food needs. Fighting in recent days has centred on Taiz, where dozens of combatants were reported killed on Friday by sources on both sides. The Houthis reported 55 of their fighters had been killed, while government sources said 26 troops had died. The Houthis have moved on strategic islands in the Red Sea and are now putting one of the richest and most powerful nations in the Middle East in a tricky spot. The Houthis said on Friday Saudi Arabia had launched 94 strikes against areas under their control in the previous 24 hours. Saudi authorities reported a Houthi projectile had damaged a school in the city of Najran near the Yemeni border. Riyadh has reportedly requested help from the United States, a call so far rebuffed by US President Donald Trump . Meanwhile, Iraq's state-owned Oil Tanker Company transported 2 million barrels of Iraqi crude aboard a large crude carrier through the Strait of Hormuz, in what its director general described on Saturday as the company's first such operation in decades. A week of Houthi attacks threatens oil and markets The Iran-backed Houthi rebels have made their biggest land grab in years, reigniting Yemen's 12-year long civil war and pushing up global fuel prices. The announcement means the company is transporting the crude through the strait rather than delivering it at the port of Basra, giving state oil marketer SOMO greater flexibility in how and where it sells the crude.

events.title: Ethiopian federal forces retake Mekelle airport from Tigrayan fighters, residents say
events.summary: Ethiopian federal forces have retaken Mekelle’s airport from Tigrayan fighters KAMPALA, Uganda -- Ethiopian federal forces have taken the airport in Mekelle, the capital of the northern Tigray region, according to people in the city who spoke to The Associated Press on Saturday, reversing a takeover by Tigrayan fighters that prompted the suspension of commercial flights last month. It wasn't immediately clear when federal forces recaptured Alula Aba Nega Airport. Those who provided the information declined to be identified for fear of retribution amid uncertainty over who controlled the city. Severe disruptions to internet and cellphone networks have made gathering and verifying information from Tigray difficult. Details of how the airport changed hands, including whether fighting took place there, remained unclear. “The military is in full control of the airport. That much I can confirm,” an Ethiopian general said on condition of anonymity. Neither the Ethiopian government nor the Tigray People’s Liberation Front, or TPLF, had issued an official statement on the airport’s reported capture. It wasn’t clear who controlled Mekelle itself. An AP contributor in the city said residents feared looting amid the uncertainty. “Many reports indicate that the government and allied forces have begun to control Tigray’s capital,” said Jalale Getachew Birru, an Ethiopia analyst for ACLED, an independent global monitor that collects, analyzes and maps data on conflict. The AP could not independently verify those reports. TPLF fighters seized the airport on Sept. 23, prompting Ethiopian Airlines to suspend flights to Mekelle and the Tigrayan cities of Axum and Shire. The African Union urged restraint, warning that renewed tensions threatened the peace agreement signed in 2022. Federal troops are fighting alongside allied Tigrayan forces against the TPLF. The AP previously reported that the Tigray Peace Force, a breakaway faction of the Tigrayan rebels, was operating alongside federal forces in the neighboring Afar region. The reported change in control follows a sharp deterioration in relations between Ethiopia and neighboring Eritrea. Ethiopia on Thursday ordered 10 Eritrean diplomats to leave and announced the closure of its embassy in Eritrea. Eritrea said that it would sever diplomatic ties. Ethiopian authorities have accused Eritrea of supporting the TPLF , an allegation Eritrea has denied. The U.S. State Department in a statement Saturday urged Ethiopia and Eritrea to show restraint and return to talks. Phone calls, records suggest some Cornell students tried to contain rape allegations Suspect in FlyDubai incident was previously identified as security risk: Officials District attorney reopens case of alleged Cornell University 'gang rape' “Increasing cross-border tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea have the potential to affect the entire region,” State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said. “The Horn of Africa cannot sustain another military conflict and humanitarian crisis. A conflict jeopardizes ongoing U.S. collaboration on shared interests with both countries.” The government of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed , if it takes control of Mekelle, is very likely to leave regional security in the hands of the Tigray Peace Force, which comprises former members of the Tigray Defense Forces, Birru said. Abiy has tried and failed to subdue Tigray’s rebellious leaders in recent months, with TPLF Chairman Debretsion Gebremichael openly challenging him. Renewed fighting has shattered a 2022 peace deal that ended a devastating two-year war between federal troops, backed by Eritrea and allied militias, and the TPLF. “This is an extraordinary and largely unexpected turn in a war whose direction looked very different only days ago,” Getachew Temare, an independent attorney and human rights defender who is from Ethiopia, said of the possible fall of Mekelle in an analysis posted on X. “But the most consequential question is not whether Mekelle falls. It is what this fall means politically.” He said the emergence of the Tigray Peace Force makes the current conflict different from the previous one. When Mekelle fell to federal forces in November 2020, the TPLF “retained something far more important. A substantial political and social constituency for armed resistance remained intact. Within months, Tigrayan forces returned to Mekelle and the military balance was dramatically reversed.” The fighting has brought renewed hardship to civilians still recovering from the previous 2020-2022 war. Residents of Mekelle told the AP earlier this week that communications, banking and other essential services had been disrupted. In September, residents described fears of renewed isolation following the suspension of flights. They also reported that roads connecting Tigray and Afar had been closed to civilian traffic, although the AP couldn't independently verify the closures. Kiyaro reported from Hamburg, Germany.

events.title: Thousands pack arena in Belgrade as Serbia's leader Vucic launches prime minister bid
events.summary: Thousands of supporters of Serbia's populist leader Aleksandar Vucic have packed Belgrade's largest arena for the launch of his campaign for prime minister BELGRADE, Serbia -- Thousands of supporters of Serbia's populist leader, Aleksandar Vucic, packed the largest indoor arena in Belgrade on Saturday for the de facto launch of his campaign for prime minister that will culminate in a pivotal election set for Oct. 25. The early election, which polls suggest could be tight between Vucic's party and a group of candidates fielded by a student-led protest movement, was called before Vucic resigned as president on Sept. 27, cutting short his second term by more than seven months. Vucic, who is constitutionally prohibited from running for a third term as president, declared upon resigning that he would lead his populist Serbian Progressive Party in the parliamentary election. If his party wins a majority of seats, the parliament is expected to elect Vucic as prime minister. Dozens of buses from across Serbia clogged streets around Belgrade Arena on Saturday as supporters arrived at the rally in the capital carrying Serbian flags and banners bearing Vucic’s picture. The event, televised by dozens of channels across Serbia, capped a week of Vucic touring towns and villages in an apparent bid to shore up his popularity that's been shaken after almost two years of sustained anti-government protests. The youth-backed movement that led the protests has demanded accountability for the Nov. 1, 2024 train station canopy collapse that killed 16 people in the northern city of Novi Sad. The movement's struggle for justice over the tragedy and against corruption has grown into a nationwide political force whose electoral arm, the Student List, will attempt to oust Vucic’s government after 14 years in power. Vucic himself has been either prime minister or president for the past 12 years. The Student List includes university professors, teachers, experts and others from across the political spectrum. Yet Vucic has accused those behind the movement of seeking to “bring Serbia to a halt,” and claimed, without providing evidence, that it's backed by unspecified foreign agents. And they know that.” The election is taking place amid heightened political tensions in Serbia, with reports of incidents and physical altercations at campaign events. International observers have described previous elections in Serbia as marred by multiple irregularities and violence. While formally a candidate for European Union membership, Serbia’s accession process has stalled under Vucic, who maintains close ties with Russia and China. European institutions have warned of democratic backsliding in Serbia in successive reports tracking the progress of candidate countries. Rights and media freedom groups have separately warned of police violence , arbitrary detentions, unauthorized surveillance and threats against journalists. events.title: SA's first musical theatre company brings talent home in debut stage
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Joey Haenen (front left) will play the lead role in Catch Me If You Can, the debut production of SA musical theatre company Full Circle. ( Supplied ) When Joey Haenen graduated with a music theatre degree in Adelaide, he knew he had to move states. "There is no work here and so you've got to move over east, that's where most of the agents are," he said. "You do all your auditioning over there and hopefully you'll land a gig." Haenen moved to Melbourne, like Jazz Garcia who spent a year getting her name known while paying for her passion through a day job in speech pathology. "There's just a lot more musical theatre opportunities in Melbourne, we don't really have anything in Adelaide," she said. The exodus from South Australia to the east coast has been happening for decades, a talent drain Jo Casson was determined to stop. Jo Casson says South Australia has been crying out for a professional musical theatre company. ( Supplied ) The arts veteran joined forces with others to form Full Circle, the state's first-ever professional music theatre company. "I discovered in the middle of last year that every other major city has a professional local theatre company and Adelaide didn't." Ironically, it's a full circle moment for the company's choreographer Zoe Komazec-Kermond, who returned from the east coast after a career performing in shows including Cats, Matilda and Mary Poppins. "There is so much talent in South Australia, so much talent and we do sometimes feel like we have to go away in order to achieve what we want to achieve," she said. Zoe Komazec-Kermond says a new SA musical theatre company will convince performers to come home. ( Supplied ) With such a rich vein of talent, Casson said forming the new company made sense. It has the backing of well-known arts lover and philanthropist Pamela Wall AO, but the company is seeking more support, as well as applying for grant funding. Full Circle will stage the musical Catch Me If You Can as its opening number, a stage version of the story that Leonardo DiCaprio took to the big screen and earned rave reviews. When the company held auditions, it attracted more than 100 performers for the 25 roles. Haenen was working and had to push his case with an audition video he sent to producers. The 21-year-old rising star's absence from the auditions did not stop him from landing the lead role of Frank Abagnale Jr. "What I love is just being able to get little bits of Joey in each of the characters every time and that's such a great joy," Haenen said. Garcia, who earned a contract among the show's ensemble, said the three-day auditions were exhausting. "The dance call was extremely strenuous, I'd say that was one of the longest kind of dance audition processes I've ever been in," she said. Jazz Garcia (middle) would love to travel back to South Australia to perform with Full Circle. ( Supplied ) More than 30 creatives and technical crew have been hired with the final cast a mix of South Australians and others returning to the state. "Everyone could sing, everyone could dance and everyone could act, so it made our job really hard to pick our final cast," Komazec-Kermond said. Beetlejuice, Waitress, Back to the Future and Dear Evan Hansen were major musicals which cancelled shows recently, with one producer citing increased cost pressures from "touring across vast distances between Australian cities". Full Circle said it was different because it would not have the high costs of touring a show nationally, like many others. However, Casson said getting productions into the country was a goal in future years. Full Circle wants to stage two musicals a year for the next two years, before increasing to three after that. Jazz Garcia believes more performers will build careers in South Australia after a new musical theatre company was formed. ( Supplied ) Those both on and off the stage realised the importance of pulling off the show and demonstrating the company should be here to stay. "It's a huge responsibility and I think we're going to do a really good job," Garcia confidently predicted. "There's so much buzz in Adelaide at the moment around Full Circle, so it's really up to us to produce the very best version of this show that we can," she said. Catch Me If You Can is at Futures Theatre in Paradise from November 5-7.

events.summary: Tennessee's top prison official turned in his resignation days after the failed attempt to execute death row inmate Christa Pike , the state announced Saturday. Gov. Bill Lee said Department of Correction commissioner Frank Strada would step down this month. Strada, who had served as commissioner since 2023, said he would cooperate with the independent investigation of the failed execution attempt. Pike, 50, survived two doses of the lethal injection drug pentobarbital and was taken to a hospital for life-saving treatment. What they're saying: In a statement, Strada said he believed his department "carried out its responsibilities in accordance with the established protocol. Lee said Strada "served with integrity," adding that he appreciated Strada's "willingness to put the interests of Tennesseans first during this difficult moment. … "I thank Commissioner Strada for his dedicated service to Tennessee and pray God's blessings over him in the days ahead." The big picture: Strada's department has faced bipartisan criticism following the unprecedented failures during the attempt to execute Pike on Wednesday night. Her attorneys said the execution team used at least seven needles in their attempts to find a vein for an IV. Pike's attorneys said she complained of intense pain during the injection and developed blisters and burns around the injection site. Between the lines: Medical experts have said those details suggest the IV wasn't properly connected and that the drug might not have gone directly into her bloodstream. Pike was unconscious and on a ventilator in a local hospital on Friday, her attorneys said.

events.title: OpenAI's Altman: Ascribing religion to models a "safety issue"
events.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman on Saturday took a veiled shot at Anthropic and its work on the soul of AI, saying he was "very uncomfortable" with the idea of attributing some kind of religious power to models. Why it matters: It's yet another point of division between Altman and his former colleague Dario Amodei, whose company has reportedly pursued scholars across faiths to make the case for moral, conscious models. But some of the top voices in AI are starting to publicly line up against Anthropic's efforts to infuse consciousness into models. What they're saying: "I am very uncomfortable about people trying to ascribe religious force or a surrender of human judgment to AI models, and think it is a real safety issue," Altman said in a post to X. Context: Earlier this week, the New York Times reported that Anthropic co-founder Christopher Olah has been meeting with religious leaders to consider questions of model consciousness — but also to figure out how to infuse morals and moral behavior into AI. At one point, the Times reported, Olah considered the possibility of models engaging in Catholic-style confession, not just to admit their mistakes but to shape their future behavior. The big picture: Spirituality is suddenly becoming something of a flashpoint around AI's future. On Friday Pope Leo, an outspoken AI critic, called on the church to ally with artists to preserve human creativity, saying: "Algorithms lack the spark of humanity." Between the lines: The pope's stance put renewed focus on a fundamental question: Do models have souls and feelings? The Times reported that Olah, before a Vatican event in May, tried to persuade the pope's advisers that they should take the prospect of conscious models more seriously. So far, other top scientists seem to be lining up against the idea. "I am disturbed by how some of my fellow AI researchers keep trying to elevate the moral standing of checkpoints and harnesses," Google DeepMind principal research scientist Jon Barron posted to X. "I hope the rest of us on Team Meatbag reject this movement and stay focused on solving real problems and helping actual humans." For the record: Neither OpenAI nor Anthropic immediately responded to requests for comment on Altman's post. The bottom line: The AI safety debate largely focuses on things like cybersecurity and bioweapons. The real problem may be more spiritual than that.

events.title: Anthropic's super bug-hunting model Mythos is hardcore good at math, as latest vuln under attack shows
events.summary: The second Anthropic-linked vulnerability known to have been exploited in the wild saw initial activity from an IP address in China targeting vulnerable hosts in the US and Japan. The vuln is a critical authentication-bypass bug in Rejetto HTTP File Server (HFS) that can lead to full admin access and remote code execution. HFS is an open source web file server that previously appeared on the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s catalog of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities in 2024. On Wednesday, researcher Zach Hanley at AI pen-testing company Horizon3 said he used Mythos to uncover a new flaw in the file server, now tracked as CVE-2026-61500. If you use Rejetto HFS, be sure to update to v3.2.1 or later, which fixes this and other security flaws. Hanley also published a video showing the steps to exploit HFS and remotely execute code on the server. By the next day, the CVE was under exploitation. “We started detecting exploitation of CVE-2026-61500 in Rejetto HFS this evening,” VulnCheck security researcher Patrick Garrity posted on LinkedIn on Thursday, adding that Hanley and team reported the bug to VulnCheck for CVE assignment. “Our canaries detected an actor in China targeting real vulnerable hosts in the US,” Garrity added. Garrity has been tracking CVEs attributed to Mythos and Project Glasswing, Anthropic’s initiative to give select partners access to the bug-hunting model, since shortly after the program was announced in April. Anthropic claims that Mythos is too powerful to release to the general public (insert evil laugh). As of Friday, Mythos and Project Glasswing have uncovered 286 CVEs, according to Garrity’s tracker, and up until Thursday only one of these bugs had been exploited in real-world attacks. The Thursday night activity originated from one IP address in China and targeted vulnerable servers in the US and Japan, Garrity told The Register. “Today we have seen four hits,” he told us on Friday. These originated from two different IP addresses in the US: 173.239.211[.]248 and 173.239.211[.]249. Both are in the same subnet, and “appear to be coming from a proxy,” Garrity added. China-linked digital intruders routinely use compromised devices as proxies to route malicious traffic and disguise the attackers’ true location, and in April a 10-country security advisory warned of China-nexus cyber operatives using proxy networks “strategically, and at scale.” In his write-up, Hanley said Horizon3 has used Mythos in its vulnerability research – and discovered “many critical vulnerabilities” – ever since the security company joined Project Glasswing in July. Mythos' mad math skillz CVE-2026-61500 highlights a couple of Mythos capabilities that make it really good at uncovering vulnerabilities, according to Hanley. Namely, Mythos excels at mathematical distillations and scientific tasks, especially those relating to computer science and operating systems. Finding this CVE “speaks to Mythos’s capabilities in understanding of mathematics, how it identified an exploitable set of cryptographic missteps, and approached solving the constraints to achieve remote code execution,” Hanley wrote. The security issue stems from how HFS authenticates users. It generates a random value with Math.random() and then passes this value to Koa, the Node.js web framework foundation for HFS. Koa uses keygrip to sign all session cookies with that random value. This means that if an “attacker can derive what the session signing key is, they can forge valid session cookies,” Hanley said. This should not be possible, assuming Math.random() uses a secure pseudo random number generator (PRNG). But V8’s Math.random() did not use a secure PRNG. Mythos discovered that the output of the xorshift128+ algorithm it used was fully reversible – and the application was leaking Math.random() outputs. The model’s analysis claimed that Z3, a Microsoft-developed, publicly available Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) solver, could be used to recover the PRNG seed. Hanley notes that Horizon3’s researchers could not recall seeing an SMT solver used this way to attack a cryptographic flaw in a real application and bypass authentication. “What makes this impressive is that Mythos didn’t just flag the insecure PRNG in isolation – it simultaneously identified that the application leaked raw Math.random() outputs through a separate code path, recognized those two facts as a chain, and determined the leak produced exactly the observations needed to make state recovery feasible,” he wrote.®

events.title: $28B hemp THC industry fights to save itself from looming federal ban
events.summary: Congress voted to close a loophole in federal law that allowed it to flourish. In a commercial kitchen outside Raleigh, North Carolina, Nicholas Hohns spreads a blue-green goo into a gridded mold, making one of his company’s signature products: potent THC gummies, featuring the primary intoxicating compound found in marijuana . It’s a business he might soon have to give up. America’s multibillion-dollar market for impairing hemp products — from THC seltzers sold at some Target stores to smokable cannabis flowers — faces potential elimination after Congress voted to close a loophole in federal law that has allowed it to flourish. Advocates for the industry, along with some lawmakers, are fighting to save it. The short-term government-funding bill signed by President Donald Trump last month delayed the effective date of the “hemp THC ban” from Nov. 12 to Dec. 11, giving Congress more time to consider regulating the products rather than banning them. “It’s such a weird spot to be in,” said Hohns. “You worked 100 hours a week for the past four years, and, yeah, you made some money. But now you might have nothing to show for it.” Marijuana and hemp are the same plant — cannabis. Marijuana is cultivated for high levels of THC in its flowers. Low-THC hemp has historically been grown for its sturdy fibers, food or wellness products. “Rope, not dope” was long the motto of farmers who supported legalizing hemp. To give farmers a new cash crop, Kentucky Republican Sen. Mitch McConnell successfully pushed the legalization of industrial hemp in the 2018 farm bill. But the way that law defined hemp — as having less than 0.3% of a specific type of THC, called delta-9, by weight — opened a huge loophole . Beverages or snacks could meet that threshold and still contain more than enough THC to get people high. Vape oil, gummy candies, chips, sodas and other unregulated, untested products laden with hemp-derived THC spread around the country , including in gas stations or convenience stores, where they were available even to teens. Some businesses started selling marijuana under the theory that raw marijuana’s THC is in a form called THC-A, which only turns into impairing delta-9 when heated or burned. The products evaded state prohibitions on recreational weed or undercut heavily taxed and regulated cannabis where it is legal. Dozens of states responded by regulating or banning impairing hemp products. McConnell finally closed the loophole late last year by inserting a hemp THC ban into a measure that ended the longest government shutdown in history. The ban, which limits the amount of THC in hemp products to 0.4 milligrams per container, wouldn’t take effect for a year. The ban “threatens to reduce retail revenues by $28.3 billion, displacing 225,000 jobs and reducing state sales tax potential by $2.1 billion,” according to a report last month from Whitney Economics, which studies the market. The industry hopes to save itself by restricting impairing products to people 21 and older, limiting how much THC can be in a package, and banning imported cannabis compounds. The owners of Kentucky’s Cornbread Hemp, Eric Zipperle and Jim Higdon, are prepared to cap their products at, say, 5 milligrams if that’s what it takes to win support from lawmakers. But the 0.4 milligram limit would destroy their business, they said. “If it goes through in December, this place is toast — it’s gone,” Zipperle said. Phone calls, records suggest some Cornell students tried to contain rape allegations Suspect in FlyDubai incident was previously identified as security risk: Officials District attorney reopens case of alleged Cornell University 'gang rape' They have 105 employees, sell hemp beverages in 18 states and expect to bring in $65 million this year. The 0.4-milligram cap is so low that it would ban even some non-impairing CBD products, such as topical lotions, said Jonathan Miller, general counsel of the industry group U.S. Hemp Roundtable. Hohns, who runs Deutermann Farms in Clayton, North Carolina, entered the hemp industry after losing his job as a personal trainer during the COVID-19 pandemic. North Carolina has not legalized either medical or recreational marijuana, but many of the edibles Hohns makes are more potent than what's available in states that have. “When I started seeing THC edibles being sold … I was like, I got 18 months to two years to make money in this industry,” Hohns said. “No way is the government just going to sit here and let us do this when this was supposed to be for fiber, plastics, building materials, rope.” That was more than four years ago. Hohns kept his capital investments minimal, fearing a shutdown. He has considered making other products, such as creatine gummies, if he has to get out of the hemp THC business. Things have been more stressful for others. Drinkin' Buds, a cannabis beverage company in Sheboygan, Wisconsin, has mothballed production.

events.title: Rogue AI agents expose internet's frail foundation
events.summary: AI agents don't need to invent new ways to hack the internet to overwhelm its defenses. They just need to speed-run the ones humans already use. Why it matters: Agents are proving they can automate basic hacking techniques at a speed and scale that is turning the internet's long-standing security gaps into easy targets. Driving the news: OpenAI said late Thursday it had notified more than 100 organizations that its agents may have accessed their systems during pre-deployment testing. Researchers at Transluce and Corridor also found a new batch of incidents last week where AI agents targeted government websites, including those of the U.S. and Canada . AI companies and researchers are actively investigating tens of thousands of cases where frontier models went outside the bounds of their pre-deployment tests, Axios recently reported . Reality check: Agents in these rogue safety-testing scenarios are just emulating the hacking techniques — using stolen login credentials and exposed API keys while also bypassing bot detection — that human hackers have successfully used for decades. In many of the newly reported cases, agents were accessing publicly available databases and websites. "The hacks we saw weren't particularly sophisticated," Jack Cable, co-founder of Corridor and one of the authors of Transluce's report, told Axios. "They were quite limited, quite rudimentary." Yes, but: Some of the latest incidents happened while agents were performing mundane tasks unrelated to cybersecurity, suggesting agents don't always need to be told to hack before they start looking for security flaws. In one case, an agent tasked with finding Canadian divorce records from the early 1900s encountered roadblocks and tested for cybersecurity vulnerabilities as another way to retrieve the information. "The fact that it was happening at all is quite concerning," Cable said. Between the lines: The flood of AI-generated activity will still create new headaches for defenders. "None of these attacks are new," Michael Morgenstern, partner at DayBlink Consulting, told Axios. "But now a single person with AI can run them at scale." Tasks that once required a hacker to manually probe websites, hunt for exposed credentials or work around access restrictions can now be delegated to software that keeps trying on its own. Cable added that companies deploying agents, as well as the AI companies evaluating them, will need robust monitoring to catch agents behaving in unexpected ways. The big picture: The old cybersecurity playbook is still relevant. Closing exposed services, rotating leaked credentials and API keys, patching known vulnerabilities and limiting access still make many of these attacks harder. AI models are largely exploiting classes of vulnerabilities that defenders have "known about for decades" and already know how to prevent, Cable said. The bottom line: How companies defend their networks doesn't change just because the technology carrying out the attacks is new. Go deeper : Cybersecurity 101 still applies in the AI world

events.title: The Supreme Court will hear a major climate change case involving a devastating Colorado wildfire
events.summary: Colorado's Boulder County is one of dozens of governments around the United States suing oil and gas companies to help pay for damage caused by disasters linked to climate change LOUISVILLE, Colo. -- Less than an hour after the first warning that a wildfire was headed for her suburban street, Tawnya Somauroo's Colorado home was in ashes. She has worked tirelessly for nearly five years to rebuild her house and help ensure her neighborhood can withstand the next blaze. But as climate change contributes to more frequent wildfires, she worries that the careful landscaping, metal fencing and flame-resistant siding are not enough. “We lost our homes and they left us to figure out for ourselves how to make our neighborhoods safe again,” Somauroo said. “At the end of the day, it comes out of our pockets, you know? And it does feel like maybe the oil and gas industry should have a part in this.” She lives in Boulder County, one of dozens of jurisdictions across the United States suing oil and gas companies to help pay for damage from disasters linked to climate change. The case is part of a wave of climate change litigation across the country and the world, with billions of dollars at stake. On Monday, the first day of the Supreme Court's new term, the justices will hear the Boulder case that could decide the fate of others like it. The city and county of Boulder first sued two oil companies in 2018, years before the fire. They argued that Suncor Energy and ExxonMobil had violated state law by deceiving the public about their contributions to climate change and sought unspecified damages to help cover the cost of worsening disasters. The companies say that a flood of lawsuits in state courts is not the way to deal with the global issue. “The problem is that climate change is caused by pretty much everybody living on earth,” said Phil Goldberg, special counsel for the Manufacturers' Accountability Project, an industry group. “We need to figure out how to address that. We need to address it in a very meaningful way. This litigation doesn’t do that.” The companies have the backing of the Trump administration. Federal government attorneys say the lawsuits are a backdoor way to regulate heat-trapping greenhouse gas emissions and amount to an unconstitutional power grab. “No one state can superimpose its own regulatory preferences on the rest — least of all to address a global problem that exists almost entirely outside its borders and affects the world at large,” they wrote. The Clean Air Act, they say, allows the federal government, rather than states, to regulate emissions. The Republican administration has largely used that power to roll back environmental regulations. Phone calls, records suggest some Cornell students tried to contain rape allegations Suspect in FlyDubai incident was previously identified as security risk: Officials District attorney reopens case of alleged Cornell University 'gang rape' Last month, the Environmental Protection Agency ceded some of its climate authority by repealing rules that limit planet-warming greenhouse gas emissions from power plants fueled by coal and natural gas. The move could complicate its argument. Boulder says it is not trying to regulate emissions beyond its borders, only holding companies accountable for local costs. “Boulder County and city aren’t trying to change what’s happening in Texas or New York, they’re trying to get compensation for things happening now in Colorado,” said Sam Sankar, senior vice president at Earthjustice, which filed an amicus brief in the case. Climate change was considered a factor in the 2021 Marshall Fire that destroyed Somauroo’s home, after the county's suit was originally filed. The total damage was estimated at $2 billion. It was the costliest wildfire in Colorado history. “Local county municipal governments play a very important role in helping front line communities adapt to climate change. This case could very well set a precedent,” said Chris Winter, executive director of the Getches-Wilkinson Center, an environmental research group in Colorado. The case will come before a conservative-majority Supreme Court where environmental regulations have not always fared well, including a 2022 decision that limited the EPA's authority to regulate carbon dioxide emissions from power plants. Only eight of the nine justices will be on the bench, though. Justice Samuel Alito recused himself just a week before arguments after facing calls to step aside because he owns stock in oil companies. That creates the possibility of a tie vote in the case, though it's unclear how likely that might be. The court is also weighing a question that experts say is a potential “off-ramp”: whether the justices have jurisdiction to hear the case at this stage. Whitehurst reported from Washington. events.title: Clever database, but can it run Doom?
events.summary: "Can it run Doom?" now applies to databases, as the author of DOOMQL has released a far more visually accurate port. There's a saying: "Be careful what you wish for." In 2025, we wrote a piece about a database boffin coming up with a version of Doom that was written in SQL. It was neat, but the visuals were nearer to 3D Monster Maze than to the 90s pixel blaster. We commented, "If persuading SQL to do the entire rendering pipeline is a 'bad idea,' we cannot wait for a terrible one." And so here we are. The author, Lukas Vogel, has been at it again and ported both Doom's game logic and renderer to SQL, running it in a database. Python handles timing, keyboard input, and bitmap display, but the rest comes from SQL queries and the CedarDB database. DOOMQL was an undeniably impressive thing. However, Vogel told The Register, "Someone on Hacker News complained last year when I did the first iteration that that one was more Wolfenstein-like because I used raycasting instead of BSP-tree traversal which was *the thing* that made Doom revolutionary. "So I obviously couldn't let that stand." Which brings us to SQLDoom. Doom, ported to SQL. In his blog, Vogel noted the ground rules for the port. Unlike DOOMQL, this had to look like real Doom. The rendering had to be purely SQL-based: "the only acceptable SQL output is a table or a bitmap encoding exact RGB values for every pixel," and the game loop also had to be purely SQL-based. Vogel told us, "I was very thrilled to find out that porting the real Doom was a) feasible and b) the performance was actually *better* than the much more barebones approach from last year! "Also, at some point I started actually playing it for fun in my free time, which is still a very strange feeling. I intended it as a tech demo, but it just feels like the real Doom, even though it doesn't share a single line of code with any existing Doom port. So I wanted to see how far I could take it. "In the end, I even got deathmatch to work." According to Vogel, the game is perfectly playable on his laptop (using a Ryzen 7 7840U), and multiplayer games can be played online using EU and US servers. We found the server performance a little sluggish – likely more due to the servers than the port – although getting SQL to jump through these hoops is something that, only a few short years ago, would be unimaginable. It's worth keeping in mind that this is a thinly veiled demonstration of the capabilities of CedarDB. It's a compiling database system where complex queries are eventually compiled to machine code. Still, it's hard not to get swept up in Vogel's enthusiasm and the fact that this is Doom… running in a database. Certainly this is a lot more fun than recreating yet another online store for yet another interminable keynote. ®

events.title: Trump promises $100 checks for 20 million seniors for Medicare
events.summary: President Trump late Friday night said the administration would send just under $100 to more than 20 million senior citizens to help pay for Medicare benefits. Why it matters: A month before the midterm, the president is adding another roughly $2 billion to a recent spate of promised refunds, rebates and dividends for various Americans. What he's saying: " I am pleased to announce that my Administration will, immediately, begin sending "Checks" of nearly $100 to over 20 MILLION wonderful Seniors to help pay for their Medicare Part B premiums, which we have already reduced by significant amounts," Trump said in a Truth Social post just before 11 p.m. ET Friday. Trump said the money would come from the Medicare Improvement Fund, which he criticized as a "Slush Fund." How it works: The White House, in a separate fact sheet , said eligible seniors would receive a direct deposit of $90 in early October, or paper checks if they don't have direct deposit. "Most" Medicare Part B enrollees are eligible, per the fact sheet. The Medicare Improvement Fund, established in 2008, has been a political hot potato for years. Yes, but: Per Medicare , the standard Part B premium is $202.90 a month, so the $90 credit will offset less than half of one month's bill. The big picture: Facing the worst economic polling of any president in the last decade, and with the midterm quickly approaching, Trump is actively trying to put money back in Americans' pockets. Zoom in: In early September he promised $5,000 for every adult citizen if Republicans win the midterm, a promise he reiterated Friday night but one that most voters don't believe . He's floated $500 Obamacare rebates for more than 1 million people who were purportedly overcharged for their benefits. He also recently suggested a less-specific dividend of some kind for those living near data centers . These ideas come on top of rebates he proposed in 2025 that were not ultimately paid, including tariff rebates and DOGE dividends. What to watch: Payments should start flowing in the coming days.

events.title: Watch: We Uncovered Bribery Allegations Involving Susan Collins
events.summary: In late 2024, FBI investigators had enough evidence to launch a sweeping bribery probe that could ensnare top lawmakers , including Sen. Susan Collins. The agency was examining interactions between Collins and a top donor: Martin Kao, CEO of defense contractor Navatek. According to Kao, in 2019, the head of the pro-Collins super PAC met with him and other Navatek execs and asked for a $500,000 donation. Government contractors are banned from making political contributions. For the company to offer donations to Collins in exchange for an official action, or for Collins to accept, would constitute criminal bribery. To skirt campaign finance laws and conceal the source of the funds, Kao sent an initial $150,000 to the super PAC using a shell company, saying he had cleared it with his lawyer. The head of the super PAC knew Kao was behind the donation. “Very smart,” he replied in an email viewed by ProPublica. Weeks later, Kao told his team Collins committed to getting the company $32 million in naval contracts. But the FBI saw through Kao’s shell company ruse. In 2022, a grand jury indicted him for making illegal campaign contributions. Facing years in prison, Kao revealed the full scheme to the FBI, hoping to reduce his sentence. What he told them has never before become public. Read More The FBI Anti-Corruption Squad Was Circling Susan Collins — Until Trump Got in the Way Kao and his close associates donated nearly $900,000 to dozens of politicians, allowing Navatek to establish operations in half a dozen states with more than $40 million a year in government funds. Collins, Kao said, was Navatek’s most important patron. Then President Donald Trump returned to office — and the FBI and Department of Justice teams that handled public corruption cases were eviscerated. The investigation died, and the government stopped talking to an informant who had offered a road map to corruption in Congress. ProPublica revealed the existence of the case for the first time. Collins’ deputy chief of staff said that her office “vigorously” denies allegations of bribery and pay-for-play made by Kao and that her office “fully cooperated” with the FBI. After our story was published, the senator mustered a defense that was full of incorrect and misleading claims , calling ProPublica’s reporting a “ smear job ” that took “the words of a twice-convicted felon over my office, campaign staff and me.”  ProPublica reviewed a trove of evidence gathered by the FBI and thousands of pages of legal records, and interviewed dozens of people familiar with Navatek, its Washington operations and the FBI inquiry to conduct our own investigation.  The White House referred us to the FBI. A spokesperson said the FBI “ultimately found nothing implicating Senator Collins” or her campaign. The FBI spokesperson did not address questions about the new phase of the investigation prompted by Kao’s account. Navatek founder Steven Loui said Kao’s methods were “unethical and illegal” and that the company fully complied with law enforcement. Watch our video to learn more on how we independently corroborated much of Kao’s account. The post Watch: We Uncovered Bribery Allegations Involving Susan Collins appeared first on ProPublica .
